name: Accounting Fundamentals
description: Debits, credits, and how the books actually get built.
intro: Accounting is the record-keeping system behind every financial statement, and understanding it, even at a basic level, makes everything else in finance click into place faster. This deck starts from the actual mechanics: what double-entry bookkeeping means, how debits and credits work, and how the books get built up from a single transaction. It is written for someone who has never taken an accounting class, not as a shortcut around learning it, but as a clear first pass.

cards.q: Someone tells you to go through a company’s books before the meeting. What are the books, literally?
cards.takeaway: The books are a set of accounts, each one a running tally of a single thing a company owns or owes.
cards.a: When people say a company’s books they mean its accounting records, and the basic unit of those records is an account: a running tally of one specific thing, such as cash in the bank, inventory sitting in a warehouse, or money owed to a supplier. A midsize business might keep hundreds of them. The complete collection is called the general ledger, and every financial statement you will ever look at is built by totalling those accounts and arranging the results. So asking for the books means asking for the underlying tallies rather than the polished summary.

cards.q: Your staffer sketches Assets = Liabilities + Equity on a napkin and says all of accounting comes back to that one line. What does the equation actually say, and why can it never go out of balance?
cards.takeaway: Everything a company owns was funded either by money it borrowed or by money its owners put in.
cards.a: Assets are everything the company owns that has value, like cash, buildings and inventory. Liabilities are what it owes to outsiders, mostly loans and unpaid bills. Equity is what would be left over for the owners if every asset were sold and every debt repaid. If Calder Foods raises $100,000 from its owners and borrows $400,000, it holds $500,000 of assets funded by $400,000 of liabilities and $100,000 of equity. The equation holds by construction: the left side lists what the company has, the right side lists where every dollar of it came from.

cards.q: A founder tells you her company did $40 million last year. Your MD wants to know whether that’s revenue or profit before anyone starts a model. What’s the difference?
cards.takeaway: Revenue is what customers paid you, profit is what is left after every cost of earning it.
cards.a: Revenue, also called sales or the top line, is the total amount customers were charged for goods and services during the period. Profit is what survives after subtracting costs: first the direct cost of the things sold, then salaries, rent, marketing, interest on any debt, and tax. A company with $40 million of revenue and $39 million of costs earned $1 million, while a smaller company with $12 million of revenue and $6 million of costs earned far more. Interviewers press on this because anyone who treats the two words as interchangeable will misread every income statement they touch.

cards.q: What do “debit” and “credit” actually mean in accounting?
cards.takeaway: Debit means left, credit means right — which one grows an account depends on the account type.
cards.a: Debit and credit aren't inherently "increase" or "decrease" — they just mean the left and right side of an account. What each one does depends on the account type: debits increase assets and expenses (and decrease liabilities, equity, and revenue), while credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue (and decrease assets and expenses). Memorize which accounts move which way, and the rest of double-entry bookkeeping follows from that.

cards.q: What is double-entry bookkeeping?
cards.takeaway: Every transaction hits two accounts of equal value, so the books always stay in balance.
cards.a: Every transaction gets recorded twice, once as a debit and once as a credit, always for the same amount. That's what keeps the accounting equation, Assets = Liabilities + Equity, in balance no matter how many transactions pile up. It also builds in a natural error check: if total debits and credits ever stop matching, you know something was recorded wrong somewhere — the same logic that has to hold in every model you'll ever build off a company's books.

cards.q: What is a T-account?
cards.takeaway: A T-account is a quick sketch of one account: debits on the left, credits on the right.
cards.a: A T-account is a simple visual for tracking one account's activity — shaped like a T, with the account name on top, debits on the left side, and credits on the right. It isn't a formal accounting record; it's a scratch tool for seeing how a transaction will flow through an account before it's entered into the ledger — the same quick sketch you'll reach for when tracing an entry through a set of financials.

cards.q: What is the difference between a journal entry and the general ledger?
cards.takeaway: Journal entries record transactions in order; the ledger re-sorts them by account.
cards.a: A journal entry is the raw, chronological record of a transaction: it shows exactly which accounts were debited and credited as the transaction happened. The general ledger then reorganizes those entries by account, pulling every transaction that touched "Cash" or "Revenue," for example, into one place so you can track that account's running balance. Think of the journal as the diary and the ledger as the filing system built from it — the distinction that matters when you're handed a target's books and need to trace a number back to the transaction that created it.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics pays $30,000 in cash for a forklift. Write the journal entry on the whiteboard for me: what are the two lines, and how do you know which side each account goes on?
cards.takeaway: Debit what the company gains, credit what it gives up, and the two amounts have to match.
cards.a: Two lines. Debit Equipment for $30,000, because equipment is an asset and debits increase assets, then credit Cash for $30,000, because cash is also an asset and credits decrease it. The company is no richer or poorer than it was that morning, one asset simply turned into another, which is why the accounting equation still balances. Had Northbay bought the forklift on credit instead, the second line would be a $30,000 credit to accounts payable, the liability that tracks bills owed to suppliers, and both assets and liabilities would rise together.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail ships $2 million of goods in December and collects the cash in February. Which year does that sale belong to, and why is accrual accounting the standard rather than simply tracking cash?
cards.takeaway: Accrual books revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, not when cash moves.
cards.a: December, because accrual accounting records revenue once the company has actually done the work and delivered the goods, and records the costs of earning that revenue in the same period, a rule known as the matching principle. Cash accounting instead records everything only when money changes hands, which is simpler but lets one slow-paying customer swing a whole year of reported profit. Accrual gives a truer picture of how a period really went, which is why it is required for any company of size, and it is also what creates the gaps between profit and cash that the cash flow statement exists to explain.

cards.q: What are accounts receivable and accounts payable, and why does almost every real business have both sitting on its balance sheet?
cards.takeaway: Receivables are sales you have not been paid for, payables are bills you have not paid yet.
cards.a: Accounts receivable is money customers owe for goods or services already delivered, so it sits on the balance sheet as an asset, a claim on cash that has not arrived yet. Accounts payable is the mirror image, bills from suppliers that have been received but not yet settled, recorded as a liability. Both exist because accrual accounting books the sale or the cost when the work happens while the cash follows weeks later. Comparing how fast those two balances turn over is one of the quickest ways to see whether a business collects from its customers sooner than it pays its own suppliers.

cards.q: A software company you’re diligencing collects a full year of subscription fees every January. Why can’t it record all of that as revenue in January, and what appears on the balance sheet instead?
cards.takeaway: Cash collected before the work is done is a liability, not revenue, until you actually deliver.
cards.a: Because it has the cash but has not earned it yet. If a customer pays $12,000 in January for twelve months of service, the company recognizes $1,000 of revenue in January and parks the other $11,000 as deferred revenue, a liability representing service it still owes, releasing $1,000 into revenue each month as it delivers. Deferred revenue is the rare liability you like to see growing, since it means customers are paying ahead of the work. It is also why a subscription business can be sitting on a pile of cash long before that cash has become profit.

cards.q: You're on the deal team for Kessler Industrial's sale process, and the seller's controller hands your group Q3 financials that haven't been closed out yet. Before the numbers go into the model, your VP wants to know: what is an adjusting entry, and why is it needed at the end of a period?
cards.takeaway: Adjusting entries true up the books so revenue and expenses land in the right period.
cards.a: An adjusting entry updates account balances at the end of a period to capture revenue that's been earned, or an expense that's been incurred, but hasn't been recorded yet — think accrued interest, or a prepaid expense that's now been used up. They're needed because plenty of transactions span multiple periods, and without them, revenue and expenses would land in the wrong period and distort the financial statements. In a deal context that's not academic: financials handed over mid-period, like the ones Kessler's controller just sent, need these entries booked before you can trust them enough to build a model on top of.

cards.q: You're building the base-case LBO model for the Thornfield Manufacturing deal, and your associate wants a simple capex and depreciation schedule rather than something modeled asset-by-asset. What is depreciation, and why is straight-line depreciation the simplest method?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life instead of expensing it all at once.
cards.a: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset, like equipment or a building, across its useful life instead of expensing the full purchase price the year it's bought, matching the expense to the years the asset actually helps generate revenue. Straight-line depreciation is the simplest version: it expenses an equal amount every year, which makes it easy to calculate and forecast, even though many assets really lose value faster in their early years than a straight line implies. That simplicity is exactly why it's the default assumption in a base-case model unless there's a specific reason to build something more granular.

cards.q: Your model has one line for depreciation and another for amortization. What’s the difference between them, and does either one actually move cash out the door?
cards.takeaway: Same idea, different assets: depreciation covers physical ones, amortization covers intangible ones.
cards.a: Mechanically they are the same move, taking the cost of something the company bought and spreading it across the years it stays useful rather than expensing it all at once. Depreciation applies to tangible assets you can physically touch, such as machinery, vehicles and buildings. Amortization applies to intangible assets, things with no physical form like a patent, a software license or a customer list picked up in an acquisition. Neither one moves cash: the money left when the asset was bought, so both are non-cash expenses that reduce reported profit in years when nothing is actually paid, which is why both get added back on the cash flow statement.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a contra account and a regular account?
cards.takeaway: A contra account runs opposite its partner account, shrinking it instead of growing it.
cards.a: A regular account moves in its natural direction — assets and expenses grow with debits, for example. A contra account is paired with a related account but moves in the opposite direction, reducing that account's reported balance instead of adding to it. Accumulated depreciation is the classic example: paired with a fixed asset account, it carries a credit balance and lowers the asset's book value on the balance sheet — the exact line you'll be linking to a depreciation schedule when you build out a model's balance sheet.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics is profitable every quarter but keeps running short of cash, and your VP tells you to look at working capital first. What is working capital, and what would it tell you here?
cards.takeaway: Working capital is short-term assets minus short-term bills, the cash locked up running the business.
cards.a: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, where current means expected to turn into cash, or fall due, within a year. On the asset side that is mostly cash, receivables and inventory, the goods a company is holding to sell. On the liability side it is mostly payables and other bills coming due shortly. A profitable company can still be starved of cash if too much of its money is sitting in unsold inventory and uncollected receivables. Keep one distinction straight, because interviewers test it: that is the accounting definition. When a banker models working capital they normally mean operating, or net, working capital, which deliberately excludes cash and any short-term debt, since those are financing items rather than part of running the business. Measured that way, the figure isolates the cash that growth actually eats.

cards.q: Calder Foods buys a rival for $500 million when the rival’s identifiable net assets are worth $320 million at fair value. Where do the extra $180 million go on the balance sheet?
cards.takeaway: Goodwill is the premium a buyer pays above the fair value of what the target actually owns.
cards.a: They become goodwill, an intangible asset that only exists because one company bought another. The buyer first restates the target’s identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, meaning what they would fetch today rather than whatever the old books said, and anything the purchase price exceeds that net figure becomes goodwill, $180 million in this case. Be careful about what actually sits inside that residual. Identifiable intangibles belong in the $320 million, not in the goodwill: under IFRS 3, and equally under US GAAP’s ASC 805, things like brand names and customer relationships are recognised separately whenever they are separable or arise from contractual or legal rights. What is left in goodwill is the genuinely unmeasurable part, an assembled workforce and expected synergies, neither of which can be recognised on its own. Goodwill is not amortized on a schedule, it is tested at least annually for impairment and written down if the deal proves worth less than what was paid.

cards.q: Your team is comparing Ferrow Retail against a public comp for a pitch book, and Ferrow uses LIFO while the comp uses FIFO. Before the margins can be compared apples-to-apples, your VP wants a quick explanation: what’s the difference between FIFO and LIFO inventory valuation?
cards.takeaway: FIFO sells your oldest inventory first; LIFO sells the newest — and rising prices make the choice matter.
cards.a: FIFO (first in, first out) assumes the oldest units in inventory get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects older, typically cheaper, costs. LIFO (last in, first out) assumes the newest units get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects more recent, typically higher, costs. When prices are rising, that difference shows up on the financials: FIFO tends to report higher profit and a higher inventory value, while LIFO reports lower profit but a smaller tax bill. That’s exactly why you can’t line up Ferrow’s margins against a FIFO comp without adjusting for the accounting difference first. One point that matters the moment you look outside the US: LIFO is a US GAAP concept and is not permitted under IFRS at all. IAS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average cost for inventories that are ordinarily interchangeable, so if a comp is on LIFO, it is a US filer.

cards.q: During diligence on the Halstead Foods acquisition, you notice the target capitalized a cost that arguably should have been expensed, flattering reported EBITDA. Before flagging it to your MD, make sure you can explain: what is the difference between capitalizing a cost and expensing it?
cards.takeaway: Capitalize a cost if its value lasts years; expense it if the benefit ends this period.
cards.a: Capitalizing a cost means recording it as an asset on the balance sheet and spreading it over time through depreciation or amortization, because it creates value beyond the current period — buying equipment, for instance. Expensing a cost means recording the full amount immediately on the income statement, because the benefit is used up in the current period, like office supplies. The choice affects both the balance sheet and how quickly a cost hits reported profit — and it's a classic spot for quality-of-earnings adjustments in diligence, since capitalizing a cost that should have been expensed makes near-term EBITDA look better than it really is.

cards.q: Two competitors run nearly identical operations and report clearly different net income, and neither has done anything wrong. Your MD asks how that’s possible. What do you tell her?
cards.takeaway: Accounting rules leave real choices, so two honest companies can report different profits.
cards.a: Because the rules leave room for judgement. One might use FIFO while the other uses LIFO, so identical rising input costs land in cost of goods sold differently. One might depreciate the same machine over ten years and the other over seven, changing the annual expense on identical equipment. One might capitalize a software build the other expenses outright. None of that is fraud, it is policy choice, which is why analysts spend so long normalizing financials before comparing two companies, and why this question is really testing whether you understand that reported profit is an opinion built on assumptions while cash is much closer to a fact.

name: Reading Financial Statements
description: How the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement fit together.
intro: Every finance and consulting interview eventually touches the three financial statements, the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, because they are how a business actually gets described in numbers. This deck is built for someone who has never opened a company’s annual report: it walks through what each statement shows, why they exist as three separate documents instead of one, and how a single transaction ripples across all three. By the end, you should be able to hear "walk me through the financial statements" and actually enjoy answering it.

cards.q: You can look at only one of the three statements, and you need to know whether Ferrow Retail can pay its bills next month. Which do you pick, and what is each of the three actually for?
cards.takeaway: Balance sheet shows what you have now, income statement how you did, cash flow why cash moved.
cards.a: You’d take the balance sheet, because it’s the only one that shows what the company holds and owes right now: cash in the bank, bills due shortly, debt coming up for repayment. The income statement is built to answer a different question, how profitable the company was over a stretch of time, and a profitable company can still run out of money. The cash flow statement explains where cash came from and went during that period, which tells you whether the business generates cash rather than whether it has any today.

cards.q: What’s the key difference between the balance sheet and the income statement in terms of time?
cards.takeaway: The income statement covers a stretch of time; the balance sheet freezes one exact moment.
cards.a: The income statement covers a period, a quarter or a year, showing what happened over that stretch. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one exact moment, showing what the company owns and owes as of that date. Think of it like the difference between a video and a photo: one captures a stretch of activity, the other captures a single instant.

cards.q: What is the accounting equation?
cards.takeaway: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity, everything owned was funded by debt or by owners.
cards.a: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Everything a company owns, its assets, was funded either by borrowing (liabilities) or by owners' investment and retained profit (equity). The balance sheet has to balance to this equation at all times, which is exactly where its name comes from.

cards.q: What does accrual accounting mean, and how is it different from cash accounting?
cards.takeaway: Accrual accounting counts revenue when it's earned, not when the cash actually shows up.
cards.a: Accrual accounting records revenue when it's earned and expenses when they're incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands, so a sale made on credit counts as revenue immediately. Cash accounting only records a transaction once cash physically moves. Nearly every company you'll model uses accrual accounting, because it matches revenue to the period it was actually generated in, giving a truer picture of performance than the cash sitting in the bank that day.

cards.q: Your staffer drops Ferrow Retail’s income statement on your desk and asks you to read it from the top line to the bottom line. What is each step telling you?
cards.takeaway: Each step down the income statement subtracts another layer of cost, ending at net income.
cards.a: Revenue at the top is everything the company sold before any costs. Subtract cost of goods sold, the direct cost of making or buying the things that were sold, and you get gross profit. Subtract operating expenses, the cost of running the business itself like salaries, rent, and marketing, and you get operating income, which is profit from operations before financing and tax. Subtract interest on debt and taxes and you reach net income, the bottom line that belongs to the owners.

cards.q: What’s the difference between cost of goods sold and operating expenses, and why does it matter which one a cost gets booked to?
cards.takeaway: COGS is the cost of the thing you sold, operating expenses are the cost of running the company.
cards.a: Cost of goods sold is the cost tied directly to what was sold in the period: raw materials, factory labor, the wholesale price of inventory. Operating expenses are the costs of running the business regardless of any single sale, like head office salaries, rent, marketing, and research. Moving a cost between the two doesn’t change net income at all, but it does change gross profit, so a company that classifies aggressively can make its product look more profitable than a peer. Classification varies enough by company that you check the footnotes before trusting a comparison.

cards.q: A client asks why your page shows three different margins for Calder Foods rather than just one. What does each margin tell her that the others don’t?
cards.takeaway: Gross, operating, and net margin show what’s left after each successive layer of cost.
cards.a: A margin is just a profit line divided by revenue. Gross margin, gross profit over revenue, shows pricing power and how cheaply the company can make what it sells. Operating margin, operating income over revenue, adds the cost of actually running the business, so it captures how efficient the whole operation is. Net margin, net income over revenue, comes after interest and tax, so it reflects how much debt the company carries and where it pays tax. That’s why operating margin usually gives the cleaner read across peers.

cards.q: What does it mean when a balance sheet line is labeled current rather than non-current?
cards.takeaway: Current means settled within twelve months, non-current means everything longer.
cards.a: Current means the item is expected to turn into cash or be paid off within twelve months: cash, receivables owed by customers, inventory on the shelf, payables owed to suppliers, and the slice of debt due this year. Non-current covers everything with a longer horizon, like factories and equipment, goodwill, and long-term borrowings. The split exists so a reader can see at a glance whether what’s coming due soon is covered by what’s turning into cash soon, which is the first thing anyone checks before worrying about the long-dated items.

cards.q: The Windmere Foods deal has a working capital adjustment built into the purchase agreement, and your associate asks you to explain what working capital actually measures before you build the mechanism into the model. What do you tell them?
cards.takeaway: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, a quick read on short-term liquidity.
cards.a: Working capital measures how easily a company can cover its near-term obligations: current assets minus current liabilities. A positive number means the company has enough short-term assets, cash, receivables, inventory, to meet what it owes in the near future. Read the number against the business model rather than judging it by its sign. Supermarkets, restaurants and subscription businesses collect from customers before they pay suppliers, so they run negative working capital as a matter of course and it is a strength, not a warning. What diligence actually flags is an unexplained deterioration from how that particular business normally runs, or receivables and inventory swelling faster than sales. It is why working capital pegs and adjustments show up in almost every purchase agreement.

cards.q: You're staffed on the Kestrel Components sale process, and the VP asks you to walk the client's newly hired CFO through how the three financial statements tie together before the first management presentation. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: Net income is the thread that stitches the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement together.
cards.a: You'd start with the income statement, which shows profitability over a period: revenue minus expenses equals net income. Then the balance sheet, a snapshot of what the company owns and owes at one specific moment, assets, liabilities, and equity. Then the cash flow statement, which tracks how cash actually moved during that same period. Net income is what ties them together: it flows into the cash flow statement's starting line and into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

cards.q: What are the three sections of the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Operating, investing, and financing activities add up to explain exactly why cash changed.
cards.a: Operating activities capture cash generated or used by the core business. Investing activities cover cash spent on or received from things like equipment or acquisitions. Financing activities capture cash from debt, equity raises, dividends, or buybacks. Add all three together in the model and you get the full explanation for why the cash balance changed over the period.

cards.q: How does depreciation affect the income statement differently than the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation cuts net income as an expense, then gets added straight back on the cash flow statement.
cards.a: Depreciation reduces net income on the income statement because it's recorded as an expense, even though no cash actually leaves the business that period. On the cash flow statement, it gets added back in the operating section, since that statement's whole job is to reflect real cash movement, not accounting expense, which is exactly the line the deal team double-checks first when a cash flow build doesn't tie out.

cards.q: During diligence on the Talbrook Industries acquisition, the target's net income looks strong but its cash balance keeps falling. Your associate asks you to explain why the two numbers can diverge in the same period.
cards.takeaway: Net income books revenue the moment it's earned; cash flow only counts money that's actually landed.
cards.a: Net income includes non-cash items like depreciation, and under accrual accounting it counts revenue as soon as it's earned, not when the cash actually arrives. Cash flow only counts money that has physically moved. That's exactly how a target can show a healthy profit on paper while its cash balance falls, if customers haven't paid yet or cash is tied up sitting in inventory, which is precisely the kind of gap diligence is meant to catch.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics earns 40 million and pays a 10 million dividend in the same year. Your associate asks what that does to equity on the balance sheet. What do you tell her?
cards.takeaway: Net income minus dividends is what actually gets added to retained earnings each period.
cards.a: Equity rises by 30 million. Net income lands in retained earnings, the running total of every dollar of profit the company has kept since it was founded, and dividends are then subtracted from it. So opening retained earnings plus net income less dividends equals closing retained earnings. Note that a dividend never appears on the income statement, since it isn’t a cost of doing business but a distribution of profit already earned, and it shows up instead as an outflow in the financing section of the cash flow statement.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail grew revenue 30% but its operating cash flow fell. The associate says look at working capital. How does a change in working capital actually show up in cash flow?
cards.takeaway: Cash tied up in receivables and inventory is subtracted, cash owed to suppliers is added back.
cards.a: The rule is simple once you see it: an increase in a current asset uses cash, and an increase in a current liability provides it. If receivables rise, customers have taken the goods but not paid, so that increase gets subtracted in the operating section. If inventory rises, cash went out to buy stock still sitting in a warehouse. If payables rise, the company is holding cash it hasn’t paid suppliers yet, so that gets added. Fast growth eats cash precisely because the buying and the lending come before the collecting.

cards.q: The Overton Digital pitch materials quote an EV/EBITDA multiple, and the analyst next to you asks what EBITDA actually captures before it goes into the comp set. What do you tell them?
cards.takeaway: EBITDA adds interest, taxes, and D&A back to net income to isolate pure operating performance.
cards.a: EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, essentially operating profit before the effects of financing decisions and non-cash accounting charges. It shows up everywhere in comps and LBO models because it lets you compare operating performance across companies with different capital structures or tax situations, stripping those differences away to leave the core business result.

cards.q: Your MD says the whole pitch rests on how much cash Calder Foods actually keeps, not what it books as profit. What is free cash flow, and how do you build it from the statements?
cards.takeaway: Free cash flow is what’s left after paying for the spending needed to keep the business running.
cards.a: Free cash flow is the cash a business has left once it has paid for the capital spending it needs, meaning the money laid out on equipment, property, and software. The quickest version straight off the statements is cash from operating activities minus capital expenditures, both of which are printed lines. In models people often build unlevered free cash flow instead: operating income after tax, plus depreciation and amortization, less capital spending, less the increase in working capital. Definitions genuinely vary between firms, so say which one you’re using.

cards.q: Talbrook Industries’ operating income jumped 40%, but the footnotes mention a legal settlement and the sale of a factory. Why does that change how you read the number?
cards.takeaway: Strip out one-time items before you compare a year to last year or a company to its peers.
cards.a: One-time or non-recurring items, things like a lawsuit payout, a restructuring charge, or a gain on selling a plant, sit inside the reported figures but say nothing about how the business will perform next year. Analysts pull them out to get a normalized number that can be compared across years and against peers, and the footnotes are where the detail to do that lives. Be skeptical while you do it: management has every incentive to label a recurring cost as one-time, which is why adjusted EBITDA add-backs get argued over line by line in diligence.

cards.q: An investor at the table says he doesn’t care about EBITDA. What’s the honest case against it, and when is it a poor stand-in for cash flow?
cards.takeaway: EBITDA ignores the capital spending, interest, and taxes a company genuinely has to pay.
cards.a: Adding depreciation back treats worn-out equipment as if it were free, so a business that has to spend heavily on machinery just to stand still can show strong EBITDA while keeping almost no cash. It also ignores interest, which is a real payment for a company carrying debt, ignores tax, and ignores cash swallowed by working capital. On top of that it isn’t a defined accounting measure, so companies set their own adjusted definitions. It remains a useful screen for comparing operations, but free cash flow is the number that tells you what’s left.

cards.q: Your interviewer leans back and says depreciation goes up by 10, the tax rate is 25%, walk me through all three statements. Where do you start?
cards.takeaway: Net income falls by the after-tax amount, cash rises by the tax saved, and the balance sheet still ties.
cards.a: Income statement first: operating income falls by 10, so pre-tax income falls by 10, taxes drop by 2.50, and net income falls by 7.50. Cash flow statement next: start at net income down 7.50, add back the full 10 of depreciation because no cash left the business, so cash from operations and the cash balance both rise by 2.50. Balance sheet last: cash is up 2.50 while plant and equipment is down 10, so assets fall 7.50, and retained earnings falls 7.50 too, so it balances. That 2.50 is the tax shield.

name: Ratio Analysis
description: Liquidity, leverage, profitability, efficiency: the numbers you pull first and what they mean.
intro: When an interviewer asks how you would assess a company, they want ratios, and they want you to say what each one tells you rather than just name it. This deck covers the handful that come up: the liquidity ratios that say whether a company can pay its bills, the leverage ratios that say how much debt it carries, the profitability ratios that say how good the business is, and the efficiency ratios that say how hard its assets work. Every one is explained from the statement it comes from, so you can rebuild it under pressure instead of remembering a formula.

cards.q: What is a financial ratio, and why do analysts use ratios instead of the raw numbers?
cards.takeaway: A ratio turns two numbers into one that can be compared across companies, years and sizes.
cards.a: A ratio divides one figure from the financial statements by another so the result means something on its own. Calder Foods making £40m of profit tells you little; £40m on £400m of sales, a 10% margin, tells you how good the business is, and lets you compare it with a rival ten times its size. Ratios strip out scale, so you can line a company up against its peers, against its own history, and against what a lender or investor expects. The skill is not calculating them, it is knowing which one answers the question being asked.

cards.q: What is the current ratio, and what does it tell you?
cards.takeaway: Current assets over current liabilities: whether the company can cover what it owes in the next year.
cards.a: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, both from the balance sheet. Current assets are cash and things that turn into cash within a year, like receivables and inventory; current liabilities are what falls due in the same window. A ratio above one means the company could, in principle, pay everything due this year from what it has. Below one is a warning, though some businesses run there comfortably, like supermarkets that get paid in cash before they pay suppliers. A very high ratio can also mean cash or stock sitting idle.

cards.q: What is the quick ratio, and why would you use it instead of the current ratio?
cards.takeaway: The quick ratio drops inventory, because stock is the current asset that may not turn into cash when you need it.
cards.a: The quick ratio, sometimes called the acid test, is current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities. It asks the same question as the current ratio but is stricter: if the company had to pay everything due this year without selling any stock, could it? Inventory is the current asset most likely to be worth less than the balance sheet says, or to sell slowly, which is why it is excluded. For Ferrow Retail, with warehouses full of seasonal clothing, the two ratios can differ a lot; for a software company with no stock they are the same.

cards.q: What is the debt-to-equity ratio, and what does a high number mean?
cards.takeaway: Total debt over shareholders' equity: how much of the company is funded by lenders rather than owners.
cards.a: Debt to equity is total borrowings divided by shareholders' equity, both from the balance sheet. It shows how the company is financed. A ratio of 2 means lenders have put in twice what the owners have. Higher leverage magnifies returns to shareholders when things go well and losses when they do not, because interest has to be paid regardless. What counts as high depends on the industry: Redhill Utilities, with steady regulated cash flows, can carry far more than a fashion retailer whose sales swing with the season. Compare with peers, not against a universal number.

cards.q: What is net debt to EBITDA, and why do lenders prefer it to debt to equity?
cards.takeaway: Net debt over EBITDA says how many years of operating cash it would take to repay the debt.
cards.a: Net debt is total borrowings minus cash. Dividing it by EBITDA, a rough measure of the cash the operations generate before interest, tax and non-cash charges, tells you how many years of that cash would clear the debt. A company at 2x could pay off its debt in about two years of earnings; at 6x it is heavily levered. Lenders like it because it compares debt with the thing that actually services debt, cash flow, rather than with equity, which is an accounting number that can be distorted by write-downs and buybacks. Loan agreements often set a maximum on it.

cards.q: What is interest cover, and what level starts to worry a lender?
cards.takeaway: EBIT over interest expense: how many times the company's operating profit covers its interest bill.
cards.a: Interest cover is operating profit, EBIT, divided by the interest expense for the year. It answers a simple question: if profits fell, how far could they fall before the company could not pay its interest? Cover of 8x is comfortable; below 2x means a modest bad year could tip the company into default, and lenders will price the loan accordingly or refuse it. Bramwell & Co. reporting EBIT of £60m against £30m of interest has cover of 2x, and its bankers would be watching. Cover is the ratio that connects the income statement to the credit story.

cards.q: What are gross margin, operating margin and net margin, and why look at all three?
cards.takeaway: Each margin strips out one more layer of cost, so the gaps between them show where the money goes.
cards.a: Gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold, divided by revenue: what is left after making the product. Operating margin also takes off overheads like rent, salaries and marketing: what is left from running the business. Net margin takes off interest and tax too: what is left for shareholders. Looking at all three shows where a company is strong or weak. Calder Foods with a 45% gross margin but a 4% operating margin has a good product and a bloated cost base. A rival with 30% and 8% is worse at making things and better at running the company.

cards.q: What is return on equity, and why can a high ROE be a warning sign as well as a good one?
cards.takeaway: Net income over shareholders' equity: the return owners earn on their money, which leverage can flatter.
cards.a: Return on equity is net income divided by shareholders' equity. It tells owners what they earn on what they have put in and left in the business. A steady 15% is good; 30% is exceptional. The catch is that borrowing raises it: if a company funds itself mostly with debt, the equity base is small, so even ordinary profits look like a big return on it. That is why a high ROE alongside a high debt-to-equity ratio is a lender's story, not a great-business story. Return on capital employed, which uses debt plus equity in the denominator, strips that effect out.

cards.q: What is return on capital employed, and why do many analysts prefer it to ROE?
cards.takeaway: EBIT over debt plus equity: how well the business uses all the money in it, whoever provided it.
cards.a: Return on capital employed is operating profit divided by the total capital in the business, debt plus equity, or equivalently total assets minus current liabilities. Because it uses profit before interest and capital from all sources, it is not flattered by how the company is financed. Two companies with the same operations will show the same ROCE whether one borrowed heavily and the other did not, whereas their ROEs would differ. A ROCE well above the company's cost of capital means every pound invested in the business is creating value; below it, growth destroys value.

cards.q: What is asset turnover, and how does it explain why a supermarket and a luxury brand can earn the same return?
cards.takeaway: Revenue over total assets: how many pounds of sales each pound of assets produces.
cards.a: Asset turnover is revenue divided by total assets. It measures how hard the assets work. A supermarket has a low margin but turns its assets many times a year, because stock flies off the shelves; a luxury watchmaker turns its assets slowly but earns a huge margin on each sale. Multiply margin by turnover and you get return on assets, so two very different businesses can arrive at the same return by different routes. That decomposition, called DuPont analysis, is a favourite interview question because it shows whether you understand what drives returns rather than just naming them.

cards.q: What are receivable days, inventory days and payable days, and what does the working capital cycle tell you?
cards.takeaway: How long the company waits to be paid, holds stock, and takes to pay suppliers, and therefore how much cash is tied up.
cards.a: Receivable days is receivables divided by revenue, times 365: how long customers take to pay. Inventory days is inventory over cost of sales, times 365: how long stock sits before it sells. Payable days is payables over cost of sales, times 365: how long the company takes to pay suppliers. Add the first two and subtract the third and you get the cash conversion cycle, the number of days the company's own cash is tied up. Northbay Logistics with 60 receivable days and 30 payable days is lending its customers a month of cash. Shortening the cycle frees cash without any change in profit.

cards.q: What is earnings per share, and why does a company's EPS matter more to the share price than its total profit?
cards.takeaway: Net income divided by shares outstanding: the profit that belongs to each share, which is what a shareholder actually owns.
cards.a: Earnings per share is net income divided by the number of shares. A shareholder does not own the company's profit, she owns a share of it, so the number that matters to her is profit per share. It is why a company can grow profit and still see its share price fall: if it issued lots of new shares to do it, each share's slice shrank. It is also why buybacks lift the share price, since fewer shares means more profit per share. Diluted EPS also counts shares that could exist from options and convertibles, and is the more honest figure.

cards.q: What is the price-to-earnings ratio, and what does a high one actually tell you?
cards.takeaway: Share price over EPS: how many years of current earnings the market is paying for, which reflects expected growth.
cards.a: The P/E ratio is the share price divided by earnings per share, or equivalently market capitalisation over net income. At 15x, investors are paying £15 for every £1 of this year's profit. A high P/E does not mean a share is expensive so much as that the market expects earnings to grow fast; a low one means it expects little growth, or sees risk. Comparing P/Es only makes sense between similar companies. The ratio also breaks when earnings are near zero or negative, which is why analysts fall back on EV/EBITDA for loss-making or heavily indebted companies.

cards.q: What is dividend yield, and what is the payout ratio?
cards.takeaway: Yield is the dividend as a percentage of the share price; payout is the dividend as a share of profit.
cards.a: Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the share price. It tells an investor the cash return they get for holding the share, like interest on a bond. The payout ratio is dividends divided by net income, the share of profit paid out rather than reinvested. A high yield with a payout ratio above 100% means the company is paying more than it earns, which cannot last, and the market is usually pricing in a cut. Redhill Utilities paying out 70% of steady earnings is normal; a growth company paying nothing and reinvesting everything is normal too.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail has a current ratio of 0.8, net debt to EBITDA of 4.5x and interest cover of 1.8x. What is the picture, and what would you ask next?
cards.takeaway: Tight liquidity, heavy leverage and thin cover together say the company is one bad season from trouble.
cards.a: Each number alone could be explained away: retailers often run current ratios below one, and 4.5x leverage is high but survivable for a stable business. Together they tell one story. Ferrow owes more this year than it has coming in, carries four and a half years of earnings in debt, and has less than two pounds of operating profit for every pound of interest. A weak Christmas would push cover below one. The questions to ask next are when the debt matures, whether the loans have covenants tied to these ratios, and how much of the current liabilities is trade credit that can be stretched.

cards.q: An interviewer asks how you would compare Calder Foods with a listed rival using ratios. How do you structure the answer?
cards.takeaway: Pick one ratio from each family, compare against the peer and against the company's own history, and say what the differences mean.
cards.a: Go family by family so you never freeze. Profitability: gross and operating margin, to see which company has the better product and the leaner cost base. Returns: ROCE, to see which one turns capital into profit more efficiently. Leverage: net debt to EBITDA and interest cover, to see which balance sheet is safer. Liquidity: current or quick ratio. Efficiency: inventory and receivable days, to see who runs tighter. For each, say the number, say what it means, and say why it might differ, since a lower margin could be a worse business or a deliberately cheaper strategy. That is the whole answer.

name: Corporate Finance & Investment Basics
description: Time value of money, NPV, IRR, and how companies decide where to put capital.
intro: This deck is about how companies actually decide where to put their money, using ideas like the time value of money, net present value, and internal rate of return. These concepts sound abstract until you realize interviewers use them to test whether you can reason about a decision the way a finance team actually would. Expect a mix of "what does this term mean" and "how would you use it to make a call," both of which come up in real interviews.

cards.q: What is the time value of money, and why does it matter?
cards.takeaway: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can already be earning a return.
cards.a: Money in hand today is worth more than the same amount later, because it can be invested right away to start earning a return, and because inflation and risk chip away at what a future dollar can actually buy. This is the foundational idea behind discounting, NPV, and virtually every valuation method bankers build: you can't compare a dollar today to a dollar in five years, or line up cash flows from different points in a deal timeline, without adjusting for that gap first.

cards.q: What does “opportunity cost” mean, and why does it come up in almost every finance decision?
cards.takeaway: Opportunity cost is the value of the best thing you gave up in order to do the thing you chose.
cards.a: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option you passed up when you committed money, time, or people to something else. If Calder Foods puts $10mm into a new depot, the real cost isn’t only the $10mm, it’s whatever that $10mm would have earned in its best alternative use, maybe paying down debt or upgrading an existing line. That’s why finance rarely asks “is this good?” and almost always asks “is this better than the next thing we could do with the same money?”, and it’s the reason a discount rate exists at all.

cards.q: A client sees $100,000 due in three years shown as roughly $79,000 on your summary page and asks why. What’s the difference between present value and future value?
cards.takeaway: Future value grows a sum forward at a rate, present value shrinks a future sum back to today.
cards.a: Future value asks what a sum today becomes if it grows at some rate, so $79,000 growing at 8% a year turns into about $100,000 in three years. Present value runs the same arithmetic backwards, asking what a future sum is worth in today’s dollars, so $100,000 three years out discounted at 8% is that same $79,000. They are two views of one relationship, and the rate is what links them. Models are almost always built in present value, because that is the only basis on which cash flows from different years can be added together.

cards.q: What’s the difference between simple and compound interest, and why does compounding matter so much over a long horizon?
cards.takeaway: Simple interest earns only on the original sum, compound interest earns on the interest as well.
cards.a: Simple interest pays a fixed amount on the original principal every period, so $1,000 at 10% simple interest earns $100 a year and reaches $2,000 after ten years. Compound interest pays on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so year two earns 10% on $1,100 rather than on $1,000, and after ten years the same $1,000 is worth about $2,594. The gap widens the longer money sits, and that is the engine underneath discounting: if money grows on a compounded basis going forward, it has to be brought back on a compounded basis too.

cards.q: You’re setting up the discounting row on a project model and an intern asks where the 9% came from. What does a discount rate actually represent?
cards.takeaway: A discount rate is the return available elsewhere at the same risk, so it sets the price of waiting.
cards.a: A discount rate is the annual return an investor could earn from an alternative use of the same money at the same level of risk, and it is what converts future dollars into today’s dollars. Two things push it up: the plain cost of waiting, which even a risk-free government bond compensates you for, and a risk premium for the chance the cash never shows up at all. So that 9% is really a claim about how risky this project’s cash flows are. Move it a point or two and the present value swings noticeably, which is why it is usually the first assumption an MD questions.

cards.q: You're on the deal team pitching Bramwell & Co., a mid-market packaging manufacturer, on a $40mm plant expansion. Your VP asks you to walk him through what Net Present Value is and how you'd use it to tell the client whether the expansion is worth funding.
cards.takeaway: NPV converts a project's future cash flows into today's dollars and nets out what it cost to get started.
cards.a: NPV takes the expansion's expected future cash flows, discounts each one back to present value using Bramwell's cost of capital, and adds them all up. Then it subtracts the initial $40mm outlay, leaving the net value the project is actually expected to create. The decision rule follows directly: recommend the project if NPV is positive, since it's expected to earn more than the cost of capital, and recommend against it if NPV is negative.

cards.q: What is the payback period, and what's its main limitation?
cards.takeaway: Payback period tells you how fast you get your money back, but ignores everything after that.
cards.a: The payback period is simply how long it takes for a project's cumulative cash flows to add back up to the initial investment. Its main blind spot is that it ignores the time value of money, treating a dollar in year one the same as a dollar in year four, and it ignores any cash flows after the payback point. Bankers will sometimes use it as a quick sanity-check gut number, but it's usually paired with NPV or IRR rather than used as a stand-alone decision tool.

cards.q: You're building the returns page for a leveraged buyout of Ferrow Retail ahead of the investment committee meeting. The senior associate asks you to explain what the IRR line in the model actually represents.
cards.takeaway: IRR is the discount rate that makes a deal's NPV exactly zero, its own break-even return.
cards.a: IRR is the discount rate at which the deal's projected cash flows produce an NPV of exactly zero, so it's essentially the LBO's built-in break-even rate of return. To judge whether the Ferrow Retail deal clears the bar, you'd compare its IRR against the fund's required return, or hurdle rate: if the projected IRR beats that hurdle, the deal is generally worth pursuing.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics has already spent $6mm on a warehouse build that now looks marginal, and the CFO says they can’t walk away after committing that much. Where’s the flaw in that reasoning?
cards.takeaway: Money already spent and unrecoverable should have no weight in a go or no-go decision made today.
cards.a: The $6mm is a sunk cost, meaning it is gone whether Northbay finishes the warehouse or stops this afternoon, so no decision made now can bring it back. The only question that matters is whether the cash still to be spent will create more value than that same cash would somewhere else, which means running the NPV on the remaining outlay and the remaining cash flows and leaving the $6mm out entirely. Interviewers like this one because the instinctive answer, protecting money already committed, is precisely the wrong one.

cards.q: Why do riskier investments have to offer higher expected returns?
cards.takeaway: Nobody takes on more uncertainty for free, so higher risk has to come with a higher required return.
cards.a: An investor can always park money somewhere very safe, such as short-term government debt, so anything with a real chance of losing money has to offer more than that to attract funding at all. The extra return demanded on top of that risk-free rate is the risk premium, and it grows with how uncertain the payoff is. Notice that this is an expected return rather than a promise: a risky project offers a higher return precisely because it might not deliver one. Every hurdle rate and every discount rate you build is an application of this single idea.

cards.q: What is the difference between a bond and a stock, at a basic level?
cards.takeaway: A bond is a loan with a promised repayment; a stock is ownership with no promises either way.
cards.a: A bond is essentially a loan: an investor gives a company or government money, and in return it promises to pay back the principal plus periodic interest (coupons) on a fixed schedule. A stock is different: it represents partial ownership in a company, with no promised repayment at all. Its value simply depends on the company's future performance and however the market chooses to price that, which is exactly why equity and debt sit on opposite ends of the risk-return spectrum in a deal's financing mix.

cards.q: Your MD wants a one-line capital structure summary for Halloway Industrial ahead of tomorrow's board deck: how much of the balance sheet is funded with debt versus equity, and why the mix is worth flagging.
cards.takeaway: Capital structure is just the mix of debt and equity a company uses to fund itself.
cards.a: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity Halloway uses to fund its operations and growth. That mix matters because it shapes the company's cost of capital, risk, and flexibility: debt is generally cheaper and doesn't dilute ownership, but it comes with fixed repayment obligations regardless of how the business performs, while equity carries no repayment obligation but costs more and dilutes existing owners.

cards.q: Your MD asks you to sanity-check the WACC on the Corven Aerospace model before the 9am call. Walk him through what "cost of capital" actually means and why it's the number sitting at the center of that check.
cards.takeaway: Cost of capital is the minimum return a company must earn on anything it invests in, or it's destroying value.
cards.a: Cost of capital is the return Corven has to offer to attract funding, whether that's interest paid to lenders (cost of debt) or the return shareholders expect (cost of equity), and it rises with how risky investors perceive the company to be. Think of it as a hurdle rate: any project or investment Corven takes on needs to earn more than this just to be worth doing, which is exactly why a WACC that's out of line with the company's risk profile is worth flagging before it goes in front of the client.

cards.q: A junior notices the Marden Chemical model carries cost of debt at 5% and cost of equity at 11%, and asks why equity is the more expensive of the two. What do you tell her?
cards.takeaway: Equity holders are paid last and promised nothing, so they demand a bigger return than lenders do.
cards.a: Lenders sit at the front of the line. They are owed a contractual interest payment, they get repaid before shareholders see anything, and if the company fails their claim is settled first, so their risk is lower and the return they will accept is lower. Shareholders are last in line, with no promised payment and no guarantee of getting their money back, and they price that uncertainty into a higher required return. Interest is also usually tax-deductible while dividends are not, which pushes the effective cost of debt lower still.

cards.q: What is diversification, and why does it reduce risk?
cards.takeaway: Diversification spreads money across assets that don't all move together, smoothing out the bumps.
cards.a: Diversification means spreading your money across multiple assets whose returns don't move in lockstep, so when one investment dips, others are likely holding steady or gaining, cushioning the blow. Because different assets react differently to the same events, a diversified portfolio typically ends up with lower overall volatility than any single holding inside it.

cards.q: What is the difference between systematic and unsystematic risk?
cards.takeaway: Systematic risk hits the whole market and can't be diversified away; unsystematic risk is company-specific and can.
cards.a: Systematic risk is market-wide, things like interest rate moves or a recession, and it affects nearly every asset at once, so no amount of diversification eliminates it. Unsystematic risk is specific to a single company or industry, like a product recall or a lawsuit, and this is the risk diversification actually protects against: spread your holdings widely enough, and one asset's specific problems just get absorbed by the others. It's also why beta in a WACC calculation only ever measures the systematic piece.

cards.q: Two mutually exclusive projects land on your desk: one has the higher NPV, the other the higher IRR, and you can only fund one. Your VP asks which you’d recommend and why.
cards.takeaway: When NPV and IRR disagree on projects you must choose between, follow the NPV.
cards.a: IRR is a percentage, so it says nothing about how much money is actually at stake, and a small project can post a spectacular rate of return while creating less value than a large project earning a modest one. IRR also quietly assumes interim cash flows get reinvested at the IRR itself, which is usually optimistic, and it can produce more than one answer when cash flows swing between negative and positive. NPV measures dollars of value created at the company’s real cost of capital, so when the two conflict, NPV is the one you follow.

cards.q: Ardsley Media is sitting on $200mm of cash with no obvious acquisition in sight. Your MD asks you to lay out what management can actually do with it.
cards.takeaway: Spare cash can be reinvested, used to cut debt, or handed back, and the best use is whatever earns most.
cards.a: There are four basic doors. Ardsley can reinvest in the business through new projects, capacity, or an acquisition, which is the right call whenever those uses have a positive NPV. It can pay down debt, lowering interest expense and financial risk. Or it can return the cash to shareholders, either as a dividend or by buying back its own shares. The discipline underneath all of it is that reinvestment only wins if it clears the cost of capital, since a company earning less than that on new projects is destroying value and would serve its owners better by handing the money back.

cards.q: What’s the difference between paying a dividend and buying back stock, and why might a company prefer one over the other?
cards.takeaway: Both hand cash to shareholders, but a dividend pays everyone while a buyback shrinks the share count.
cards.a: A dividend is a cash payment made to every shareholder on a per-share basis, and once a company starts one, cutting it later reads as a distress signal, so the market treats it as close to a commitment. A buyback has the company purchase its own shares in the market, which reduces the share count so each remaining share owns a larger slice of the same business, and it can be slowed or paused quietly. Buybacks therefore give management more flexibility, though they only create value if the shares are bought below what they are actually worth.

name: Financial Markets & Instruments
description: How stocks, bonds, and other instruments actually trade.
intro: This deck covers how stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments actually trade, the difference between where a security is first issued and where it changes hands afterward, and the basic mechanics behind the markets you hear about in the news. It is aimed at giving you enough grounding to talk about markets confidently in an interview, not at making you a trader. No assumed background beyond general curiosity about how finance works.

cards.q: What does it actually mean to own a share of stock?
cards.takeaway: A share is a small ownership slice of a company, not a loan to it.
cards.a: A share of stock is a unit of ownership in a company. If Calder Foods has 50 million shares outstanding and you hold 500 of them, you own one hundred-thousandth of the business, which comes with a claim on that same fraction of its profits and, usually, a vote on matters put to shareholders. You aren’t lending the company anything and nobody promises you your money back. Your return comes from the shares being worth more later, or from dividends, cash the company chooses to pay out to its owners.

cards.q: What is a bond, and what do the words coupon, par value and maturity mean?
cards.takeaway: A bond is a loan on fixed terms, set interest payments plus a set date to get your money back.
cards.a: A bond is a loan you make to a company or a government, packaged so that it can be bought and sold. The par value, also called face value, is the amount the issuer promises to repay at the end, conventionally $1,000 per bond. The coupon is the fixed interest paid along the way, so a 5% coupon on a $1,000 bond is $50 a year. Maturity is the date the last coupon and the par value come back. You get no ownership and no upside beyond those promised payments.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a primary market and a secondary market?
cards.takeaway: Primary market money goes to the company; secondary market money just moves between investors.
cards.a: In the primary market, a company sells brand-new securities directly to investors for the first time, an IPO being the classic example, and the company keeps the proceeds — this is the deal-side work an ECM (equity capital markets) team executes. In the secondary market, investors simply trade those already-issued securities amongst themselves, like on the NYSE or Nasdaq, and the issuing company isn't even a party to the transaction. Only the primary market actually raises new capital for the company; the secondary market just lets ownership change hands.

cards.q: Your group is staffed on the IPO for Ferrow Retail Group, a private-equity-backed retailer. Before the kickoff call, a first-year analyst asks you: what is an IPO, exactly?
cards.takeaway: An IPO is a private company's first sale of shares to the public, becoming publicly traded.
cards.a: An IPO, or initial public offering, is the process by which a private company like Ferrow Retail sells shares to the public for the first time and becomes a publicly traded company. It lets the company raise capital from a much broader pool of investors, but in exchange, existing owners give up some ownership and the company takes on the disclosure and reporting obligations that come with being public.

cards.q: A friend asks what actually happens when she taps buy on her phone and the shares appear in her account. What does a broker do, and what does an exchange do?
cards.takeaway: The broker takes your order and routes it, the exchange is the venue where it meets the other side.
cards.a: A broker is a firm licensed to place orders on your behalf and to hold the resulting shares and cash in your account, since an individual can’t walk onto an exchange and trade directly. The exchange is the venue itself, a regulated marketplace that collects everyone’s buy and sell orders into one order book and matches them by price. So the sequence is you instruct the broker, the broker routes the order to an exchange or another trading venue, the exchange pairs it with someone willing to take the other side, and the fill comes back to your account.

cards.q: What is the bid-ask spread?
cards.takeaway: The bid-ask spread is the gap between what buyers offer and what sellers demand.
cards.a: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security, and the ask is the lowest price a seller is willing to accept; the difference between the two is the spread a trading desk watches all day. A narrow spread usually signals a liquid market with plenty of active buyers and sellers, while a wide spread signals lower liquidity or more uncertainty about fair value.

cards.q: You buy Northbay Logistics at the market and the fill comes back three cents worse than the price on your screen. What’s the difference between a market order and a limit order?
cards.takeaway: A market order guarantees you trade, a limit order guarantees your price, never both.
cards.a: A market order says fill me now at the best price available, so it trades immediately but you accept whatever the ask happens to be at that instant, which is why the fill can drift a few cents from the last quote you saw. A limit order sets the worst price you’ll accept, buy at $49.80 or better, and it simply rests in the order book until someone trades against it or you cancel. The trade-off is certainty of execution against certainty of price, and in a thinly traded name with a wide spread that difference gets expensive fast.

cards.q: What is a market maker?
cards.takeaway: Market makers quote both sides of the market constantly, earning the spread instead of betting on price direction.
cards.a: A market maker is a firm that continuously quotes both a bid and an ask price for a security, standing ready to buy or sell at those prices at any time — it's the kind of two-sided flow you'd see running through a bank's trading desk. That constant two-sided quoting is what supplies liquidity to the market. Their profit comes from capturing the bid-ask spread across that flow of trades, not from predicting which way the price will move.

cards.q: You're building the comps set for the Ferrow Retail deal and need to size up each comparable company. Your analyst asks you to explain what market capitalization is and how it's calculated.
cards.takeaway: Market cap is share price times shares outstanding, a company's total public equity value.
cards.a: Market capitalization is the total value of a company's outstanding shares, calculated simply as the current share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. It's the standard way to categorize company size — large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap — and to compare the relative size of publicly traded companies at a glance, exactly what you'd use to screen comps for a pitch like this one.

cards.q: What is a market index, and what do people mean by active versus passive investing?
cards.takeaway: An index is a rules-based basket used as a scoreboard, and passive funds just buy the whole basket.
cards.a: An index is a defined basket of securities whose combined value is tracked over time, usually weighted by market capitalization so the largest companies count for the most. You can’t buy the index itself, it’s a scoreboard for how a slice of the market performed. Active investing means a manager picks individual holdings hoping to beat that scoreboard and charges a higher fee for the attempt, while passive investing means holding a fund that simply owns the basket at very low cost. Most active managers fail to beat their index after fees over long stretches, which is why passive money has grown so quickly.

cards.q: Redhill Utilities is raising money and you can buy either its bonds or its shares. As the investor, how do the two differ in risk, return, and where you stand if the company fails?
cards.takeaway: Debt is paid first for a capped return, equity is paid last with no ceiling on the upside.
cards.a: Buying the bonds makes you a lender: you get fixed coupons, your principal back at maturity, and legal priority, meaning that if Redhill is wound up, creditors are paid out of the proceeds before shareholders see anything. The most you can make is the yield you were promised. Buying the shares makes you an owner: nothing is promised, you sit last in line and can be wiped out entirely, but you’re entitled to everything left over once the lenders are satisfied, and that has no upper limit. Same company, two very different risk profiles.

cards.q: What is preferred stock, and where does it sit between debt and common stock?
cards.takeaway: Preferred stock pays a fixed dividend and ranks ahead of common shares but behind every lender.
cards.a: Preferred stock is an ownership stake that behaves partly like a bond. It normally pays a fixed dividend, and in a wind-down preferred holders are paid after all lenders but before common shareholders, the ordinary shares people mean when they just say stock. In exchange for that steadier income and better place in the queue, preferred holders usually give up their vote and most of the upside if the business does well. Because it sits between debt and equity, bankers call it hybrid capital, and it shows up constantly in private equity deals and rescue financings.

cards.q: You're on the DCM team pricing a new bond for Bramwell & Co. Overnight the bond's price drops, and a client asks why the yield just moved — how do you explain the relationship between a bond's yield and its price?
cards.takeaway: A bond's yield and price always move in opposite directions.
cards.a: A bond's yield is the return an investor actually earns from holding it, and it moves inversely to the bond's price: when price falls, like it just did on Bramwell's bond, yield rises, because the same fixed coupon payments now represent a bigger percentage return on the lower price paid. Pay less for the same future cash flows and your return goes up; pay more and it goes down. This inverse relationship is one of the most fundamental mechanics in fixed income markets.

cards.q: S&P just assigned Bramwell & Co.'s new bond issuance a rating one notch below investment grade. Your associate asks you to explain to the client what a credit rating tells investors and why it matters for pricing the deal.
cards.takeaway: Lower credit rating means higher default risk, so investors demand a higher yield.
cards.a: A credit rating, assigned by agencies like Moody's or S&P, is their estimate of how likely an issuer like Bramwell is to default on its debt. Ratings range from investment-grade at the safer end down to high-yield, or “junk,” at the riskier end. Because risk and return are linked, a rating this low means Bramwell will have to offer a higher yield to compensate investors for taking on that extra default risk.

cards.q: At the morning meeting someone says the curve just inverted and the desk reacts. What is the yield curve, and why does an inverted one get that much attention?
cards.takeaway: The yield curve plots yield against maturity, and inversion means short-dated debt yields more than long.
cards.a: The yield curve plots the yield on one issuer’s bonds, usually a government’s, against how long each one has until it matures, from a few months out to thirty years. Normally it slopes upward, because lending for longer leaves more time for inflation and trouble, so investors demand more to do it. An inverted curve slopes down, with short maturities yielding more than long ones, which implies the market expects interest rates, and typically growth, to be lower in future. Inversions have preceded most recent recessions, though the signal is imprecise and the lag has varied a lot.

cards.q: Rates move a quarter of a point and Bramwell’s thirty-year bond falls far more than its two-year. Your associate asks why maturity changes how much a bond’s price moves. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: The longer you wait for the money, the more a change in rates moves the bond’s price today.
cards.a: A bond’s price is just the present value of its future payments, and discounting bites harder the further out a payment sits. Raise the discount rate a quarter of a point and a payment arriving in thirty years loses much more of its value than one arriving in two, so the long bond drops far more for exactly the same move in rates. That sensitivity is called duration, roughly the weighted average time until you receive your money, and it’s the standard measure of interest-rate risk on a fixed income desk. A lower coupon lengthens duration too.

cards.q: What is a derivative, and what are options and futures examples of?
cards.takeaway: A derivative's value comes from something else entirely; options and futures are the two classic examples.
cards.a: A derivative is a financial contract with no value of its own; its value is derived from an underlying asset, like a stock, commodity, or index — the kind of exposure a derivatives or structuring desk trades all day. Options and futures are both derivatives, but they work differently: an option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a set price, while a futures contract is an obligation, both sides are locked in to buy or sell it at a set price on a set future date.

cards.q: A hedge fund client, Talbrook Capital, wants to protect a long position in Ferrow Retail stock ahead of earnings. Your VP asks you to walk through the difference between a call option and a put option before the call.
cards.takeaway: Calls profit when the price rises above the strike; puts profit when it falls below it.
cards.a: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset, like Ferrow Retail stock, at a set strike price before expiration, and investors buy calls when they expect the price to rise. A put option gives the holder the right to sell at the strike price, which is the side Talbrook would look at to hedge against a drop, and investors buy puts when they expect the price to fall. Either way, it's a right, not an obligation, so the holder can just let the option expire worthless if exercising it wouldn't be profitable.
