cards.q: Calder Foods beats its earnings forecast and the stock still falls 6% by lunchtime. A client calls asking how that’s possible. How do you explain it?
cards.takeaway: Prices move on the gap between results and expectations, not on whether the news itself was good.
cards.a: A share price already reflects what the market collectively expects, so what moves it is the surprise, the difference between what was reported and what investors had priced in beforehand. If traders were positioned for a much bigger beat, or if management guided next year down, an objectively good quarter is still a disappointment against that bar and the stock sells off. This is what people mean when they say something is already priced in, and it’s why a stock can fall on good news and rally on bad news that simply turned out to be less bad than feared.

name: Markets & Macro Awareness
description: Rates, inflation, FX and what they do to markets, so you can talk about the news coherently.
intro: Every spring week and internship interview has a moment where they ask what is going on in markets, and most first-years either freeze or recite a headline. This deck gives you the handful of ideas that connect the headlines: what interest rates actually do, why inflation is the number everyone watches, what moves a currency, and how all of it feeds through to stocks, bonds and deals. It assumes you have never read the Financial Times. By the end you will be able to hold a two-minute conversation about the economy without bluffing.

cards.q: What is a central bank's policy rate, and why does everyone care about it?
cards.takeaway: The policy rate is the price of money for the whole economy, set by a committee eight times a year.
cards.a: The policy rate is the interest rate a central bank sets for the shortest-term borrowing between banks. In the UK it is Bank Rate, set by the Bank of England; in the US it is the federal funds rate, set by the Federal Reserve. Everything else prices off it. When it moves, mortgage rates, savings rates, corporate borrowing costs and government bond yields all shift, which is why a quarter-point change gets front-page coverage. In an interview you are expected to know roughly where the rate is, which way it moved last, and what the central bank said about where it goes next.

cards.q: What is inflation, how is it measured, and why do central banks target 2%?
cards.takeaway: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise, measured by a basket of goods, and 2% is the level that keeps money stable without freezing the economy.
cards.a: Inflation is the rate at which the general level of prices rises over a year. It is measured with a price index, in the UK the Consumer Prices Index, which tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services. Central banks target roughly 2% because a little inflation keeps wages and prices adjusting smoothly, while high inflation eats savings and makes planning impossible, and falling prices (deflation) make people delay spending. When inflation runs well above target, the central bank raises rates to slow it down; when it falls well below, it cuts to support demand.

cards.q: How does raising interest rates actually bring inflation down?
cards.takeaway: Higher rates make borrowing dearer and saving more attractive, so demand cools and prices stop rising as fast.
cards.a: Raising rates works through demand. Mortgages and loans cost more, so households have less to spend; companies find projects harder to justify, so they invest and hire less; saving pays more, so money sits rather than circulates. With less spending chasing the same goods, businesses lose the ability to keep raising prices. The effect is slow, typically a year or more to work through fully, which is why central banks talk about acting before inflation has fully shown up, and why they sometimes overshoot in both directions.

cards.q: Why do higher interest rates tend to push share prices down?
cards.takeaway: A share is worth the present value of future cash, and a higher discount rate makes distant cash worth less today.
cards.a: A company's shares are worth what its future cash flows are worth today, and you get from the future to today by discounting at a rate. When interest rates rise, that discount rate rises, so the same future cash is worth less now and the valuation falls. The effect is largest for companies whose profits sit far in the future, which is why fast-growing tech stocks tend to fall hardest when rates rise. There is a second channel too: when a safe government bond pays more, investors need less persuading to leave equities.

cards.q: When rates rise, which sectors tend to win and which tend to lose?
cards.takeaway: Banks usually benefit; anything valued on distant growth or bought with borrowed money usually suffers.
cards.a: Banks tend to benefit because they earn the gap between what they pay on deposits and what they charge on loans, and that gap usually widens as rates rise. Insurers earn more on the money they hold. On the other side, growth stocks lose value because their profits are far in the future, property and utilities suffer because they carry a lot of debt and compete with bonds for income-seeking investors, and highly leveraged companies see interest costs eat their earnings. In an interview, one sentence on each side shows you understand the mechanism rather than the headline.

cards.q: What is GDP, and what does it mean when people say the economy is in recession?
cards.takeaway: GDP is the value of everything an economy produces in a period; a recession is that number shrinking for two quarters in a row.
cards.a: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a period, usually reported quarterly. When it grows, businesses sell more, hire more and pay more tax; when it shrinks, the reverse. The common definition of recession is two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, though economists also look at jobs and spending before calling one. For a bank, GDP matters because deal activity, loan demand and defaults all track it, so a forecast of slowing growth shows up in every conversation about pipelines.

cards.q: Why do central banks watch the jobs market so closely when they are worried about inflation?
cards.takeaway: Tight labour markets push wages up, and wages feed straight into prices.
cards.a: When unemployment is low, employers compete for workers by raising pay. Higher wages are good for households but they are also a cost for businesses, who pass them on in prices, and they give people more to spend, which supports demand. That is why strong jobs data can send markets down: investors read it as a sign the central bank will keep rates higher for longer. The reverse also holds, which is why a rise in unemployment can rally bonds and, sometimes, equities, as the market anticipates cuts.

cards.q: What actually moves a currency's exchange rate?
cards.takeaway: Money flows toward higher interest rates, stronger growth and safety, and a currency rises when money flows in.
cards.a: A currency is just something people buy and sell, and its price rises when more people want it. The biggest driver is interest rates: if UK rates are higher than US rates, holding pounds pays more, so money flows in and sterling tends to strengthen. Growth matters because strong economies attract investment. Risk matters because in a crisis money runs to the dollar, the Swiss franc and the yen as safe havens. Trade balances, politics and central bank comments all move the rate too, which is why FX reacts to almost every piece of news.

cards.q: Sterling falls 10% against the dollar. Calder Foods imports most of its ingredients in dollars and Bramwell & Co. sells engineering kit to American customers. What happens to each?
cards.takeaway: A weaker currency hurts importers and helps exporters, and the effect shows up in margins before it shows up in revenue.
cards.a: Calder Foods now needs 10% more pounds to buy the same dollars' worth of ingredients, so its costs rise. It either raises prices, and risks losing customers, or absorbs the hit and its margin falls. Bramwell & Co. gets the mirror image: its American customers pay in dollars, and each dollar now converts into more pounds, so its revenue and margin rise without it doing anything, and it could cut its dollar prices to win share. This is why the FTSE 100, full of exporters and companies earning abroad, often rises on a weak pound while domestically focused firms fall.

cards.q: What is quantitative easing, and what is quantitative tightening?
cards.takeaway: QE is the central bank buying bonds to push long-term rates down; QT is letting them run off to push rates back up.
cards.a: When the policy rate is already near zero and the economy still needs help, a central bank can buy government bonds in large quantities. That pushes bond prices up and yields down, lowers long-term borrowing costs and pumps money into the financial system. That is quantitative easing, used heavily after 2008 and in 2020. Quantitative tightening is the reverse: the central bank stops reinvesting the bonds it holds, or sells them, which drains money from the system and nudges long-term rates up. Both work on the long end of the curve, whereas the policy rate works on the short end.

cards.q: The Fed cuts rates by more than the market expected. Walk through what happens to bonds, equities, the dollar and gold that afternoon.
cards.takeaway: A surprise cut lifts bond prices, usually lifts equities, weakens the dollar and helps gold, because the surprise is what the market reprices.
cards.a: Markets price what they expect, so only the surprise moves prices. A bigger cut than expected means future rates are lower than everyone assumed. Bond yields fall and bond prices rise. Equities usually rise because the discount rate fell, unless the size of the cut makes investors worry the Fed sees a recession coming, in which case the reaction can reverse. The dollar weakens because holding it now pays less. Gold rises because it pays no interest, so lower rates make it relatively more attractive. Knowing that the surprise is what matters, not the cut itself, is the thing interviewers listen for.

cards.q: What is a credit spread, and what does it tell you when spreads widen?
cards.takeaway: The spread is the extra yield a company pays over government bonds for its risk; widening spreads mean the market is getting nervous.
cards.a: A credit spread is the difference between the yield on a company's bond and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity. It is the price of the risk that the company does not pay you back. When investors get nervous about the economy, they demand more compensation for that risk, so spreads widen; when they are confident, spreads tighten. Because of that, spreads are one of the cleanest gauges of market mood. A desk saying that high-yield spreads have blown out is saying that the market thinks defaults are coming.

cards.q: What do people mean by risk-on and risk-off?
cards.takeaway: Risk-on is money moving into assets that pay more but can lose more; risk-off is money running to safety.
cards.a: Risk-on describes a market where investors are confident, so they sell safe assets and buy ones with higher expected returns: equities, high-yield bonds, emerging-market currencies, commodities. Risk-off is the reverse: money leaves those assets for government bonds, the dollar, the yen, the Swiss franc and gold. Most days are a mix, but a big piece of news, a bank failure or a strong jobs number, can flip the whole market into one mode. Being able to say which mode the market is in, and why, is most of what talking about markets in an interview involves.

cards.q: Oil jumps 20% in a month. Who wins, who loses, and why does the central bank care?
cards.takeaway: Energy producers win, energy users lose, and because oil feeds into the price of almost everything, the central bank sees inflation coming.
cards.a: Oil producers and the countries that export it earn more for the same barrels. Airlines, shipping companies, chemicals firms and anyone with a big fuel bill see costs rise, and consumers have less to spend after filling up. Because fuel is an input to transport, plastics, food and heating, an oil spike pushes up the prices of goods across the economy, which shows up in inflation a few months later. That is why a central bank watches oil: it has to decide whether the rise is a one-off it can look through, or the start of something it needs to raise rates against.

cards.q: An interviewer asks what is going on in markets right now. How do you structure the answer?
cards.takeaway: Rates, inflation, growth, then one story you actually follow, in under two minutes.
cards.a: Use a fixed structure so you never freeze. First, rates: where the central bank is and which way it is leaning. Second, inflation: the latest number and whether it is moving toward the target. Third, growth: is the economy expanding, slowing or in recession, and what the jobs market says. Then one specific story you have genuinely followed, whether a sector, a deal, a currency move or a company, with a view on why it matters. Finish with what you think happens next and why. Nobody expects you to be right; they want to see you can think in cause and effect and that you actually read.

cards.q: They ask you to talk about a recent deal or market event. How do you prepare one so it holds up to follow-up questions?
cards.takeaway: Pick one, know the numbers, know the rationale, and have a view on whether it makes sense.
cards.a: Choose one deal or event from the last few months that connects to the bank or team you are interviewing with. Learn the basics cold: who bought what, for how much, how it was paid for, and the headline multiple or premium if there was one. Then the why: what the buyer says it gains, whether the market agreed on the day, and what the risks are. Finally, form an opinion, because the follow-up will be whether you would have done the deal. Two stories prepared this way beat ten headlines you can only name.

cards.q: Your team is advising Ferrow Retail on its IPO. Rates have risen, the VIX is elevated and two recent listings have traded down. Why does the macro backdrop matter for the deal, and what might you advise?
cards.takeaway: IPOs need calm markets and confident investors, so the backdrop decides whether the window is open and at what price.
cards.a: An IPO asks investors to buy something new at a price set today, which they will only do when they trust prices will hold. Higher rates lower what they will pay for growth, so the valuation range comes down. The VIX, a measure of expected equity volatility, being elevated means big daily swings, and nobody wants to price a deal into that. Recent listings trading below their offer price make investors demand a bigger discount. The honest advice is often to wait for a window: a few weeks of calmer markets and a couple of successful deals. If the company cannot wait, it prices lower and sells less.

cards.q: What is the difference between monetary policy and fiscal policy, and why does the mix between them move markets?
cards.takeaway: Monetary policy is the central bank and interest rates; fiscal policy is the government and its taxes and spending.
cards.a: Monetary policy is what the central bank does with interest rates and its bond holdings. Fiscal policy is what the government does with taxes, spending and borrowing. They can pull in the same direction or against each other. A government spending heavily while the central bank is trying to cool inflation means rates stay higher for longer, and more government borrowing means more bonds to sell, which pushes yields up. That combination worried markets in the UK in 2022, when a budget of unfunded tax cuts sent gilt yields sharply higher and the pound down within days. Knowing that episode is a good example to have ready.

name: Earnings & Guidance
description: What happens on results day, why stocks fall on a beat, and how to read what a company says about its future.
intro: Four times a year every listed company reports its results, and the way the share price reacts confuses almost everyone at first. This deck explains the machinery: what consensus is, what a beat and a miss actually mean, why guidance often matters more than the numbers, how the market prices the surprise rather than the result, and what to look for in a company's statement. It is the practical half of talking about markets, the part that lets you explain why Calder Foods fell 6% on a record quarter.

cards.q: What is an earnings release, and what is in it?
cards.takeaway: The quarterly or half-yearly statement of results, with the numbers, the management commentary and the outlook.
cards.a: An earnings release is the announcement a listed company puts out each quarter, or each half-year in the UK, reporting how it performed. It contains the headline numbers, revenue, profit and earnings per share, usually compared with the same period a year earlier; a commentary from the chief executive explaining what drove them; the financial statements in summary form; and an outlook or guidance section saying what management expects next. It is released before the market opens or after it closes, and is usually followed by a call where analysts question management. The share price reacts to all of it, not just the headline.

cards.q: What is consensus, and where does it come from?
cards.takeaway: The average of analysts' forecasts for a company's results, which is the number the market has already priced in.
cards.a: Consensus is the average, or sometimes the median, of the forecasts published by the analysts who cover a company. If fifteen analysts expect Calder Foods to earn between 40p and 46p a share, consensus might be 43p. Because investors read those forecasts, the share price before results already reflects roughly that expectation. So results are judged not against last year but against consensus: the question is not whether the company did well but whether it did better or worse than everyone assumed. Consensus figures are collected by data providers like Bloomberg and Refinitiv, and companies often publish a compiled version themselves.

cards.q: What does it mean to beat or miss, and why does a beat not guarantee the share price rises?
cards.takeaway: A beat is a result above consensus; the price only rises if the beat is bigger than what the market had quietly hoped for.
cards.a: A beat is reporting a number above consensus; a miss is below. In principle a beat is good news, but the market often expects one, especially from companies that reliably guide conservatively and then beat. If investors had been positioned for a big beat, a small one disappoints, and the price falls. The market also looks past the headline: a company can beat on earnings through a one-off tax gain while revenue misses, or beat this quarter while cutting guidance for the next. The move on the day reflects the whole package against what was already priced in, not the single number.

cards.q: What is guidance, and why does it often move the share price more than the results themselves?
cards.takeaway: Guidance is management's forecast for the coming period, and shares are priced on the future, not the quarter just finished.
cards.a: Guidance is management's own forecast for the next quarter or year: a range for revenue, profit or margin, sometimes for capital spending or cash flow too. It matters more than the results because the results are history and the share price is a bet on the future. A quarter that beats by 2% while guidance for next year is cut by 10% is a bad day. Companies are careful with guidance because missing it destroys credibility, so many guide conservatively, which is why the same companies beat quarter after quarter. Reading whether guidance was raised, held or lowered is the first thing to do on results day.

cards.q: Calder Foods reports record profit, beats consensus by 3%, and the shares fall 6% by lunchtime. Explain to a client what happened.
cards.takeaway: The market prices the surprise, not the result, and a beat that was smaller than hoped, or paired with weaker guidance, is a negative surprise.
cards.a: Start with what was priced in: the shares had run up 15% into results, so investors were expecting more than consensus, and a 3% beat was less than the whisper number. Then look at what else was in the statement: guidance for next year was held rather than raised, margins fell despite the profit growth, and on the call management sounded cautious about input costs. The record profit was true and already known to be likely; the new information was that growth is slowing. The price moves on new information. This is the single most useful idea in the whole topic, and interviewers love it.

cards.q: What is the whisper number?
cards.takeaway: The unofficial expectation among investors, usually higher than published consensus, that a company really has to beat.
cards.a: Published consensus is the average of analyst forecasts, which can be stale because analysts update slowly and some are deliberately cautious. The whisper number is what active investors actually expect, formed from more recent data, conversations and the way the shares have traded. For a company with a habit of beating, the whisper sits above consensus, so a beat against consensus can still be a miss against the whisper, and the shares fall. There is no official source for it, which is exactly why it matters: it is the expectation that is not written down, and therefore the one that surprises.

cards.q: What is the earnings call, and what should you listen for beyond the numbers?
cards.takeaway: Management's tone, what they refuse to answer, and what the best analysts push on, which shows where the doubt is.
cards.a: After the release, management hosts a call: a prepared presentation, then questions from analysts. The numbers are already public, so the value is in what is said around them. Listen for tone, whether the chief executive sounds confident or defensive; for the questions analysts ask twice, which reveal what the market is worried about; for anything management declines to quantify; and for changes in language from last quarter, a business that was growing strongly now growing solidly. Traders often move the price during the call, and transcripts are read for months afterwards. Preparing one call properly is a strong interview story.

cards.q: What are adjusted earnings, and why should you be sceptical of them?
cards.takeaway: Earnings with items management calls one-off stripped out, which is useful until the one-offs happen every year.
cards.a: Companies report statutory earnings under accounting rules and, alongside them, an adjusted figure that removes items they say do not reflect the underlying business: restructuring costs, impairments, share-based pay, acquisition expenses. Sometimes that is fair, since a one-time factory closure really does distort the year. But the choice of what to exclude is management's, and companies that adjust out restructuring costs every single year are describing a permanent cost as a one-off. Compare adjusted with statutory over several years; a gap that never closes tells you the adjusted number is flattering.

cards.q: What is a profit warning, and why does the share price react so violently to one?
cards.takeaway: A statement, outside the normal calendar, that results will fall short of expectations; the market punishes the surprise and the loss of trust.
cards.a: A profit warning is an unscheduled announcement that profits will be materially below what the market expects. UK rules oblige companies to issue one as soon as they know, rather than wait for results day. Shares often drop 20% or more, for two reasons. The first is the information: expectations were wrong and have to be reset. The second is credibility: management either did not see it coming or did not say so, and investors now doubt everything else they were told. There is an old market saying that profit warnings come in threes, because the problem that caused the first is rarely fixed by the second.

cards.q: What is the difference between organic growth and reported growth, and why do analysts strip out acquisitions and currency?
cards.takeaway: Organic growth is what the existing business did on its own; reported growth includes what was bought and what exchange rates did.
cards.a: Reported revenue growth is the simple change from last year. Organic, or like-for-like, growth removes the effect of businesses acquired or sold during the period and of currency movements, so it shows how the underlying operations performed. Bramwell & Co. reporting 12% growth is less impressive if 8% came from a company it bought in March and 3% from a weaker pound flattering its dollar sales. Analysts and interviewers focus on organic growth because it is repeatable; acquisitions and currency are not. Retailers report the same idea as like-for-like sales, stripping out new store openings.

cards.q: Why do companies buy back their own shares around results, and how does it affect earnings per share?
cards.takeaway: Fewer shares means the same profit is spread over less, so EPS rises even if profit does not.
cards.a: A buyback is a company using cash to purchase its own shares in the market and cancel them. Profit is unchanged, but it is now divided among fewer shares, so earnings per share rises. Because analysts and the press focus on EPS, buybacks can make a flat year look like a growing one, and companies know it. They are also a way of returning cash to shareholders without committing to a dividend that would be embarrassing to cut. The question to ask is whether the company is buying back because the shares are cheap or because it has run out of better uses for the money.

cards.q: What is an earnings season, and why does it matter for markets as a whole, not just individual companies?
cards.takeaway: The few weeks when most companies report; taken together, the results are the most direct reading of how the economy is doing.
cards.a: Earnings season is the period, starting a couple of weeks after each quarter ends, when the bulk of listed companies report. The big US banks usually open it. Individually each result moves one stock; together they move the market, because they answer the question macro data can only approximate: are companies actually making more money? A season where most companies beat and raise guidance can lift an index even with poor economic headlines, and a season of margin pressure and cautious outlooks can sink one. Bank results in particular are read as a signal about credit and the consumer.

cards.q: How do results feed into a bank's day-to-day work, in advisory and in research?
cards.takeaway: Research analysts rewrite their models and ratings; deal teams update comps, pitch books and the story they tell clients.
cards.a: In research, results day is the busiest day of the quarter: the analyst updates the forecast model within hours, publishes a note on whether the thesis has changed, and may raise or lower the rating and price target. In investment banking, every result changes the inputs to comps and precedents, so valuations in live pitches are refreshed, and a client's strong or weak quarter changes the timing advice on a sale or a capital raise. A sudden fall after a miss can also make a company a takeover target, which is where the coverage banker's phone starts ringing.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail reports a 4% revenue miss but raises full-year profit guidance. What is the market likely to do, and why?
cards.takeaway: Probably up, because guidance about the future outweighs a miss on the past, but the reason matters.
cards.a: The revenue miss says sales were weaker than expected; the raised profit guidance says management expects to earn more than the market assumed for the whole year. Investors weigh the future more heavily, so the likely reaction is positive, provided the raise is credible. The detail decides it. If profit is rising because Ferrow closed loss-making stores and cut costs, the market will believe it. If it is rising because of a one-off property sale, it will not. And if the revenue miss is the start of a trend, the guidance may not survive the next quarter. Say all three and you have answered like an analyst.

cards.q: What should you read on a company before an interview at the bank that covers it?
cards.takeaway: The last two results releases, the guidance, the share price reaction, and one thing you think about it.
cards.a: Read the last two earnings releases, including the outlook paragraph, and note whether guidance was raised, held or cut. Check how the shares moved on each results day and work out why, using the ideas in this deck. Skim the transcript of the latest call for the questions analysts asked twice. Then form one opinion, for example that the market is underestimating the cost savings or overestimating the growth. That takes an evening, and it lets you answer both the technical question, walk me through their results, and the fit question, why this company, with the same preparation.

cards.q: Why do analysts model a company at all if consensus already exists?
cards.takeaway: Consensus is where the market is; a model is how you decide whether the market is wrong.
cards.a: A financial model is a forecast of the company's income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, built from assumptions about volumes, prices, costs and investment. Consensus is the average of many such models. The point of building your own is to have a view that differs, and to know why. If your model says Calder Foods will earn 10% more than consensus because you think its new factory ramps faster, and you turn out to be right, the shares will rise when everyone else catches up. Investing and equity research are the business of having a better forecast than consensus, which is why the model matters more than the number.

name: Valuation Basics
description: DCF, comps, and the multiples analysts actually use.
intro: Valuation is the skill of putting a number on what a company or investment is actually worth, and it is one of the most commonly tested topics in finance interviews, from "walk me through a DCF" to "how would you value this company." This deck introduces the core methods, discounted cash flow, comparable companies, and the multiples analysts lean on, in plain language first, then in the more technical form interviewers expect. No prior valuation experience assumed, just a willingness to think in terms of cash flow and comparison.

cards.q: What does it actually mean to say a company is worth $400 million, and how can two serious buyers look at the same business and land on very different numbers?
cards.takeaway: A company is worth the future cash it produces, so buyers differ whenever their forecasts differ.
cards.a: Valuing a company means estimating what someone should rationally pay today for the right to everything the business earns from here on. Two buyers can both be rigorous and still disagree, because that estimate rests on forecasts nobody can verify: how fast the business grows, how risky its cash flows feel, and what each buyer could do with the company once they own it. A rival in the same industry who can strip out duplicate warehouses honestly sees more value than a passive investor who changes nothing. That is why this work produces a defensible range, not a fact.

cards.q: A first-year tells you Calder Foods “trades at 9 times.” Nine times what, and what is a multiple actually telling you?
cards.takeaway: A multiple is a price per dollar of annual profit, which lets you compare companies of any size.
cards.a: A multiple is just a ratio: what a company is valued at, divided by some measure of what it produces in a year, usually a profit figure. If Calder is valued at $900 million and earns $100 million of operating profit a year, that is 9 times, meaning a buyer is paying nine dollars for every dollar of annual profit. Dividing by profit strips size out of the comparison, so a $900 million company and a $4.5 billion one can sit in the same table. A higher multiple usually means the market expects faster growth or sees less risk.

cards.q: Marlstone Capital is evaluating a buyout of Ferrow Retail and wants to know the total price tag versus what's left for shareholders. What's the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
cards.takeaway: Enterprise value is the whole business; equity value is just the shareholders' slice.
cards.a: Enterprise value represents the value of the whole business — what Marlstone would need to pay to acquire Ferrow outright, including taking on its debt and stripping out its cash. Equity value is just the value belonging to shareholders (what market cap represents). The bridge between them: enterprise value = equity value + debt − cash.

cards.q: A client asks why your team is quoting Halsey Aerospace's value on an EV/EBITDA basis instead of just comparing share prices. What does EV/EBITDA measure, and why use enterprise value instead of market cap?
cards.takeaway: EV/EBITDA compares total company value to operating earnings, ignoring how the company is financed.
cards.a: Enterprise value is used instead of market cap because it also accounts for debt and cash, making it possible to compare companies fairly even when they have very different capital structures: market cap alone ignores how much of the business is funded by debt. EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) strips out financing and accounting choices, so you're comparing pure operating performance, which is exactly why the multiple travels well across a set of comps.

cards.q: What is a P/E ratio, and what does a high P/E typically signal to a banker sizing up a target?
cards.takeaway: P/E shows how much investors pay today for each dollar the company currently earns.
cards.a: The price-to-earnings ratio divides a company's share price by its earnings per share. A high P/E usually signals that the market expects strong future earnings growth, since investors are willing to pay more today for the same current profit; it can also simply mean the target is overvalued relative to its fundamentals, so P/E alone doesn't tell you which story is true.

cards.q: Your associate drops a metric you've never used, EV/EBIT, into the comps tab and asks whether the numerator should be enterprise value or share price. How do you decide which metrics pair with which?
cards.takeaway: Match the top of the ratio to whoever owns the bottom of it, before interest or after.
cards.a: Ask who has a claim on the number in the denominator. Revenue, EBITDA and EBIT are all measured before interest is paid, so lenders and shareholders both still have a claim on them, and the numerator has to be enterprise value, the value of the whole business. Net income and earnings per share are what is left after lenders are paid, so they belong to shareholders alone and pair with equity value or share price. Market cap over EBITDA quietly compares a shareholder claim with a whole-company profit, and interviewers use exactly that mismatch to see whether you understand the bridge.

cards.q: You're building a comps page where one company is loaded with debt and another has none. Why lead with EV/EBITDA rather than P/E, and when would you still want the P/E column on the page?
cards.takeaway: EV/EBITDA compares businesses whatever their debt load, P/E compares what shareholders keep after it.
cards.a: EV/EBITDA takes debt out of both halves of the ratio, so a heavily borrowed company and a debt-free one can be judged on operating performance alone, which is why it usually leads an industrials or consumer comps page. P/E is not useless, though: it reflects interest and taxes, which is what an actual public shareholder experiences, and it is the default where borrowing is part of the operating model rather than a financing choice, such as banks and insurers, where EBITDA barely means anything. Most teams show both and are ready to explain the gap between them.

cards.q: What is comparable company analysis (“comps”), and why do bankers reach for it before running a full DCF?
cards.takeaway: Comps value a company by comparing it to similar public companies' current pricing.
cards.a: Instead of building a value from scratch like a DCF does, comps anchor to what the market is already paying for similar businesses, typically using a ratio like EV/EBITDA or P/E, then apply that same multiple to the company being valued. It's a relative valuation method: quicker to turn around for a pitch book than a DCF, and it reflects real market sentiment, for better or worse.

cards.q: Your VP sends back the Northbay Logistics comps set saying it “isn't clean.” What actually makes a company comparable, and what quietly disqualifies one?
cards.takeaway: Good comps share a business model, size and growth profile, not just an industry label.
cards.a: Start with what the company really does, its products, its customers and how it earns money, because two firms filed under the same industry code can run completely different businesses. Then screen on size, growth rate and profit margins, since a company growing twenty percent a year will always command a higher multiple than one growing two percent, and mixing the two widens the range until it says nothing. Geography and regulation matter for the same reason. Five or six names you can defend line by line beat fifteen you cannot when the client starts pushing.

cards.q: Your VP asks why the precedent transaction multiples you pulled for the Bramwell & Co. pitch are running higher than the trading comps for the same sector. What is precedent transactions analysis, and how does it differ from comps?
cards.takeaway: Precedent transactions value a company using prices actually paid in past M&A deals.
cards.a: Unlike comps, which look at how similar companies trade on public markets day-to-day, this method looks at what acquirers have actually paid to buy similar businesses outright. Because acquisitions usually include a control premium (extra paid to gain control of the company), precedent transaction multiples tend to run higher than trading comps — which is exactly the gap your VP is asking about.

cards.q: Your VP asks you to talk her through the DCF tab before tomorrow's client call: why discount every year of projected free cash flow back to today instead of just adding the numbers up? What is a DCF actually doing?
cards.takeaway: A DCF says a company is worth all the cash it will ever generate, brought back to today's dollars.
cards.a: You forecast the company's free cash flow for the next several years, then discount each year back to present value using a discount rate (usually WACC), since a dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today: it carries risk, and that same dollar could be earning a return elsewhere. Add those discounted years together, plus a terminal value for everything beyond the forecast window, and that sum is what lands in the model as today's value.

cards.q: Your MD asks you to sanity-check the WACC on the Ferrow Retail LBO model before the 9am call. What is WACC actually representing, and why does it belong in the discount rate?
cards.takeaway: WACC is the blended cost of a company's money, part debt, part equity.
cards.a: Every company funds itself with some mix of debt and equity, and each has a cost: debt costs interest (though it's tax-deductible, making it effectively cheaper than its stated rate), equity costs the return shareholders expect. WACC blends those two costs, weighted by how much of each the company actually uses. It's used as the discount rate in the model because it represents the minimum return Ferrow's investments need to clear to be worth funding — if the WACC input is off, everything downstream is off with it.

cards.q: An analyst discounted levered free cash flow at WACC and the VP called the output nonsense. Which cash flow pairs with which discount rate, and what does each one land you on?
cards.takeaway: Unlevered cash flow at WACC gives enterprise value, levered cash flow at cost of equity gives equity value.
cards.a: Unlevered free cash flow is the cash the business throws off before any interest is paid, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders together, and the matching rate is WACC, the blended cost of both. Discount it and you get enterprise value, then subtract net debt to reach equity value. Levered free cash flow is what remains after interest and debt repayments, so it belongs to shareholders alone and gets discounted at the cost of equity, landing directly on equity value. Discounting levered cash flow at WACC counts the benefit of debt twice, which is why the VP handed it straight back.

cards.q: What is “terminal value” in a DCF, and why does it get so much scrutiny in a model review?
cards.takeaway: Terminal value covers everything a business earns after the forecast period ends.
cards.a: A DCF only forecasts explicitly for about 5–10 years, but the company is assumed to keep operating indefinitely beyond that. Terminal value estimates all of that remaining future in one lump sum, discounted back to today just like any other cash flow. It's typically the single largest piece of a DCF's total value — which is exactly why an MD will push hard on the assumptions behind it, a long-run growth rate or an exit multiple, before a number goes in front of a client.

cards.q: What are the two ways to calculate terminal value, and how do you check that they agree with each other?
cards.takeaway: Grow the last cash flow forever, or assume you sell the business at a market multiple.
cards.a: The perpetuity growth method assumes the final forecast year's free cash flow keeps growing at a modest constant rate forever, usually somewhere near long-run inflation or economy-wide growth, and capitalises it at the discount rate less that growth rate. The exit multiple method instead assumes the business is sold at the end of the forecast for a multiple of its final-year EBITDA, normally taken from the comps set. Teams usually run one as the primary and back into the other as a check: if a two percent growth rate implies a 25 times exit multiple, one of the two assumptions is wrong.

cards.q: Before the Corrigan Foods model goes into the deck your associate asks you to “add the grid.” What is a sensitivity table, and which two inputs almost always sit on its axes?
cards.takeaway: A sensitivity table shows how far the answer moves when the two shakiest assumptions move.
cards.a: A sensitivity table re-runs the whole DCF across a grid of values for two inputs and prints the resulting per-share values in a matrix. The two axes are nearly always the discount rate and whichever terminal value assumption you used, the long-run growth rate or the exit multiple, because those are the inputs the answer moves most on and the ones a client will challenge first. Watching the value swing from forty-seven dollars to seventy-seven across a perfectly plausible grid tells you far more than the base case alone, and that spread is what becomes the DCF bar on the valuation page.

cards.q: In the elevator an MD asks you to rank a DCF, trading comps and precedent transactions from highest value to lowest. What do you say, and what do you refuse to commit to?
cards.takeaway: Precedents normally sit above comps because of the control premium, and a DCF can land anywhere.
cards.a: Trading comps and precedent transactions both price a company off other companies, but comps use daily market prices for small stakes while precedents use prices paid for whole companies, which carry a control premium, so precedents sit above comps as a rule. The DCF is the one you should not commit to: it is built from your own forecasts rather than the market's, so it can land above or below either, though in practice it often comes in high because management projections are optimistic. Naming the reliable ordering and flagging the DCF as assumption-driven is the answer that survives a follow-up.

cards.q: Before the Corrigan Foods pitch book goes to print, your MD asks why the valuation page shows a range instead of one clean number. Why does a valuation usually get presented as a range (a “football field”) rather than a single number?
cards.takeaway: A valuation range, not one number, because every method rests on assumptions that can shift.
cards.a: Growth rates, discount rates, which comps are truly comparable: small changes in any of these assumptions can shift the output meaningfully. Presenting a range across multiple methods (DCF, comps, precedent transactions) is more honest about that uncertainty than putting one falsely precise number in front of a client.

cards.q: An interviewer says Ferrow Retail raises $200 million of new debt and leaves every dollar of it sitting in the bank. What happens to its enterprise value, and what happens to its equity value?
cards.takeaway: Neither one moves, because the new debt and the new cash cancel inside the bridge.
cards.a: Enterprise value is equity value plus debt minus cash, so raising two hundred million adds two hundred million to the debt line and exactly the same amount to the cash line, and the two offset: enterprise value is unchanged. Equity value does not move either, since shareholders own the same operating business plus a pile of cash the company also owes. The point being tested is that enterprise value measures the operating business itself, so a pure financing decision cannot create or destroy it. The honest nuance to add is that if investors expect the cash to be wasted, the share price can still fall.

cards.q: A junior hands you a DCF whose output lands suspiciously close to the number the client was hoping for. Where does a DCF usually get pushed, and what do you check first?
cards.takeaway: Check what share of value sits in terminal value, then the growth rate and the margin ramp.
cards.a: The three easiest places to bend a DCF are the long-run growth rate, the exit multiple and the final-year operating margin, because each is a single cell that moves the answer a lot and is hard to disprove. Start with how much of the total value sits in terminal value: much above roughly eighty percent and the forecast years are barely doing any work, so the model is really one assumption wearing a spreadsheet. Then check that the growth rate is not above long-run economic growth, which would have the company eventually swallowing the economy, and that margin expansion has a reason behind it rather than a straight line.

name: Comparable Companies
description: Building a comps set, choosing the multiples, and reading the answer they give.
intro: Trading comparables are the valuation method analysts actually run most days, and the one interviewers dig into once you have named the three methods. This deck takes you through the process: choosing the peer group, deciding which multiples matter and why, calculating enterprise value properly, adjusting for the things that make one company's numbers look unlike another's, and reading the range you end up with. It also covers the traps, from mixing enterprise and equity metrics to trusting a multiple without knowing what drives it.

cards.q: What is comparable companies analysis, and what question is it actually answering?
cards.takeaway: Comps value a company by asking what the market pays for similar businesses today.
cards.a: Comparable companies analysis, or trading comps, values a company by looking at how the stock market prices similar listed companies. You take a set of peers, work out what multiple of earnings or EBITDA each trades at, and apply that range to your company's own numbers. The question it answers is not what the company is worth in some absolute sense but what investors would pay for it today, given what they pay for its rivals. That makes it a market-based method, quick and grounded in real prices, but only as good as the peer group and the day you run it.

cards.q: How do you choose the peer group, and why is it the step that matters most?
cards.takeaway: Same industry, similar size, similar growth and margins; the multiple only means something if the peers really are alike.
cards.a: Start with companies in the same business, selling similar products to similar customers. Then narrow by size, geography, growth rate and margin, because a company growing at 20% a year will trade at a higher multiple than one growing at 3% even if they make the same thing. Five to ten names is typical. The peer group matters most because every number that follows is inherited from it: if you put a fast-growing US software company in the set for a slow UK one, your valuation will be wrong before you calculate anything. Interviewers often ask which peers you would pick and why, not how to do the maths.

cards.q: What is enterprise value, and how is it different from market capitalisation?
cards.takeaway: Market cap is the value of the equity; enterprise value is the value of the whole business, debt included, cash netted off.
cards.a: Market capitalisation is the share price times the number of shares: what the equity is worth. Enterprise value adds net debt, plus minority interests and preferred stock if there are any, and subtracts cash. It is the price of the entire operating business, regardless of who funded it. If you bought all of Bramwell & Co.'s shares for £500m and took on its £200m of debt, the business cost you £700m, minus whatever cash was in the bank. Enterprise value is what you compare across companies with different amounts of debt, because it does not change when a company borrows to buy back shares.

cards.q: Why must enterprise value multiples use metrics before interest, and equity multiples use metrics after it?
cards.takeaway: Match the numerator to the denominator: whole-business value goes over whole-business profit, equity value over equity profit.
cards.a: EBITDA and EBIT are earned by the business before lenders take their interest, so they belong to both debt and equity holders. Enterprise value is the value belonging to both, so EV/EBITDA lines up. Net income is what is left after interest, so it belongs only to shareholders, and market cap is the value of what shareholders own, so P/E lines up. Cross them and the ratio is meaningless: EV over net income compares a whole-business value with a shareholders-only profit, and a company with more debt would look cheaper for no real reason. Mixing them is the most common comps mistake and a standard interview trap.

cards.q: What is EV/EBITDA, and why is it the multiple bankers reach for first?
cards.takeaway: It compares whole-business value with cash operating profit, so it works across companies with different debt, tax and depreciation.
cards.a: EV/EBITDA is enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Because EBITDA sits above interest, it ignores how the company is financed; because it sits above tax, it ignores differences in tax rates and jurisdictions; because it sits above depreciation, it ignores differences in how old the assets are and how they are accounted for. That makes it the fairest comparison across a peer group, and usable even when a company makes an accounting loss. Its weakness is the same as its strength: it ignores capital spending, so a business that has to reinvest heavily looks better than it is.

cards.q: When would you use P/E, EV/Sales, or EV/EBIT instead of EV/EBITDA?
cards.takeaway: P/E for stable, profitable companies where equity investors think in earnings; EV/Sales when there are no profits; EV/EBIT when capital intensity differs.
cards.a: P/E is the multiple equity investors and the financial press use, and it works well for mature, profitable companies with similar capital structures, like banks, where EBITDA is meaningless anyway. EV/Sales is the fallback for companies with no profits yet, like early-stage tech or a turnaround, though it says nothing about whether the sales will ever make money. EV/EBIT is better than EV/EBITDA when peers differ in how much they spend on assets, because depreciation is a real cost of running a capital-heavy business. Some industries have their own: price per subscriber, EV per bed, EV per tonne of capacity.

cards.q: What does LTM mean, and why do analysts show both LTM and forward multiples?
cards.takeaway: LTM is the last twelve months of actual results; forward multiples use next year's forecasts, which is what buyers actually pay for.
cards.a: LTM, last twelve months, means the four most recent quarters added together, so the figure is actual and up to date rather than tied to a financial year end. Forward multiples divide today's value by forecast earnings for the next year or two, usually the average of analysts' estimates. Investors pay for the future, so forward multiples are usually the more relevant, especially for fast-growing companies whose LTM numbers understate them. Showing both makes the growth visible: a company at 20x LTM and 14x forward is expected to grow earnings by about 40%.

cards.q: What does it mean to normalise or adjust a company's earnings before running comps?
cards.takeaway: Strip out one-off items so the multiple reflects what the business earns in a normal year.
cards.a: Reported earnings often include things that will not repeat: a restructuring charge, a gain on selling a building, litigation costs, an impairment. If Calder Foods reported EBITDA of £50m including a £15m one-off legal settlement, its underlying earning power is £65m, and applying a peer multiple to £50m would undervalue it. Normalising means removing those items so every company in the set is compared on a recurring basis. Companies publish their own adjusted figures, but they tend to be generous about what counts as one-off, so analysts form their own view.

cards.q: You have a peer range of 8x to 12x EV/EBITDA. How do you decide where in the range your company sits?
cards.takeaway: Compare growth, margins, scale and risk against the peers; better than the median means above the median.
cards.a: The range is the starting point, not the answer. Line your company up against the peers on the things that drive multiples: revenue growth, margins, size, market position and risk. If it is growing faster with better margins than the median peer, it deserves a multiple toward the top of the range; if it is smaller, slower or riskier, toward the bottom. Then apply a narrower band, say 9x to 11x, to the company's EBITDA to get an enterprise value range, and subtract net debt to get equity value. Interviewers care about this reasoning far more than the arithmetic.

cards.q: Why do comps and a DCF often give different answers, and which do you trust?
cards.takeaway: Comps say what the market pays now; a DCF says what the cash flows are worth; the gap is information, not an error.
cards.a: A DCF values the company from its own forecast cash flows and a discount rate, so it reflects your assumptions and is indifferent to market mood. Comps reflect what investors are actually paying today, including whatever optimism or fear is in the market. When the DCF comes in well above comps, either your forecasts are generous or the sector is out of favour; when it comes in below, the reverse. Neither is simply right. Bankers show both, usually as a football field chart, and use the overlap as the range. Explaining the difference is the mark of understanding both.

cards.q: What is the difference between trading comps and precedent transactions?
cards.takeaway: Trading comps use stock-market prices for similar companies; precedents use prices paid in actual takeovers, which include a control premium.
cards.a: Trading comparables look at how similar listed companies are priced by the market day to day, which is the value of a minority stake. Precedent transactions look at what acquirers paid to buy whole companies in past deals. Buyers pay a premium for control, typically 20% to 40% over the share price, because they can change how the business is run and capture synergies. So precedents give higher multiples than trading comps, and are the right benchmark when valuing a company for sale, while trading comps are the benchmark for where the shares should trade.

cards.q: Why can a company trade at a lower multiple than its peers without being cheap?
cards.takeaway: A low multiple usually reflects lower growth, higher risk, worse governance or a reason the market knows and you do not yet.
cards.a: A multiple is a price per unit of earnings, and the market lowers it when it expects those earnings to grow more slowly, to be more volatile, or to be less trustworthy. Northbay Logistics at 6x when peers are at 9x might have a customer that provides half its revenue, a founder who controls the board, a pension deficit, or a history of missed guidance. Sometimes the discount really is a mispricing, which is what value investors hunt for, but the first assumption should be that the market has a reason. Saying that in an interview shows judgement rather than a calculator.

cards.q: How do you handle a company in the peer set that has a very different financial year or reports in another currency?
cards.takeaway: Calendarise the numbers to the same twelve months and convert at a consistent exchange rate before comparing.
cards.a: If one peer's year ends in March and another's in December, their annual figures cover different periods and different economic conditions, so you calendarise: use quarterly figures to rebuild each company's earnings over the same twelve months. If a peer reports in dollars and your company in pounds, convert the earnings and the market data at consistent rates, usually the average rate for the period for income statement items and the spot rate for balance sheet items. Multiples themselves are currency-free, since numerator and denominator are in the same currency, but the inputs must be built consistently.

cards.q: Talbrook Capital asks for a quick comps valuation of Bramwell & Co. Peers trade at 10x EBITDA. Bramwell has EBITDA of £80m, debt of £300m, cash of £50m and 100m shares. What is the share price implied?
cards.takeaway: Multiply to get enterprise value, subtract net debt to get equity value, divide by shares: £5.50.
cards.a: Enterprise value is 10 times £80m, which is £800m. Net debt is £300m of debt minus £50m of cash, which is £250m. Equity value is £800m minus £250m, which is £550m. Divided by 100 million shares, that is £5.50 a share. The interviewer is checking that you know to subtract net debt rather than gross debt, and that you subtract it at all: applying 10x and dividing straight by shares would give £8.00, which is the classic error. If Bramwell had preferred stock or a minority interest, those would come off too.

cards.q: What is a football field chart, and what is it for?
cards.takeaway: One chart showing the valuation range from every method side by side, so the reader sees where they agree.
cards.a: A football field is a horizontal bar chart with one bar per valuation method: trading comps, precedent transactions, DCF, sometimes an LBO analysis and the 52-week share price range. Each bar runs from the low end of that method's range to the high end. Laid side by side, the bars show where the methods overlap, which is usually taken as the most defensible valuation range, and where one method is an outlier, which prompts a question about why. It is the last page of most valuation sections in a pitch book and the picture a managing director looks at first.

cards.q: An interviewer says: walk me through how you would value Ferrow Retail using comps. Give the answer in order.
cards.takeaway: Peers, metrics, multiples, adjustments, range, then equity value per share, with one sentence on the limits.
cards.a: First, choose five to ten listed retailers similar in size, format, geography and growth. Second, gather each one's enterprise value and equity value, and their LTM and forward EBITDA, EBIT and net income, normalised for one-offs. Third, calculate EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT and P/E for each, and look at the median and the range. Fourth, judge where Ferrow sits in that range on growth, margins and risk. Fifth, apply the chosen multiples to Ferrow's own numbers for an enterprise value range, subtract net debt, and divide by shares for a price per share. Finish by noting that comps reflect today's market and should be cross-checked against a DCF and precedents.

name: Debt, Credit & Leverage
description: How companies borrow, what lenders check, and what leverage really costs.
intro: Almost every company you will ever look at borrows money, and understanding why is what separates a surface read of a balance sheet from a real one. This deck takes credit from both sides at once, the company doing the borrowing and the lender deciding whether to hand the money over. You will cover why a profitable business chooses to take on debt, what a revolver or a term loan actually is, how leverage and coverage ratios get read, and what happens when the money runs out. Every term is defined from scratch, so you do not need to have seen a loan agreement or a bankruptcy before.

cards.q: Calder Foods is profitable, sitting on cash, and carries no debt at all. Its CFO is about to sign $200 million of loans anyway. Why would a healthy company deliberately borrow money?
cards.takeaway: Debt costs less than equity and hands over no ownership, so it can lift the returns owners earn.
cards.a: Lenders get paid before shareholders and often hold a claim on specific assets, so they take less risk and accept a lower return than equity investors demand. Debt also doesn’t give away ownership: if Calder borrows $200 million and earns more on that money than the interest costs, the extra profit belongs entirely to the existing shareholders. That amplifying effect is why even cash-rich companies keep some debt on the balance sheet, and it is the same logic sitting underneath every leveraged buyout you will ever model.

cards.q: An associate tells you debt is cheaper than the interest rate suggests because of the tax shield. Walk through what she means for a company paying $10 million of interest at a 25% tax rate.
cards.takeaway: Interest is deducted before tax is calculated, so borrowing shrinks the tax bill and the real cost of debt.
cards.a: Interest expense is subtracted from profit before the tax charge is worked out, so borrowing lowers taxable income. On $10 million of interest at a 25% tax rate the company keeps $2.5 million it would otherwise have paid in tax, meaning the interest really costs $7.5 million. A 6% loan is closer to 4.5% in cash terms, which is the shorthand after-tax cost equals rate times one minus the tax rate. Equity has no equivalent break, since dividends come out of already-taxed profit, and that asymmetry is a big reason capital structures contain debt at all.

cards.q: What is the difference between a revolver, a term loan, and a bond?
cards.takeaway: Revolvers cover short-term swings, term loans fund a set need, bonds raise long money from investors.
cards.a: A revolving credit facility, or revolver, is a pre-agreed limit the company can draw on, repay, and draw again, normally used to smooth seasonal swings in working capital and mostly left undrawn as a safety net. A term loan is a fixed amount lent by a bank or a syndicate of banks for a set period, usually at a floating rate, often repaid partly in instalments and monitored closely. A bond is borrowed from many investors at once in the capital markets, typically longer-dated, lightly monitored, and repaid in a single lump at maturity.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics is negotiating two facilities at once, one secured on its truck fleet and one unsecured. What does collateral actually do for the lender, and how does it show up in the pricing?
cards.takeaway: Collateral gives a lender named assets to seize first, which raises its recovery and cuts the rate charged.
cards.a: A secured loan is backed by specific assets pledged to the lender, here Northbay’s trucks and depots. If the company stops paying, the secured lender can take and sell those assets ahead of everyone else, so it expects to get far more of its money back in a bad outcome. An unsecured lender has only a general claim on whatever is left. Because expected recovery is higher, secured debt prices meaningfully tighter, which is why companies pledge assets even though doing so limits what they can later sell or borrow against.

cards.q: Calder Foods files for bankruptcy with $600 million of cash to distribute against $900 million of claims. In what order does that money go out, and who is likely to end up with nothing?
cards.takeaway: Cash flows down a strict seniority ladder and equity is paid only once every creditor is made whole.
cards.a: Recoveries follow a waterfall: the costs of running the process first, then secured lenders up to the value of their collateral, then senior unsecured bonds, then subordinated or junior debt, then preferred shares, and common equity last. Each tier must be paid in full before the next one receives anything at all. With $600 million against $900 million of claims the money runs dry partway down, so the senior unsecured lenders take a partial recovery and everything below them is wiped out. That ranking is precisely why lenders negotiate so hard over where in the structure they sit.

cards.q: What is the difference between amortising debt and a bullet maturity, and why does the choice matter for a company’s cash flow?
cards.takeaway: Amortising debt repays principal along the way, a bullet repays the whole thing on the final day.
cards.a: Amortising debt requires the borrower to repay slices of the principal on a schedule, say 5% or 10% a year, so the balance shrinks steadily and the lender’s exposure falls with it. A bullet pays interest only until the last day, when the entire principal comes due at once. Amortising is harder on year-to-year cash flow but leaves little to deal with at the end. Bullets keep cash free for the business and are standard for bonds, at the cost of one very large obligation the company will almost certainly need to refinance.

cards.q: An MD glances at your page and says Northbay is four and a half turns levered. What is he measuring, and what does that number actually tell you about the company?
cards.takeaway: Debt divided by EBITDA says how many years of operating earnings it would take to repay the debt.
cards.a: He means the leverage ratio, total debt divided by EBITDA, which is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and serves as a rough proxy for the cash a business throws off before financing costs. At 4.5x, Northbay owes about four and a half years of that figure. Bankers say turns because each turn is one multiple of EBITDA. Below roughly 2x is usually called conservative and above 6x aggressive, but the safe level depends heavily on the industry, since a utility with contracted revenue can carry far more than a cyclical manufacturer.

cards.q: Two companies both sit at 5x debt to EBITDA, but your credit analyst is relaxed about one and worried about the other. What does an interest coverage ratio tell you that the leverage ratio does not?
cards.takeaway: Coverage asks whether this year’s earnings can pay this year’s interest, not how big the debt pile is.
cards.a: Interest coverage is EBITDA divided by annual interest expense, and it answers a different question: can the company actually meet what it owes right now? Leverage measures the size of the debt, but two borrowers with identical leverage can be paying very different rates. One borrowing at 4% might cover its interest five times over, while one paying 11% covers it barely twice, and the second is far closer to trouble. Anything under about 2x makes lenders uneasy, because a single weak quarter can leave the company unable to make a payment.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail’s loan caps leverage at 4.0x, tested every quarter, and this quarter it comes in at 4.2x. What kind of covenant is that, and what actually happens next?
cards.takeaway: Maintenance covenants are tested on a schedule and a breach hands lenders the right to call the loan.
cards.a: That is a maintenance covenant, a test the borrower has to pass on a fixed schedule whether or not it does anything at all. An incurrence covenant, more common in bonds, only bites when the company takes an action such as raising new debt or paying a dividend. Breaching a maintenance covenant is an event of default, and in principle the lenders can accelerate, meaning demand the entire loan back immediately. In practice they usually negotiate a waiver or amendment in exchange for a fee, a higher margin, or tighter terms, because pushing a viable business into bankruptcy rarely maximises their recovery.

cards.q: What is the difference between fixed-rate and floating-rate debt, and who is carrying the interest rate risk in each one?
cards.takeaway: Fixed debt locks the borrower’s cost and leaves the lender exposed, floating debt does the reverse.
cards.a: A fixed-rate loan or bond pays the same coupon for its whole life, so the borrower knows its interest bill years ahead and the lender absorbs the risk that market rates move against it. Floating-rate debt, the norm for bank loans, resets periodically at a benchmark rate plus a fixed margin, so the borrower’s cost rises and falls with the market while the lender’s return keeps pace. Floating borrowers are therefore exposed to rate rises, which is why heavily indebted companies often buy hedges that cap how far that cost can climb.

cards.q: You are drafting a credit memo and your VP says the ratios are the easy part. Beyond leverage and coverage, what does a credit analyst actually look at before agreeing to lend?
cards.takeaway: Ratios are one snapshot, real credit work is about how durable the cash flow looks under stress.
cards.a: An analyst wants to know how reliable the cash flow is, so they test how cyclical the industry is, how concentrated the customer base is, whether contracts are long-dated or repriced every year, and how much of the cost base is fixed and therefore cannot be cut in a downturn. They look hard at liquidity, meaning cash on hand plus whatever is undrawn on the revolver, because companies fail when they run out of cash rather than when a ratio slips. They also weigh asset quality, the maturity profile, and whether the owners would put fresh equity in if things went wrong.

cards.q: Northbay has comfortable leverage and pays its interest easily, but $700 million of its $900 million of debt matures in a single year. Why does your credit analyst still call that a risky structure?
cards.takeaway: Debt bunched into one year has to be refinanced whether or not markets are open when it comes due.
cards.a: Almost no company repays large debt out of its own pocket, it refinances, borrowing new money to retire the old. That works right up until the year the debt falls due happens to be a year when credit markets are shut, the rating has slipped, or rates have doubled. A maturity wall, meaning a large block of debt maturing in one narrow window, concentrates that risk on a single date instead of spreading it out. Treasurers manage it by staggering maturities and refinancing early, often a year or two ahead, and lenders read an unaddressed wall as a warning sign.

cards.q: Calder Foods is one notch inside investment grade, and a deal it is considering would push it into high yield. Beyond a higher coupon, what actually changes for the company if it crosses that line?
cards.takeaway: Dropping to high yield costs more, restricts more, and changes who is willing to hold the debt.
cards.a: The higher coupon is the obvious cost, often a few percentage points. Less obvious is that high-yield bonds come with far more restrictive documentation, limiting extra borrowing, dividends, asset sales and acquisitions, plus call protection that makes repaying early expensive. The investor base changes too, from insurers and index funds that are only permitted to hold investment grade towards credit funds pricing each deal on its own merits, so demand is thinner and swings with sentiment. That is why some companies will shrink a deal, fund it with equity, or walk away entirely to protect the rating.

cards.q: A company misses an interest payment. Walk me conceptually through what happens next, and what people mean when they distinguish a restructuring from a Chapter 11 filing.
cards.takeaway: Default just breaks the contract, then the company and its creditors either negotiate a fix or go to court.
cards.a: A default is simply a breach of the debt agreement, a missed payment or a broken covenant, and it usually opens a short grace period rather than triggering immediate seizure. From there the company and its creditors can restructure out of court, agreeing to extend maturities, cut the coupon, or swap debt for equity, which is quicker and cheaper but needs nearly everyone to consent. If they cannot agree, Chapter 11 puts the company under court protection, where an automatic stay pauses collection while a plan is negotiated, and the same seniority waterfall decides who takes losses and who ends up owning the business.

cards.q: Rates have risen sharply since Ferrow Retail last financed itself. Your MD asks how that changes what the company should be doing about its debt. Where do you start?
cards.takeaway: Higher rates hit floating debt immediately and every maturity that has to be refinanced later.
cards.a: Start with whatever is already floating, because that cost repriced the moment rates moved and it feeds straight into interest coverage. Then look at the maturity profile, since anything coming due gets refinanced at today’s rates rather than the ones it was issued at, so a bond struck at 4% can roll into 8% and double the interest bill overnight. Higher rates also raise the bar for investment, so projects that cleared a low hurdle rate no longer do. Companies often respond by borrowing less, paying debt down, hedging, or shortening maturities if they expect rates to fall back.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail reports record EBITDA and is still comfortably inside every covenant, yet it runs out of money by December. Your MD asks how that is possible. How do you answer?
cards.takeaway: EBITDA is not cash, and companies fail when the cash runs out rather than when earnings look weak.
cards.a: EBITDA deliberately ignores the things that actually drain cash: interest, tax, capital spending, and working capital. A retailer growing quickly has to buy inventory and pay suppliers long before customers pay it, so reported profit climbs while the bank balance falls. Add an amortisation payment, a revolver the bank declines to renew, or a maturity landing in a closed market, and a genuinely profitable business can miss a payment. That gap between accounting earnings and cash actually available is the most useful thing to carry out of credit work, and it is why analysts build all the way down to free cash flow instead of stopping at EBITDA.
