name: Capital Structure & Leverage
description: Debt versus equity, the cost of each, WACC, and why more leverage is not simply more risk.
intro: Every company has to decide how to fund itself, with money from lenders or money from owners, and the mix shapes everything from its cost of capital to whether it survives a downturn. This deck explains the choice: why debt is cheaper than equity, why it stops being cheaper past a point, what WACC is and how it is used, what the Modigliani-Miller idea says and why it matters even though its assumptions are unrealistic, and how a company actually settles on its structure. It connects the credit deck to the valuation and LBO decks, and it answers the interview question that follows any DCF: what discount rate, and why.

cards.q: What is capital structure?
cards.takeaway: The mix of debt and equity a company uses to fund its assets.
cards.a: Capital structure is how a company pays for what it owns: some money borrowed from lenders, which is debt, and some put in by owners or retained from profits, which is equity. Bramwell & Co. with £300m of loans and £700m of shareholders' equity has a capital structure of 30% debt, 70% equity. The mix determines who gets paid first, how much the company must pay out regardless of how it is trading, and what return each provider of money expects. Changing it, by borrowing to buy back shares or issuing shares to repay debt, changes the risk and the value of the company even if the business itself is untouched.

cards.q: Why is debt cheaper than equity?
cards.takeaway: Lenders get paid first and get paid a fixed amount, so they take less risk and demand less return; interest is also tax-deductible.
cards.a: A lender has a contract: interest on set dates, principal back at maturity, and first claim on the assets if the company fails. A shareholder has none of that; she gets whatever is left after everyone else, if anything. Less risk means a lower required return, so debt at 6% is normal when equity investors want 10% or more. On top of that, interest is deducted before corporation tax is calculated, so at a 25% tax rate a 6% loan really costs the company 4.5%. Dividends are paid from taxed profit and get no such relief. Cheaper and tax-advantaged is why companies borrow at all.

cards.q: If debt is cheaper, why not fund the company entirely with debt?
cards.takeaway: Because more debt makes both the debt and the equity riskier, and past a point the rising cost of distress outweighs the tax saving.
cards.a: As a company borrows more, its interest bill rises relative to its profits, and a bad year that was once uncomfortable becomes fatal. Lenders see that and charge more for each additional loan, and shareholders, who now sit behind a bigger pile of claims, demand a higher return too. There are also the costs of financial distress: customers and suppliers pull back from a company that might fail, good staff leave, and management spends its time on the bank rather than the business. At some level of debt those costs grow faster than the tax benefit, and the overall cost of capital starts rising again. That level is the optimal structure.

cards.q: What is the cost of equity, and how is it usually estimated?
cards.takeaway: The return shareholders require for the risk they take, typically estimated with the capital asset pricing model.
cards.a: The cost of equity is the return investors need to be persuaded to hold the company's shares rather than something safer. It is not a cash cost the company pays, like interest, but it is real: if the company earns less than it, the shares fall. The standard estimate is the CAPM: the risk-free rate, usually a government bond yield, plus the company's beta times the equity risk premium. Beta measures how much the shares move with the market; a beta of 1.2 means 20% more volatile than average. With a 4% risk-free rate, a beta of 1.2 and a 5% premium, the cost of equity is 10%.

cards.q: What is the cost of debt, and why is it taken after tax?
cards.takeaway: The interest rate the company would pay to borrow today, reduced by the tax relief on interest.
cards.a: The cost of debt is the rate at which the company could raise new borrowing now, not the rate on loans it took out years ago. It can be read from the yield on its traded bonds, or estimated as the risk-free rate plus the credit spread appropriate to its rating. Because interest is deductible, the effective cost is the rate times one minus the tax rate: a 6% pre-tax cost at 25% tax is 4.5% after tax. That after-tax figure is what goes into WACC, since the tax saving is a real cash benefit of borrowing that the equity does not get.

cards.q: What is WACC, and what is it used for?
cards.takeaway: The weighted average cost of capital: the blended return the company must earn on its assets to satisfy both lenders and shareholders, and the discount rate in a DCF.
cards.a: WACC combines the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by how much of each the company uses, measured at market values. If Bramwell is 30% debt at 4.5% after tax and 70% equity at 10%, WACC is 0.3 times 4.5 plus 0.7 times 10, which is 8.35%. It is the minimum return the company's investments must earn to create value, so it is the hurdle rate for projects and the discount rate for the company's free cash flows in a DCF. It is the single number an interviewer is most likely to ask you to build from scratch.

cards.q: Why does WACC use market values of debt and equity rather than book values?
cards.takeaway: Investors' required returns are on what their claims are worth today, not on what the accounts recorded years ago.
cards.a: The weights in WACC represent how much of the company's value each investor group owns, and the return they require is a percentage of that value. A company whose shares have risen fivefold since it listed has an equity book value far below its market value; using the book figure would understate the equity weight and the resulting WACC. Debt is usually close to book value unless the bonds trade at a large discount, so the practical difference is on the equity side. For a private company with no market value, analysts estimate it from comparable companies or use a target structure.

cards.q: What does the Modigliani-Miller theorem say, and why is it useful if its assumptions are unrealistic?
cards.takeaway: In a world with no taxes or distress costs, capital structure does not change firm value; the theorem tells you that taxes and distress are the whole story.
cards.a: Modigliani and Miller showed that in a perfect market, with no taxes, no bankruptcy costs and no information problems, the value of a company does not depend on how it is financed. Slicing the same cash flows into debt and equity in different proportions changes who gets what, not the total. Borrowing more raises the cost of equity exactly enough to offset the cheaper debt, so WACC stays flat. Nobody thinks the assumptions hold. The point is what happens when you relax them: the tax deductibility of interest makes debt add value, and the costs of distress make too much debt destroy it. That is the whole modern theory in one sentence.

cards.q: What is financial leverage, and how does it magnify returns to shareholders in both directions?
cards.takeaway: Funding assets with debt means the same operating result produces a bigger swing in the return on the owners' smaller stake.
cards.a: Suppose Ferrow Retail's assets earn 10%. Funded entirely with £100m of equity, shareholders earn 10%. Funded with £50m of equity and £50m of debt at 6%, the assets still earn £10m, the lenders take £3m, and shareholders earn £7m on £50m, which is 14%. Leverage lifted their return. Now suppose the assets earn only 4%: £4m, minus £3m of interest, leaves £1m on £50m, a 2% return, against 4% unlevered. The interest is fixed, so every swing in operating profit lands entirely on the equity. That is why levered equity is riskier and why lenders care about cover.

cards.q: What is a credit rating, and how does it feed back into capital structure decisions?
cards.takeaway: An agency's grade for how likely a borrower is to repay; a lower grade means dearer debt, so companies manage their structure to keep a target rating.
cards.a: Agencies like Moody's and S&P grade companies from AAA down to D on their ability to repay. Investment grade, BBB- and above, means access to the deepest pools of lenders at low spreads; below that is high yield, where borrowing costs jump and some investors cannot buy at all. Because the rating drives the cost of debt, many companies manage their leverage to hold a target, often BBB, and will issue equity or cut dividends rather than lose it. The rating agencies publish the ratios they look at, net debt to EBITDA and interest cover among them, so the target rating becomes a constraint on the whole structure.

cards.q: What is the pecking order theory, and what does it predict about how companies actually raise money?
cards.takeaway: Companies prefer retained profits, then debt, then equity as a last resort, because issuing shares signals the shares are overpriced.
cards.a: The pecking order theory says managers fund investment first from cash the business generates, then by borrowing, and only then by issuing new shares. The reason is information: managers know more than investors, and would only sell shares if they thought the price was full, so an equity issue is read as a signal and the price falls. Debt carries less of that signal because its value depends less on the company's private prospects. The theory predicts that profitable companies carry little debt, because they never need it, which is what you observe, and that share issues are rare and greeted badly, which is also what you observe.

cards.q: Why do companies in different industries carry such different amounts of debt?
cards.takeaway: Stable, asset-heavy businesses can borrow a lot; volatile or intangible ones cannot, because lenders want predictable cash and something to seize.
cards.a: Lenders look for two things: cash flows steady enough to cover interest every year, and assets they could sell if the company failed. Redhill Utilities has both, regulated revenues and a network of pipes and cables, so it can run at five times EBITDA. A software company has neither, its revenue can halve if a product fails and its assets are people and code, so it carries little debt and funds itself with equity. Retailers sit in between, and cyclical businesses like airlines borrow against aircraft but suffer in downturns. When you see a leverage ratio, ask what industry before asking whether it is high.

cards.q: What is a leveraged recapitalisation, and why would a company do one?
cards.takeaway: Borrowing a large sum to pay shareholders a special dividend or buy back shares, swapping equity for debt to lower the cost of capital or fend off a bidder.
cards.a: A leveraged recap is a deliberate change in structure: the company takes on significant new debt and hands the cash to shareholders. The business is unchanged but is now funded with more debt and less equity. Companies do it when they think they are under-levered, because the tax shield on the new debt adds value and the remaining shares are worth more each; or as a defence, because a company already loaded with debt is a less attractive takeover target. The risk is the same as any leverage: if the business then weakens, the debt that looked comfortable becomes a problem. Private equity does the same thing to companies it already owns, called a dividend recap.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co. is considering funding a £200m acquisition with either new shares or a new loan. What are the arguments each way?
cards.takeaway: Debt is cheaper and avoids dilution but adds fixed obligations and rating risk; equity is safer but dilutes and signals the shares are full.
cards.a: Debt: the after-tax cost is lower, so the deal adds more to earnings per share; existing shareholders keep their full stake; and the interest shield adds value. Against it: leverage rises, interest cover falls, the rating agencies may downgrade, and a bad year after the deal is more dangerous. Equity: the balance sheet stays strong and the company keeps borrowing capacity for the next opportunity. Against it: shareholders are diluted, the deal adds less to EPS, and the market may read the issue as management thinking the shares are overpriced. Most companies use a mix, sized to hold their target leverage and rating after the deal.

cards.q: How does capital structure connect to an LBO?
cards.takeaway: An LBO is an extreme capital structure choice: fund most of the purchase with debt, use the company's cash to repay it, and let leverage magnify the equity return.
cards.a: A leveraged buyout is capital structure theory turned into a business model. The private equity buyer funds perhaps 60% of the price with debt secured on the company itself, so its own equity cheque is small. The company's cash flows then pay down that debt over five years or so, which shifts value from lenders to the equity as the debt shrinks. When the company is sold, the equity has grown far faster than the business did, because leverage magnified the return. Everything in this deck applies: the deal only works on a business with steady cash flows, the debt costs more as leverage rises, and too much of it turns a good business into a distressed one.

cards.q: An interviewer asks: what discount rate would you use for Calder Foods' DCF, and how would you get it? Give the answer in order.
cards.takeaway: WACC, built from the CAPM cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted at market values, with a sentence on each input.
cards.a: Use WACC, because the free cash flows in a standard DCF belong to all providers of capital. Cost of equity from the CAPM: the current government bond yield as the risk-free rate, a beta from Calder's own share price or from comparable food companies if it is private, and an equity risk premium of around 5%. Cost of debt from the yield on Calder's bonds or the risk-free rate plus a spread for its rating, taken after tax. Weights from the market value of its equity and debt, or a target structure if the current one is unusual. Combine, and say the number, and then say which input you are least sure of, since that is the follow-up.

name: M&A Fundamentals
description: How deals actually get done, from the first pitch to goodwill.
intro: Mergers and acquisitions are how companies buy, sell and combine with one another, and it is the work most people picture when they picture investment banking. This deck starts with the plain-language version, what a merger actually is, why anyone would pay above market price, and what a bank does on the sell-side versus the buy-side, then builds toward the mechanics interviewers push on: consideration, synergies, accretion and dilution, goodwill, and where a premium has to be earned back. You have already met valuation and the financial statements, so the focus here is deals themselves. No deal experience assumed.

cards.q: What is the difference between a merger and an acquisition, and why do bankers lump them together as one thing?
cards.takeaway: A merger combines two companies into one, an acquisition is one company buying and absorbing another.
cards.a: In an acquisition, one company, the acquirer, buys control of another, the target, and the target stops existing as an independent business. A merger is the friendlier-sounding version, where two companies combine, sometimes under a new name, and the shareholders of both end up owning a piece of the combined company. In practice the line is blurry, which is why bankers use M&A as a single umbrella term: almost every deal announced as a merger of equals still has a side that pays a premium and a side that collects it.

cards.q: Your MD is prepping a pitch for Northbay Logistics and asks you to lay out why a company would buy another company at all. What is actually on that list?
cards.takeaway: Acquirers buy to get scale, capability, market access, or earnings faster than they could build them.
cards.a: Almost every acquisition comes down to buying something faster than you could build it. That might be scale, where the combined company spreads the same head office and factory costs over more revenue, or capability, where the target owns technology or a team the buyer would need years to develop. It might be market access, buying a foothold in a region or a customer segment, or diversification into steadier earnings. Less flattering motives exist too, including a chief executive who simply wants a bigger company to run, and naming that one is often what an interviewer is listening for.

cards.q: What do bankers mean by sell-side and buy-side on an M&A deal, and what is the bank actually doing in each?
cards.takeaway: Sell-side means running a process to sell a company, buy-side means helping a buyer find and buy one.
cards.a: On a sell-side mandate the bank works for the company being sold, or its owners, and runs the process: setting the price expectation, preparing the marketing materials, deciding which buyers get approached, and squeezing the best terms out of whoever is still standing at the end. On a buy-side mandate the bank works for the acquirer, helping it identify targets, value them, structure and finance a bid, and negotiate. Sell-side fees are usually a percentage of deal value paid at closing, which is why banks compete hard for those mandates.

cards.q: A private equity fund and a large competitor are both circling Calder Foods. How would you expect a strategic buyer and a financial buyer to think about price differently?
cards.takeaway: A strategic buyer can pay for synergies, a financial buyer pays only for what the business earns on its own.
cards.a: A strategic buyer is an operating company, often a competitor, supplier or customer, that will fold the target into its own business. Because the two operations end up combined, it can afford to pay for savings and growth that only exist once they are one company. A financial buyer is an investment firm, typically private equity, that buys the company to own it separately for a few years and sell it on, so it can only pay for what the business generates by itself, plus whatever borrowing and operational improvement add. That is why strategics often win competitive auctions on price.

cards.q: Calder Foods shares trade at $40 and its board has just agreed to be bought at $52. Why would any acquirer pay well above a price anyone could buy the stock at this morning?
cards.takeaway: A control premium is the extra an acquirer pays to own and run the whole company rather than a slice of it.
cards.a: The control premium is the amount paid above where the shares traded before news of a deal moved the price, and it commonly lands somewhere in the twenty to forty percent range, though it varies a lot by sector and situation. Buying one share gets you a passive slice; buying the whole company gets you the right to redirect its cash, replace its management, and combine it with your own operations. Shareholders also have no reason to sell at the market price, since they can get that any day of the week, so the premium is the price of persuading them to let go.

cards.q: A potential buyer for Northbay Logistics calls and asks your team to send over “the book.” What are a teaser, an NDA and a CIM, and why do they arrive in that order?
cards.takeaway: The teaser is anonymous bait, the NDA buys silence, and the CIM is the full book on the business.
cards.a: The teaser is a one or two page anonymous summary, a description and a few financials with the company’s name stripped out, sent broadly to see who bites. A buyer that wants more signs a non-disclosure agreement, a contract promising not to share what it learns or use it against the seller. Only then does it receive the confidential information memorandum, the fifty to hundred page book covering the business, its market, its customers and its numbers, which is what a first-round bid actually gets based on.

cards.q: Your staffer wants you to be able to describe a live sell-side deal to a client tomorrow. Walk me through an M&A process from the first pitch through to closing.
cards.takeaway: A sale runs pitch, marketing, first bids, diligence, final bids, signing, and only then closing.
cards.a: It starts with banks pitching for the mandate and one being hired. The team prepares the teaser and the CIM, approaches buyers, and collects non-binding first-round bids. A shorter list then gets management presentations and access to the data room, the online archive where the seller’s contracts, financials and legal files sit for diligence, before submitting binding bids. The winner negotiates the purchase agreement and signs it. Closing, when the money and the ownership actually move, comes weeks or months later, once regulators and shareholders have given their approvals.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail has agreed to buy Calder Foods and can pay in cash, in its own shares, or a blend of the two. What does each choice signal to the market?
cards.takeaway: Cash signals confidence, stock shares the risk and hints the buyer thinks its own shares are pricey.
cards.a: Cash is simple: the seller’s shareholders receive a fixed amount and walk away, so every bit of the risk that the deal disappoints sits with the buyer. Stock means they receive shares in the combined company, keeping some of the upside but also carrying part of the downside, and their real proceeds move with the buyer’s share price until closing. The market usually reads cash as confidence and stock as a hint that the buyer thinks its own shares are richly valued, which is one reason an acquirer’s stock often falls on the announcement of a large all-stock deal.

cards.q: At a basic level, what is the difference between buying a company’s assets and buying its stock, and why do buyers and sellers usually want different ones?
cards.takeaway: An asset deal lets a buyer pick what it takes, a stock deal takes the whole company, liabilities included.
cards.a: In a stock purchase the buyer acquires the target’s shares, so it gets the company exactly as it stands, every contract, every employee and every liability, including the ones nobody has found yet. In an asset purchase the buyer names the specific assets and liabilities it wants and leaves the rest behind in a shell the seller still owns. Buyers tend to prefer asset deals, since they sidestep unknown liabilities and often get to write assets up for tax purposes, while sellers prefer stock deals for the clean exit and generally better tax treatment. The details turn on local tax law, so lawyers drive that call.

cards.q: Your VP says the model needs $80 million of synergies to justify the price on Calder Foods. What are synergies, and why will the board believe the cost ones more than the revenue ones?
cards.takeaway: Cost synergies are savings the buyer controls, revenue synergies depend on customers behaving as hoped.
cards.a: Synergies are the value that only exists once two companies are combined. Cost synergies are expenses that disappear, one head office instead of two, one finance team, better purchasing terms from suppliers, and a buyer can usually name the specific line items and when they land. Revenue synergies are extra sales, selling the target’s product to your customers or the reverse, and they depend on customers choosing to behave as hoped rather than on decisions the buyer controls. Boards and analysts routinely haircut or ignore the revenue number for exactly that reason.

cards.q: The first question a CFO asks about any deal is whether it is accretive. What do accretion and dilution actually mean, and why does that question come before everything else?
cards.takeaway: A deal is accretive if the buyer’s earnings per share end up higher after it than they would be alone.
cards.a: Earnings per share is net income divided by shares outstanding. In a deal, the buyer adds the target’s earnings and any synergies, subtracts the cost of paying for it, meaning interest on new debt or the interest given up on cash spent, then divides by a share count that grows if part of the price is paid in stock. If that figure beats what the buyer would have earned per share standing alone, the deal is accretive, and if it falls short, dilutive. It is a crude test that says nothing about whether the price was sensible, but it is the number the market reacts to first.

cards.q: Your VP gives you only the two P/E ratios and asks whether an all-stock deal will be accretive before you open Excel. What is the rule of thumb, and why does it work?
cards.takeaway: In an all-stock deal, a buyer with a higher P/E than the price it pays for the target is usually accretive.
cards.a: In an all-stock deal the buyer is paying with its own shares, so the question is whether the earnings it buys are cheaper than the earnings it gives up. A price-to-earnings ratio is what investors pay for a dollar of profit, so a buyer trading at twenty times earnings that acquires a target at fourteen times is buying profit more cheaply than the market prices its own, and earnings per share rises. The rule only holds if you use the P/E implied by the offer price rather than the target’s trading price, and it ignores synergies, so treat it as a first read rather than an answer.

cards.q: You have been handed the sources and uses page for a $900 million acquisition of Northbay Logistics. What is that schedule showing, and why must the two sides tie?
cards.takeaway: Sources and uses lists every dollar the deal needs and every dollar funding it, and the two totals must match.
cards.a: Uses lists everything the money has to pay for: the equity purchase price for shareholders, any of the target’s debt that must be repaid at closing because it cannot legally survive a change of ownership, and the advisory, legal and financing fees. Sources lists where those dollars come from: new debt raised, cash already on the balance sheet, the buyer’s own shares issued as payment, sometimes equity the seller rolls into the new company. The two sides tie by construction, since the financing is sized to whatever the uses total, and a page that does not balance is the fastest way to lose an MD’s trust.

cards.q: Where does goodwill come from in an acquisition, and what is purchase price allocation actually doing?
cards.takeaway: Goodwill is whatever is left of the price once the target’s identified assets are marked to fair value.
cards.a: When a deal closes, the buyer cannot simply carry the target’s old balance sheet forward. Purchase price allocation restates the target’s assets and liabilities at fair value, which usually means writing property up and recognizing intangibles the target never booked itself, such as brand names and customer relationships. Whatever the purchase price exceeds that fair value of net identifiable assets becomes goodwill, an asset standing in for everything paid that cannot be pointed at directly. Under US accounting it is not amortized but tested for impairment, and a goodwill writedown is about as close as a company comes to publicly admitting it overpaid.

cards.q: Calder Foods’ board has now rejected Ferrow’s offer twice, and Ferrow is considering going straight to the shareholders. What makes a deal hostile, and what can a board actually do about it?
cards.takeaway: A deal is hostile when the acquirer goes around a board that said no and appeals to shareholders directly.
cards.a: A friendly deal is negotiated with the target’s board, which then recommends it to shareholders. A deal turns hostile when the board refuses and the acquirer goes around it, either with a tender offer, an approach made directly to shareholders to buy their shares, or a proxy fight to replace the directors with ones who will agree. Boards can respond with a poison pill, a plan letting every other shareholder buy cheap new stock the moment a bidder crosses an ownership threshold, or by finding a friendlier rival bidder. Hostile attempts are a small minority of deals, and most that succeed end up negotiated anyway.

cards.q: Two of the three largest players in a market announce they are combining. What does the regulatory review look for, and what can it actually do to the deal?
cards.takeaway: Regulators ask whether the combined company could raise prices, not whether the deal is a good idea.
cards.a: Before a deal can close, competition authorities examine whether the combined company would meaningfully weaken competition in any market it touches. They look at how concentrated the market becomes, how closely the two companies actually compete for the same customers, and how easily a new entrant could appear to discipline prices. The outcomes are a clean approval, an approval conditional on remedies such as selling an overlapping business to a third party, or a challenge that kills the deal outright. Big deals often need clearance in several countries at once, which is much of why signing and closing sit months apart.

cards.q: Interviewers like to say most acquisitions destroy value. Is that actually true, and how would you answer without just agreeing with them?
cards.takeaway: Acquirers frequently overpay, so the average deal disappoints, but the spread across deals is very wide.
cards.a: The evidence is more specific than the slogan. Studies of share price reactions around announcements consistently find that target shareholders capture most of the gain, because the premium is handed to them on day one, while acquirer shareholders on average earn close to nothing and often slightly less, particularly in large stock-funded deals. Averages hide a wide spread, though: smaller cash-funded purchases of adjacent businesses with concrete cost savings tend to do fine. The framing worth offering is that value transfers to the seller at signing, and the buyer only earns it back if the synergies actually arrive.

cards.q: Calder Foods trades at 8x EBITDA and Ferrow has agreed to pay 12x. Your MD asks where those extra four turns have to come from for the deal to make any sense. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: A premium only pays off if synergies or structure earn back the turns paid above standalone value.
cards.a: Standalone, the market says the business is worth eight times its EBITDA, so those four extra turns are a bet on something the market is not currently pricing. The honest sources are synergies, since savings raise combined EBITDA and pull the effective multiple back down, structure, meaning cheap debt or a tax step-up that lowers the real cost of the purchase, or a genuine view that the comparable companies are mispricing the asset. If Ferrow pays 12x on $100 million of EBITDA and delivers $40 million of savings, it has really paid about 8.6x, and that is the number your MD wants to hear.

name: LBOs & Private Equity Basics
description: How buyouts work, from borrowed money to the returns math.
intro: Private equity is the business of buying whole companies, usually with a great deal of borrowed money, improving them for a few years and then selling them on. The leveraged buyout is the transaction at the centre of it, and it is the most heavily tested topic in private equity interviews, from what makes a good LBO candidate to walk me through a paper LBO on this napkin. This deck starts with what a PE firm actually does and why debt magnifies returns, then builds up through sources and uses, the capital structure, and the returns arithmetic interviewers expect you to do in your head. No prior exposure to buyouts assumed.

cards.q: You mention you are interviewing at a private equity firm and a friend asks what that even is. What do private equity firms actually do?
cards.takeaway: A private equity firm buys whole companies with investors’ money, improves them, and sells them years later.
cards.a: A private equity firm raises a large pool of money from outside investors, uses it to buy entire companies outright, holds each one for roughly three to seven years while trying to make it more profitable, and then sells it. The profit is the gap between what the firm paid and what it eventually sells for. The key difference from owning shares in a public company is control: because the firm owns the whole business, it can change management, strategy, pricing and cost structure directly rather than voting from the sidelines.

cards.q: Before you get anywhere near the technicals, your interviewer wants the intuition. How is a private equity firm buying a company like a person buying a house with a mortgage?
cards.takeaway: Put in a small slice of your own money, borrow the rest, and the whole asset’s gain lands on your slice.
cards.a: Say you buy a house for 500, putting in 100 of your own cash and borrowing 400 as a mortgage. Sell it later for 600, repay the 400, and you walk away with 200. The house went up only 20 percent, but your money doubled, because the lender’s return was fixed at the interest rate and every extra pound of gain landed on you. That borrowed money is called leverage, and a buyout works on exactly this arithmetic, with a company in place of the house and its cash flow in place of your salary paying the mortgage.

cards.q: What actually happens in a leveraged buyout, step by step?
cards.takeaway: A sponsor buys a company mostly with borrowed money, the company repays that debt, and the sponsor sells later.
cards.a: A private equity firm, usually called the sponsor, agrees a price for a target company and funds the purchase with a large slice of borrowed money plus a smaller cheque of equity from its own fund. The crucial mechanic is that the debt is placed on the acquired company’s balance sheet and serviced out of that company’s own cash flow, not out of the sponsor’s pocket. Over the holding period the company pays interest and chips away at principal, and at exit the sale proceeds repay whatever debt remains, with everything left over belonging to the sponsor.

cards.q: A candidate tells your interviewer that private equity firms invest their own money. She pushes back. Where does the money in a PE fund really come from, and how does the firm get paid?
cards.takeaway: Outside investors supply nearly all the capital, and the firm earns a fee plus a share of the profits.
cards.a: The capital comes from limited partners, or LPs: pension funds, endowments, insurers and wealthy families who commit money to a fund but take no part in running it. The firm itself is the general partner, or GP, which manages the fund and typically invests one to two percent of the total alongside its LPs. The classic economics are roughly two percent a year in management fees on the capital committed, plus carried interest of about twenty percent of the profits once returns clear a hurdle rate, a minimum annual return often set near eight percent. Actual terms vary by firm and by fund.

cards.q: Your associate hands you a list of five companies and asks which ones might work as a buyout. What makes a company a good LBO candidate?
cards.takeaway: Predictable cash flow first, then low reinvestment needs, a defensible position, and room to improve.
cards.a: Above everything else you want steady, predictable cash flow, because the debt carries interest and principal payments that fall due whether trading is good or bad. You also want modest capital expenditure, meaning the company does not have to sink large sums into equipment or property just to keep running, since that cash is needed for the lenders. A defensible market position, long-term contracts or a recognisable brand protect the revenue, hard assets give lenders collateral to lend against, and low existing debt leaves room to add more. Cyclical businesses and cash-hungry early-stage companies are poor fits for the same reasons.

cards.q: Your VP wants a sources and uses table on the Northbay Logistics buyout by tomorrow morning. What is it, and what has to be true of it?
cards.takeaway: Uses list everything the deal has to pay for, sources list where that money comes from, and the two must tie.
cards.a: Uses set out every pound the deal must fund: the price paid for the target’s equity, the repayment of existing debt that the lenders will insist is cleared, and transaction and financing fees. Sources set out where that money comes from: each tranche of new debt, the sponsor’s equity cheque, sometimes cash already sitting on the target’s balance sheet, and occasionally equity rolled over by existing management. The two columns must equal each other exactly, and in practice sponsor equity is the plug: you fix the price and the debt the lenders will provide, then the equity is whatever is still missing.

cards.q: A junior asks why the Northbay deal has three different layers of financing instead of one big loan. What sits in an LBO capital structure, and who gets paid first if things go wrong?
cards.takeaway: Senior debt is paid first and costs least, and equity is paid last but keeps whatever upside is left.
cards.a: Senior secured debt sits at the top: it is backed by the company’s assets, carries the lowest interest rate, and is repaid before anything else. Below it sits subordinated or mezzanine debt, which is unsecured, charges a higher rate to compensate, and sometimes comes with an equity kicker such as warrants. The sponsor’s equity sits at the bottom and receives only what is left after every lender has been paid. Layering the financing this way lets the sponsor borrow more in total than any single lender would provide, because each layer is priced for the risk it actually takes.

cards.q: Your interviewer says leverage is what makes buyout returns work, then asks what happens when a deal goes badly. Why does debt magnify both directions?
cards.takeaway: Debt has a fixed claim, so the entire swing in company value lands on the thin slice of equity underneath it.
cards.a: Take a company bought for 1,000 with 700 of debt and 300 of equity. Sell it for 1,300, repay the 700, and the equity is 600, doubled on a 30 percent rise in the business. Sell it for 700 instead and the lenders take all of it, leaving the equity at zero on an identical 30 percent move the other way. Lenders are owed a fixed amount regardless, so every gain and every loss above that fixed claim belongs to the equity, which is why interviewers treat leverage as the source of both the returns and the risk.

cards.q: Your MD glances at the returns page and asks for both the IRR and the multiple of money. What does each one measure, and why do sponsors always quote both?
cards.takeaway: MOIC says how many times your money came back, IRR says how fast, and neither is complete alone.
cards.a: MOIC, the multiple of invested capital, is simply total cash returned divided by cash invested: put in 300, take out 900, and you have made 3.0x. It says nothing about how long that took. IRR, the internal rate of return, is the annualised rate that accounts for timing, so the same 3.0x is roughly a 44 percent IRR over three years but only about 17 percent over seven. Quoting both stops either number flattering a deal on its own, since a quick small win can post a spectacular IRR on very little absolute profit.

cards.q: Where does the cash a portfolio company generates actually go each year while a sponsor owns it?
cards.takeaway: Spare cash pays down debt, and every pound of debt retired becomes a pound of sponsor equity.
cards.a: After the company covers its operating costs, working capital, capital expenditure, interest and taxes, whatever free cash flow is left usually goes straight to repaying debt, often because the loan agreement contains a cash sweep clause requiring exactly that. Since the sponsor’s equity is simply enterprise value minus debt, each pound of debt retired lifts equity by a pound even if the business is worth no more than the day it was bought. This is why the debt schedule is the beating heart of an LBO model and why an analyst is expected to be able to walk through it line by line.

cards.q: Your interviewer asks where the money in a successful buyout actually comes from. What are the three levers of value creation, and which one would you not lean on?
cards.takeaway: Returns come from debt paydown, EBITDA growth, and multiple expansion, and you control only the first two.
cards.a: Debt paydown converts the company’s cash flow into equity value, as you have seen. EBITDA growth raises the earnings that any exit multiple gets applied to, whether through higher revenue, better margins or bolt-on acquisitions. Multiple expansion means selling the business at a higher multiple of EBITDA than you paid for it, which depends largely on market conditions and how the company is positioned at the point of sale. A strong answer notes that the first two are operational and within the sponsor’s influence, while the third is close to market timing, so investment committees rarely underwrite a deal that needs it.

cards.q: The interviewer slides a blank sheet across the table and says: walk me through a paper LBO, no calculator, ten minutes. What is she actually asking for?
cards.takeaway: A paper LBO is the whole buyout arithmetic done by hand, from entry price to exit equity to returns.
cards.a: You start from EBITDA and an entry multiple to get enterprise value, split that into debt and sponsor equity, then project EBITDA forward a few years and subtract interest, taxes and capital expenditure to see how much debt gets repaid along the way. At exit you apply an exit multiple to the final year’s EBITDA, subtract the debt still outstanding, and what remains is the equity. Divide that by the equity you put in for MOIC, and annualise it for a rough IRR. The exercise tests structure and composure more than arithmetic, so state each assumption out loud and keep the numbers round.

cards.q: Halfway through a model review your VP deletes the exit multiple and asks you to justify it from scratch. Why does that single assumption carry so much weight?
cards.takeaway: Most of a buyout’s value is realised at exit, so the exit multiple quietly drives the whole return.
cards.a: Exit value is exit EBITDA multiplied by the exit multiple, and unlike a dividend along the way, the bulk of the sponsor’s cash arrives in that one moment. On a business earning 140 of EBITDA, a single turn of multiple is 140 of enterprise value, and because the debt is repaid at a fixed amount, all of that difference lands on the equity. The common convention is to assume the exit multiple equals the entry multiple, which forces the return to be earned through operations and debt paydown rather than through an assumption that the market will simply be kinder on the way out.

cards.q: Marlstone Capital has owned Calder Foods for five years and wants out. What are the usual exit routes, and what pushes a sponsor towards one over another?
cards.takeaway: Sell to a strategic buyer, sell to another sponsor, or float it, and market conditions usually decide.
cards.a: A sale to a strategic buyer, meaning an operating company in the same industry, often fetches the highest price because the buyer can fold in the business and realise synergies that no financial buyer can. A secondary buyout means selling to another private equity firm, which is quick and clean but capped by that firm’s own return requirements. An initial public offering lists the shares publicly, though the sponsor usually sells down over several tranches rather than exiting in one go, so proceeds depend on how the stock trades after listing. Size, sector appetite and the state of the debt markets drive the choice.

cards.q: Three years into the Northbay hold the company is performing well but the market for exits has frozen. Your MD mentions a dividend recapitalisation. What is that?
cards.takeaway: The company borrows fresh debt and pays the proceeds out to its owner, returning cash without a sale.
cards.a: In a dividend recapitalisation the portfolio company raises new debt and uses the proceeds to pay a special dividend up to the fund that owns it. The sponsor takes cash off the table without selling anything, which reduces the equity still at risk and lifts IRR by pulling money forward in time, though it does not change the underlying business at all. The trade-off is more leverage on a company that still has to service it, so lenders will only allow it where cash flow comfortably covers the larger interest bill, and it is often viewed as an aggressive move when trading later disappoints.

cards.q: What is a debt covenant, and why does a sponsor negotiate the terms as hard as the interest rate?
cards.takeaway: Covenants are the conditions attached to a loan, and breaching one hands the lenders leverage over the deal.
cards.a: Covenants are promises written into a loan agreement. A maintenance covenant requires the borrower to stay inside a financial test at every reporting date, most commonly a leverage ratio such as debt to EBITDA below an agreed level, or an interest coverage ratio above one. An incurrence covenant only applies when the company takes a specific action, such as raising more debt or paying a dividend. Breaching a covenant is a default, and it lets lenders renegotiate terms, demand repayment, or in serious cases take control, so headroom between the test and the forecast matters as much as the coupon. How tight covenants run varies a great deal with market conditions.

cards.q: Two bidders are circling Calder Foods, a large food group and a private equity fund. Why can either one end up as the higher bidder depending on the situation?
cards.takeaway: A strategic buyer pays for synergies it keeps forever, a sponsor is capped by the return it must earn.
cards.a: A strategic buyer folds the target into an existing business, so it can strip out duplicated costs or push products through its own distribution, and it never has to sell, which lets it rationally pay above what the company is worth on its own. A financial buyer works backwards instead: it starts from the return it has promised its LPs, assumes an exit in five years, and solves for the highest price that still clears that hurdle, so its ceiling is set by how much debt it can raise and how confident it is in the exit. When credit is cheap and plentiful, or when the target is non-core to every strategic in the sector, the sponsor wins.

cards.q: Last question of the interview. Your Northbay model shows 2.7x exiting at 8.0x EBITDA. She asks what happens if you exit at 7.0x instead, and whether the deal still works.
cards.takeaway: One turn of multiple compression comes straight off the equity, because the debt claim never shrinks.
cards.a: Exiting at 7.0x on 140 of EBITDA gives 980 of enterprise value instead of 1,120, and because the 300 of remaining debt is repaid in full regardless, the whole 140 comes out of the equity: 680 rather than 820, so 2.3x instead of 2.7x and roughly an 18 percent IRR rather than 22. Whether that still works depends on the fund’s hurdle, and many committees would call it acceptable but thin. The same arithmetic run upwards is why paying one turn too much at entry is so hard to recover from, and why every LBO model carries a sensitivity table across entry and exit multiples.

name: IPOs & Equity Capital Markets
description: How companies go public, and how those offerings get priced.
intro: Equity capital markets is the part of a bank that helps companies sell shares to investors, and the initial public offering is its signature product: the moment a private company becomes one anyone can buy on an exchange. This deck walks you through what going public actually changes, who receives the money when shares are sold, what the underwriting bank is being paid for, and how a price that starts as a wide range becomes a single number the night before trading. You’ll also meet the pieces interviewers love to probe, lock-ups, greenshoes, follow-ons and the first-day pop. No deal experience assumed.

cards.q: What does it actually mean for a company to go public, and what changes the day it does?
cards.takeaway: Going public means selling shares to public investors and living under public disclosure from then on.
cards.a: A private company’s shares are held by a small, closed group, founders, employees, maybe a private equity firm, and nobody else can buy in. Going public means selling shares to public investors so that anyone can own a piece and trade it on an exchange. From that day the company has thousands of owners it has never met, a share price that moves every second, and a legal duty to publish audited financial results on a fixed schedule. The business is the same, the accountability around it is not.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics’ founder asks why she should go public at all when a private equity firm has offered to fund the business quietly. What do you tell her about both sides?
cards.takeaway: An IPO buys capital, currency and liquidity in exchange for control, cost and permanent scrutiny.
cards.a: The case for is real money and real optionality: cash to fund growth or repay debt, a traded share price that can be used to pay for acquisitions and compensate employees, and a way for early owners to eventually sell down. The case against is just as real: underwriting fees, ongoing audit, legal and compliance costs, competitors reading your margins in a public filing, and a management team judged every quarter on numbers it cannot always control. Plenty of good companies stay private for exactly those reasons, and a thoughtful answer says so.

cards.q: You’re drafting the offering summary for Calder Foods and the CFO asks who actually receives the money from each share sold. How do you explain primary versus secondary shares?
cards.takeaway: Primary shares raise new cash for the company, secondary shares just cash out existing holders.
cards.a: Primary shares are brand-new shares the company creates and sells in the offering, so the proceeds land on the company’s balance sheet and the total share count rises. Secondary shares already exist and are being sold by current owners, founders or a private equity sponsor, so that cash goes to them and the company receives nothing and issues nothing. Most deals mix the two. If Calder sells 10 million shares, 6 million primary and 4 million secondary, only the 6 million funds the business, which is the first thing to check before you model what the proceeds pay for.

cards.q: What does the underwriting bank actually do in an IPO, and what is it being paid for?
cards.takeaway: The underwriter prepares, prices and markets the deal, then buys it and carries the risk of unsold shares.
cards.a: An underwriter is the investment bank that runs the offering. It does the diligence, helps draft the disclosure document, builds the valuation, organises the investor marketing, gathers orders, sets the final price with the company and decides which investors get shares. In the standard US structure, a firm commitment, the bank then buys the whole block from the company at the offer price less its fee and resells it, so anything it cannot place stays on its own books. That fee, the gross spread, is often around five to seven percent on a mid-size deal and lower on very large ones.

cards.q: At the kickoff meeting a client asks how long the whole IPO will take and what happens in between. Walk her through it end to end.
cards.takeaway: A traditional IPO usually runs four to nine months from kickoff to the first day of trading.
cards.a: It starts with an organisational meeting where the company, banks, lawyers and auditors agree the plan. Then comes the long stretch: diligence, audited financials and drafting the registration statement, which is filed with the regulator and goes through rounds of written comments. Once that clears, the deal launches publicly with a price range, management spends one to two weeks meeting investors, and the bank collects orders. The deal is priced the night before trading begins, and the stock opens the next morning. Market conditions and the state of the company’s accounts move that timeline more than anything else.

cards.q: What is the prospectus, or registration statement, and why does a deal team spend months on one document?
cards.takeaway: The prospectus is the company’s full public disclosure and the legal basis on which investors buy the deal.
cards.a: It is the document a company files with the securities regulator, called an S-1 in the United States, before it can sell shares to the public. Inside are the business description, audited financial statements, management’s discussion of the results, a long list of risk factors, how the proceeds will be used, and who owns what. Investors are legally entitled to rely on it, and the company and the banks can be sued if it is materially wrong or incomplete. That liability is exactly why diligence is exhaustive and why sentences get argued over line by line.

cards.q: You’re a week into the roadshow for Calder Foods when the syndicate desk says the book is three times covered. What is a roadshow, what does building a book mean, and what did they just tell you?
cards.takeaway: A roadshow builds a book of investor orders at each price, showing what demand the deal can really bear.
cards.a: The roadshow is one to two weeks of management meeting institutional investors, funds, pensions, insurers, to tell the story and answer hard questions. As those meetings happen, the bank’s syndicate desk builds the book: a running record of who wants how many shares and up to what price. Three times covered means orders total roughly three times the shares on offer, which sounds emphatic but is only a starting point. Orders are non-binding and often padded to win an allocation, so bankers discount them and weigh who is asking as heavily as how much.

cards.q: How does the IPO price actually get set, and why does the price range narrow as the deal goes on?
cards.takeaway: The range starts as a valuation estimate and narrows as real orders replace guesswork.
cards.a: Bankers start from valuation, comparable public companies and a discounted cash flow, then cut that by an IPO discount because investors want to be paid for backing a company with no trading history. That produces the range printed in the prospectus, which is deliberately an opening anchor rather than a forecast. As the book fills in, guesswork gets replaced with actual limits real investors will pay, so the range gets revised up or down and finally collapses to one number agreed the night before trading. The goal is not the highest possible price, it’s the highest price that still leaves committed buyers behind it.

cards.q: Calder Foods prices at $23 and closes its first day at $30. The CFO calls and asks whether the bank left $7 a share on the table. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: A first-day pop is partly deliberate underpricing and partly information the deal could not fully see.
cards.a: The pop is the gap between the offer price and where the stock settles on day one. On the company’s side it is straightforward arithmetic: that gap times the primary shares sold is cash the business could have raised and didn’t. On the bank’s side, a modest discount is intentional, it compensates long-term investors for taking an untested stock, encourages them to hold, and reduces the chance of a broken deal trading below issue, which damages the shareholder base and every future raise. Only a small slice of the company trades on day one, so that opening price is also thin evidence. Reasonable people genuinely disagree here.

cards.q: What is a lock-up period in an IPO, and why do underwriters insist on one?
cards.takeaway: A lock-up stops insiders selling for a set window so early supply cannot swamp a newly listed stock.
cards.a: A lock-up is a contract between insiders, founders, executives and pre-IPO shareholders, and the underwriters, agreeing not to sell shares for a period after listing, most commonly around 180 days. It exists because only a small fraction of the company is floated at IPO, so unrestricted insider selling into that thin market would overwhelm it and it would signal that the people who know the business best want out. Expiry dates get watched closely, though the effect on price is usually smaller than expected because everyone can see the date coming.

cards.q: Two weeks after Northbay Logistics prices, the syndicate desk mentions they’ve exercised the shoe. What is the greenshoe, and why does every deal have one?
cards.takeaway: The greenshoe lets underwriters sell fifteen percent extra shares and cover it from the company or the market.
cards.a: The greenshoe, formally the over-allotment option, lets the underwriters buy up to fifteen percent more shares from the company at the offer price for about thirty days after pricing. Mechanically the bank sells 115 percent of the deal on day one, leaving itself short that extra slice. If the stock trades up, it exercises the option, buys the shares from the company and delivers them, and the company raises more money. If the stock trades down, it buys shares in the open market instead, which covers the short and steadies the price. One structure, two useful outcomes.

cards.q: A founder who owns 2 million of Northbay’s 8 million shares asks what the IPO does to her stake if the company issues 2 million new shares. Walk her through it.
cards.takeaway: Issuing new shares takes nothing from you, it shrinks the fraction each share you hold represents.
cards.a: Before the deal she owns 2 million of 8 million shares, which is 25 percent. Issue 2 million primary shares and the count becomes 10 million, so her unchanged 2 million is now 20 percent. That is dilution: same certificates, smaller share of the votes and of every future dollar of earnings, and earnings per share spread thinner too. Whether she is worse off depends entirely on what the proceeds do, since a smaller slice of a better-funded company can be worth more than a bigger slice of the old one. Secondary shares cause no dilution at all, because they already existed.

cards.q: What is a follow-on offering, and why does a stock often dip when one is announced?
cards.takeaway: A follow-on sells more shares after the IPO, and both new supply and the signal usually push the price down.
cards.a: A follow-on is any offering by an already-listed company, whether the company issues new shares to raise cash, existing holders sell down, or both. It can be marketed over days or done overnight as a block. The price almost always clears at a discount to the last close, because you’re asking the market to absorb a large slug of stock at once and buyers need an incentive. There’s a signalling effect too, since management chooses when to sell and tends to do it when the shares feel fully valued. A sponsor exiting reads differently from a company funding a defined project, and interviewers will ask you to tell them apart.

cards.q: How do a direct listing and a SPAC differ from a traditional IPO, and when would a company pick one?
cards.takeaway: A direct listing floats existing shares without raising cash, a SPAC goes public by merging into a shell.
cards.a: In a direct listing, existing shares simply start trading, with no underwritten offering and, classically, no new money raised, so the opening price comes from an auction rather than a book. It suits a well-known, well-funded company whose holders mainly want liquidity. A SPAC is a listed shell that already raised cash in its own IPO and then merges with a private target, which becomes public at a negotiated price, usually faster but with sponsor shares and investor redemptions eating into the cash that actually arrives. A traditional IPO stays the default when the goal is raising real capital at a marketed price.

cards.q: Two near-identical logistics companies with the same financials price nine months apart at very different multiples. Your analyst asks how that’s possible. What’s going on?
cards.takeaway: An IPO prices off the market’s appetite in that window, not off the company’s fundamentals alone.
cards.a: An IPO is priced against what investors will pay right now, and right now moves. The comparable companies you value against trade at different multiples in different quarters, so the anchor itself shifts. Calm markets let buyers accept a slim discount while volatile ones make them demand a fat one, and higher interest rates push down what any future cash flow is worth today. Recent listings matter too: a run of deals that traded up creates appetite, a run of broken ones closes the door. Add fixed constraints like earnings blackouts and the shelf life of audited accounts, and you get real windows a company can miss.

cards.q: Curveball: Calder Foods has 40 million shares and comparable companies imply $1.5 billion of equity value. It needs $300 million of primary proceeds. How many new shares is that, and where does the IPO discount come in?
cards.takeaway: New shares equal proceeds divided by the offer price, which is the comps value less an IPO discount.
cards.a: Comps imply about $37.50 a share on the existing 40 million. You don’t offer there, though: an IPO discount of roughly ten to fifteen percent buys the demand, so call the offer price $32. Raising $300 million at $32 takes about 9.4 million new primary shares, lifting the count to roughly 49.4 million, and those new investors end up owning about nineteen percent of the company. Notice what the discount cost: $5.50 a share on 9.4 million shares is around $50 million of value handed to buyers to get the deal done. That trade, certainty of execution against price, is the whole conversation in the pricing meeting.

name: Excel for Financial Modeling
description: The modeling habits and shortcuts a first-year analyst is expected to know cold.
intro: Excel is the quiet backbone of every IB analyst seat, and interviewers use it as a proxy for whether you can actually build and check a model under time pressure, not just talk about one. This deck covers the linking discipline, formatting conventions, and modeling habits that come up constantly: keeping a 3-statement model tied together, handling circular references cleanly, building sensitivity tables, and the small checks that separate a clean model from a fragile one. If you've mostly used Excel for basic formulas so far, start here.

cards.q: It’s your first week and a VP tells you to take a first pass at the model for Calder Foods. You’ve never opened one. What actually is a financial model?
cards.takeaway: A model is a spreadsheet that turns a handful of assumptions into a projected set of financials.
cards.a: Strip away the formatting and a model is a spreadsheet that takes a small set of assumptions, how fast revenue grows, what margin the business holds, how much it spends on equipment, and projects the company’s financial statements forward five or ten years. Every projected number is a formula that traces back to one of those assumptions, so changing a single input rewrites the entire forecast in front of you. That’s the point of building one: it lets a deal team ask what a business is worth, or how much debt it could carry, and show exactly which assumptions are driving the answer.

cards.q: How should a model be laid out across tabs, and why does that structure matter more than it sounds like it should?
cards.takeaway: Inputs on one tab, calculations in the middle, outputs at the end, with information only flowing forward.
cards.a: The convention is to move left to right: an assumptions tab holding every input the model needs, then the calculation tabs, the three financial statements plus supporting schedules for debt and fixed assets, then an outputs tab carrying the handful of numbers that actually end up in the deck. Information should travel in that one direction, so a calculation tab never reaches forward into an output tab for a value. It matters because models get handed around constantly, and the first thing anyone opening yours will do is hunt for where the inputs live.

cards.q: Why do banker-built models color hardcoded inputs blue and formulas black, and what does a green cell usually mean?
cards.takeaway: Color-coding cells by type lets anyone audit a model's logic at a glance, without opening the formula bar.
cards.a: On the Street, font color is a substitute for documentation: blue marks a hardcoded input typed directly into the cell, black marks a formula that calculates from other cells, and green marks a link pulling in a value from another worksheet or workbook. That convention lets anyone glance at a tab and instantly separate the assumptions someone is allowed to change from the calculations that shouldn't be touched by hand. Breaking it, a blue cell that's secretly a formula, or a formula colored blue, is one of the fastest ways to look sloppy in front of an MD, because it hides where the model's real control panel is.

cards.q: Your associate opens your revenue build for Ferrow Retail and finds =1200*1.05 typed into a cell. The number it produces is correct. Why is she still unhappy?
cards.takeaway: A number typed inside a formula is an assumption nobody can find and nobody can flex.
cards.a: The 1.05 is a growth assumption, and burying it inside a formula makes it invisible: the cell displays black like every other calculation, so a reviewer scanning the tab has no way of knowing an input is hiding in there. When the MD asks to see 3% growth instead, you have to hunt through formulas one cell at a time rather than retyping one labelled number. The fix is to put 5.0% in its own blue input cell and write =B4*(1+$B$2). Reviewers genuinely go looking for buried hardcodes, and finding one costs you the benefit of the doubt on everything else in the file.

cards.q: You drag your growth formula across the forecast row and every year after the first comes back as zero, even though the growth rate is sitting right there in cell B2. What happened?
cards.takeaway: Copying a formula shifts every reference along with it unless dollar signs pin it in place.
cards.a: Excel references are relative by default, meaning they describe a direction rather than an address: a formula in C4 pointing at B2 really says “two rows up, one column left,” so dragging it right turns B2 into C2, then D2, both of which are empty, and anything multiplied by an empty cell is zero. Typing dollar signs, $B$2, locks the column and the row so the reference stays put wherever the formula lands, and F4 cycles a highlighted reference through the variants. The mixed forms matter too: B$2 locks only the row, which is what you want when the same formula gets copied both across and down a grid.

cards.q: Why do IB analysts build models almost entirely with the keyboard, and which shortcuts should you know cold?
cards.takeaway: Mouse-free navigation is faster and steadier, and interviewers watch for it directly in a live Excel test.
cards.a: Analysts spend most of the workweek inside Excel, so a second saved on every cell-to-cell move compounds fast, and reaching for the mouse breaks the train of thought while building a formula. Interviewers watch how a candidate moves around the sheet almost as closely as whether the final number is right, because mouse-heavy navigation is a tell for inexperience. Know cold: Ctrl+Arrow to jump to the edge of a data block, Ctrl+Shift+Arrow to select to that edge, F4 to cycle a reference between relative and absolute, Ctrl+Alt+V for Paste Special, and Ctrl+` to toggle formula view. These aren't optional polish, they're assumed baseline fluency by the time you're in the room.

cards.q: Walk me through the errors you run into most often in a model, #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE! and #N/A. What is each one actually telling you?
cards.takeaway: Each Excel error names its own cause, so the text in the cell tells you where to start looking.
cards.a: #REF! means a formula is pointing at a cell that no longer exists, almost always because someone deleted a row, a column or a whole tab, and it’s the most destructive of the four because it spreads to everything downstream. #DIV/0! means you divided by zero or by a blank, which turns up constantly in margin and growth lines for a period with no data yet. #VALUE! means you did arithmetic on text, usually a pasted figure carrying a footnote marker or a stray space. #N/A means a lookup ran but found no match, typically a name spelled differently on the two tabs.

cards.q: In your Northbay Logistics model the company should only repay its loan in years when it actually throws off spare cash. How do you write that, and where do IF statements start to get dangerous?
cards.takeaway: IF chooses between two outcomes based on a test, but MIN or MAX usually reads better than nesting them.
cards.a: An IF takes three arguments, a test, the result if the test is true, and the result if it’s false, so =IF(D18>0,D18,0) says sweep the year’s spare cash into the loan if there is any, otherwise pay nothing. You’d also want to cap that payment at the loan still outstanding, and that’s where MIN, which simply returns the smaller of two numbers, is cleaner than a second IF nested inside the first: =MIN(D18,D25). That’s the real point. Two or three IFs stacked inside each other become almost impossible to audit, so reach for MIN or MAX whenever the logic is really just a cap or a floor.

cards.q: You need to pull a comp company's EV/EBITDA multiple from a Comps tab into your output page, but the row order won't stay fixed as companies get added or re-sorted. What's the safer approach?
cards.takeaway: INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP survives inserted rows and reordering; a hardcoded row reference does not.
cards.a: Use INDEX/MATCH, or in modern Excel, XLOOKUP, rather than pointing directly at a specific row, because comps lists get re-sorted, re-ranked, or have companies added mid-deal. MATCH, or XLOOKUP's lookup argument, finds the row position of the company name, and INDEX, or XLOOKUP's return array, pulls the multiple from that row in whichever column you choose, so the formula still finds the right value even after the list changes shape. XLOOKUP is the newer single-function version of the same idea, defaults to an exact match, and can search in either direction, but INDEX/MATCH is still worth knowing cold since not every bank's template or Excel version has XLOOKUP available.

cards.q: You've pulled comps output for Ferrow Retail into a summary page using live formulas, and now need to send a static snapshot to the deal team that won't change later. What's the move?
cards.takeaway: Paste Special > Values converts live formulas into fixed numbers, severing the link to their source cells.
cards.a: Copy the range, then Paste Special (Ctrl+Alt+V, or the classic Alt+E, S, V) and choose "Values" instead of a normal paste, which pastes the calculated result as a static number and strips out the underlying formula along with any link to the source cells or tabs. That's the standard way to freeze a snapshot before sending a model externally, turning a live comps pull into a fixed exhibit that won't silently change if someone edits the source tab later, and it's also the way to break a link when copying data between workbooks so the destination file doesn't stay dependent on a file that might get moved or deleted. It gets used constantly inside a model too, for example hardcoding a final negotiated purchase price so it stops moving every time a live market-data pull updates.

cards.q: Your VP asks you to build the debt schedule for Northbay Logistics. How should each year be laid out so the balances genuinely carry forward?
cards.takeaway: Every schedule reads beginning balance, plus and minus the period’s activity, equals ending balance.
cards.a: Every roll-forward uses the same four lines: a beginning balance, the additions during the period, the reductions during the period, and an ending balance that is just those three added together. What makes it a schedule rather than a table is that the next period’s beginning balance is a direct reference to the prior period’s ending balance and nothing else, no retyping and no arithmetic in that cell. The identical block works for debt, where the activity is borrowings and repayments, for fixed assets, where it’s capital spending and depreciation, and for share count. Interviewers like it because any wrong number traces back to one line in one year.

cards.q: How would you build a clean scenario toggle in a model, say switching between a Base Case and Downside Case set of assumptions, without breaking anything downstream?
cards.takeaway: A single toggle cell, driven by one dropdown, should be the only thing every downstream formula reads.
cards.a: The clean pattern is one dedicated toggle cell, built with a data validation dropdown. Number the cases, 1 for Base and 2 for Downside, and every assumption with more than one version can be written as =CHOOSE($B$2,BaseValue,DownsideValue). If you would rather the dropdown showed the words, use =IF($B$2="Base",BaseValue,DownsideValue) instead, since CHOOSE needs a number from 1 upwards and errors on text or on zero. Either way every such formula reads that same single toggle, so flipping the dropdown once cascades through the entire model instantly. The discipline is that no downstream formula ever hardcodes its own scenario choice; everything points back to the one switch, so there's exactly one cell to check to know which case the model is currently showing.

cards.q: Your associate flags that changing the D&A assumption in your Ferrow Retail model doesn't move the ending cash balance. What's the likely problem?
cards.takeaway: In a properly linked model, one input change ripples through all three statements to the cash balance.
cards.a: In a correctly built model, D&A hits the income statement, reducing pre-tax income and taxes, flows into the cash flow statement as a non-cash add-back, and reduces the PP&E balance on the balance sheet; the cash flow statement's ending cash then becomes the balance sheet's cash line. If changing D&A doesn't move ending cash, a link is broken somewhere in that chain, most often the CFS add-back is hardcoded instead of pulling from the income statement, or the balance sheet's cash cell isn't actually pointing at the CFS's ending-cash line. Trace it cell by cell with Ctrl+[ to find precedents rather than guessing, confirming each statement genuinely pulls live from the one before it.

cards.q: Before sending your Bramwell & Co. LBO model to the MD, how do you sanity-check that it isn't secretly broken?
cards.takeaway: A visible balance check and error traps catch a broken model before your MD does.
cards.a: Every balance sheet should carry a check row, typically =Total Assets - Total Liabilities and Equity, wrapped in something like =IF(ROUND(Assets-Liabilities,0)=0,"OK","ERROR") so it's impossible to miss the moment the sheet stops balancing. Beyond that, wrap fragile formulas, lookups, divisions, anything that depends on an input existing, in IFERROR so a missing value produces a visible flag instead of a #N/A or #DIV/0! buried in a cell nobody's looking at, and scan the model with Ctrl+` or Excel's formula-auditing tools before circulating it. The habit that actually matters in an interview is naming this discipline unprompted: a model that runs without errors but was never checked for balance is not considered done on the Street.

cards.q: While building the debt schedule for the Bramwell & Co. LBO, Excel throws a circular reference warning. Why did that happen, and how do you handle it?
cards.takeaway: Interest on an average or closing debt balance creates the loop; interest on the opening balance avoids it entirely.
cards.a: The loop appears when interest expense is calculated on a debt balance that the interest itself helps determine. Compute interest on the average or closing balance for the period and you get a genuine circle: interest reduces the cash flow available to repay debt, the repayment changes the closing balance, and the closing balance changes the interest. Excel cannot resolve that on its own, so it throws a circular reference warning, or returns zeros and errors. It is worth being precise here, because it is a modelling choice rather than something inherent to debt schedules: calculating interest on the opening balance breaks the loop completely, which is why plenty of models do exactly that and never see a circular reference at all. If you do want average-balance interest, turn on iterative calculation (File > Options > Formulas > Enable iterative calculation) so Excel recalculates until it converges, and build in a circularity breaker switch, a cell or checkbox that can force interest expense to zero, so an unrelated error elsewhere does not spin the whole model into cascading #REF or #VALUE errors.

cards.q: Your MD wants a table showing the Bramwell & Co. LBO's exit IRR across a range of exit multiples and entry leverage levels. What Excel feature builds this in one shot?
cards.takeaway: A two-variable data table recalculates one output across every combination of two input ranges automatically.
cards.a: Excel's Data Table, under What-If Analysis, recalculates a single output formula across every combination of two input ranges without you writing a formula in each cell. You lay out a grid with one variable's values down the left column (say, exit multiples), the other across the top row (leverage levels), put the output formula, like IRR, in the top-left corner cell, then select the whole grid and tell Excel which cell each axis should feed as the row input and column input. Excel substitutes each combination in turn and fills the grid, which is also why large data tables can noticeably slow down recalculation. It's the standard way to hand an MD a range of outcomes instead of a single point estimate.
