cards.q: The MD wants to know what gross margin Calder Foods has to reach for EBITDA to break even. The model is built, but it only runs forwards. What do you reach for?
cards.takeaway: Goal Seek runs a model backwards, solving for the one input that lands an output on a chosen target.
cards.a: Goal Seek, under What-If Analysis, asks for exactly three things: the cell holding the output, the value you want that cell to equal, and the single input cell Excel is allowed to change. It then iterates until the output hits the target. Think of it as the mirror image of a data table: a data table shows you many outputs across a grid of inputs, while Goal Seek fixes the output and hands you back the input. Two cautions worth saying out loud in an interview, it overwrites the input cell permanently, so note the original value first, and it solves for one variable only.

cards.q: An analyst rolls off the deal and you inherit her half-finished Ferrow Retail model the night before it goes to the client. How do you get comfortable with it?
cards.takeaway: Find the inputs first, then trace one important output all the way back to them before touching anything.
cards.a: Orient before you edit. Read the tab order to see how the model is meant to flow, then find the blue cells, since those are the control panel and they tell you what the builder treated as an assumption. Pick one number that matters, ending cash or the final value, and walk it backwards with Ctrl+[ or Trace Precedents until you land on those inputs, which tells you quickly whether the plumbing is live or partly typed in. F5 then Special then Constants will surface hardcoded values typed loose into cells. It will not catch a number buried inside a formula, because that cell counts as a formula rather than a constant; for those, Ctrl+` toggles Show Formulas so you can scan a row and see them. Finally, flex an assumption whose direction you already know and confirm the outputs move the right way.

name: The Investment Banking Interview
description: The resume walk, the behavioural questions, and how to handle both well.
intro: You’ve worked through ten decks of technical material, which means the harder half of the preparation is already behind you. This deck is about the other half: the questions that have nothing to do with valuation, and the delivery that decides whether your technical work ever gets seen. None of it is about performing a character, and nothing here will tell you what your story should be, because that part is yours. What it covers is what each question is really testing, the shape of an answer that lands, and how to stay steady when a conversation goes somewhere you didn’t plan for. Read it once early, then again the week of.

cards.q: An interviewer opens with “so, tell me about yourself.” You have a resume walk prepared and ready to go. Are these the same question, and if not, how do they differ?
cards.takeaway: Tell me about yourself asks who you are now, the resume walk asks how you got here.
cards.a: They overlap, but the scope is different. Tell me about yourself invites a short, present-tense framing: what you’re doing now, what pulled you toward finance, and what you’re looking for next, usually inside a minute. The resume walk is chronological and longer, tracing the decisions that connect one line of the page to the next. If you answer the opener with a full four-minute history you’ve misread the room, and most interviewers will politely let you keep going rather than stop you.

cards.q: “Walk me through your resume.” It’s the first question in most banking interviews, and it sounds like a formality. What is the interviewer actually testing, and how should the answer be shaped?
cards.takeaway: A resume walk is a story about choices, not a list of jobs, and it should end pointing at this seat.
cards.a: Nobody needs the page read back to them, they have it in front of them. What’s being tested is whether your path has a logic to it and whether you can narrate something clearly under mild pressure, which is a fair share of what a junior banker does on a call. Move roughly forward in time, give the most airtime to the two most recent and most relevant experiences, and at each step say why you made the move rather than only what the role was. Land the last sentence on why that path leads here.

cards.q: “Why investment banking?” What does a credible answer actually contain, and which answers quietly hurt you?
cards.takeaway: A credible answer names the work you want to do, not the prestige, the pay, or the pace.
cards.a: Two things are being checked: that you understand what the job really involves day to day, and that your reasons will survive a bad month. The answers that fall flat are the interchangeable ones, that you like finance, that you’ll learn a lot, that it’s fast-paced, because they would apply equally to a dozen other jobs. Stronger answers point at something specific: the analytical work of putting a value on a business, seeing how large decisions actually get made, a moment in a class or a role that made that concrete. Pay and prestige are real motivations, they just don’t predict who stays.

cards.q: You’re interviewing with a mid-sized bank on Thursday and a much larger one on Friday, and both will ask “why us?” How do you get specific without sliding into flattery?
cards.takeaway: Name something true about the bank that would change your actual day, not its reputation.
cards.a: Telling a bank that it’s excellent tells them nothing, since every candidate says it. Useful specifics are the things that genuinely differentiate the seat: the group’s sector focus, the size of deals a first-year would touch, how lean the teams run, whether the programme is generalist or you’re placed straight into a group. Anything concrete you learned from someone who works there counts, provided you can say what you learned and not just who you spoke to. The simplest test is to paste a rival bank’s name into your answer, and if it still reads fine, you don’t have an answer yet.

cards.q: “What’s your greatest weakness?” Why does a polished answer like “I care too much about getting things right” usually cost you more than an honest one?
cards.takeaway: The weakness question tests self-awareness, so a disguised strength answers a different question badly.
cards.a: Interviewers have heard the perfectionist answer hundreds of times and read it as either a genuine lack of self-knowledge or an unwillingness to be candid, and both matter in a job where you have to flag your own mistakes quickly and without being asked. A real answer names something true but survivable, ideally not the central requirement of the role, then spends most of its length on what you’ve done about it and what changed. Strengths work the same way in reverse: claim one, then give the evidence, because an adjective with nothing behind it is only a word.

cards.q: Your interviewer asks for a time you handled a difficult deadline. What’s the shape of a strong behavioural answer, and how do you use that shape without sounding like you’re reciting it?
cards.takeaway: Set the scene fast, spend the answer on what you personally did, then close on a concrete result.
cards.a: Most behavioural answers work in three parts: a brief situation so the listener knows the stakes, then the actions you took, then the outcome. The common failure is two minutes of background and thirty seconds on your own contribution, when that middle stretch is the only part being assessed. Keep the setup to a couple of sentences, say I rather than we when describing what you did, and finish with something specific enough to picture, a number, a decision that got made, a deadline that got met. Rehearsing the shape is sensible, memorising the sentences is what makes an answer sound canned.

cards.q: “Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone on a team.” The interviewer will never check the story, so what are they actually listening for?
cards.takeaway: Conflict questions test how you talk about people you disagree with, not whether you won.
cards.a: The substance of the disagreement matters far less than how you describe the other person. An answer that casts a teammate as lazy or slow tells the interviewer roughly how you’ll sound about a colleague at two in the morning in a deal room, which is exactly the risk being screened for. What lands is a story where the other side held a reasonable position, you did something concrete to understand or resolve it, and the working relationship came out intact. A real, modest disagreement beats a dramatic one, and a resolution where you changed your own mind is not the weak version.

cards.q: “Tell me about a time you failed.” Why does the reflection at the end of that answer carry more weight than the failure at the start of it?
cards.takeaway: The failure is only the setup, what you changed afterwards is the actual answer.
cards.a: Everyone has failed at something, so the failure by itself carries almost no information. What the question separates is people who can own an outcome and learn from it from people who deflect, quietly blame someone else, or reach for something so trivial that nothing was ever at stake. Pick something that genuinely went wrong, state your own part in it without an alibi, then give the back half of the answer to what you understood afterwards and what you did differently the next time. In a job where juniors make real mistakes on live documents, that pattern is the entire point of asking.

cards.q: “Where do you see yourself in five years?” Analyst programmes typically run two or three, and everyone in the room knows it. What is the question really getting at?
cards.takeaway: Five-year questions test whether your ambitions and this job point in a compatible direction.
cards.a: There’s an honest tension here and interviewers are aware of it: the programme is finite, plenty of people move on afterwards, and nobody expects someone in their early twenties to have the next decade mapped out. What’s being checked is that the next few years are a deliberate choice rather than a default, and that you aren’t describing a plan this seat plainly cannot serve. A workable answer commits to doing the analyst job well and being genuinely useful to a team, then describes the direction you’re drawn to in terms of the work rather than a job title. Claiming you’ll be a lifer tends to read as false.

cards.q: Halfway through the interview: “so, what deal or market have you been following?” How do you talk about it in a way that shows judgement rather than just recall?
cards.takeaway: Say what happened, why it happened, and what you think, with the last part carrying the weight.
cards.a: Facts anyone could take from a headline prove nothing, because the interviewer has read the same headline. A good answer moves in three steps: what happened, in about two sentences, then why the buyer or the market did it, meaning the strategic or financial logic, then your own view, including where you think the risk sits or what would have to be true for it to work. Only that third step shows judgement. Choose something you actually find interesting and can hold up under two follow-up questions, rather than the biggest transaction of the year that you only skimmed.

cards.q: The interviewer glances at the clock and says “we’ve got five minutes left, do you have any questions for me?” What does the question you pick actually signal?
cards.takeaway: Your question shows what you think the job is, so ask something only this person could answer.
cards.a: This is still part of the assessment, and passing entirely tends to read as indifference. Questions whose answers sit on the bank’s website, or that ask what an analyst does all day, suggest you haven’t done the reading. What works is drawn from the person in front of you: how a recent staffing actually ran, what surprised them in their first year, how feedback reaches juniors in their group, what they’d want a new analyst to be good at on day one. Ask because you want to know, then listen, because the follow-up you ask says more than the opening question did.

cards.q: Mid-interview you’re asked a multi-step technical question, and for a second your mind goes completely blank. How do you think out loud instead of freezing?
cards.takeaway: Say the first true thing you know out loud, then reason forward one step at a time.
cards.a: Silence is the expensive part, because from the other side of the table thinking and drowning look identical. Buy a beat honestly, repeating the question back or asking a clarifying question is perfectly acceptable, then start from something you’re certain of and build outward one step at a time, naming each assumption as you make it. Being talked through a wrong turn is normal, and often reads better than a fast correct answer, since much of the actual job is reasoning aloud with someone more senior. Close by checking the result against common sense rather than stopping the moment a number appears.

cards.q: An interviewer asks you something technical you have genuinely never seen before. What’s the best available move, and why is answering confidently anyway the worst one?
cards.takeaway: Say what you don’t know, offer how you’d work it out, and let the interviewer take it from there.
cards.a: Every interviewer knows there are things you haven’t covered yet, so one gap is rarely fatal on its own. Bluffing is closer to fatal, because it’s usually transparent, and it suggests you might do the same on a live model where a wrong number reaches a client. Say plainly that you’re not sure, then give whatever you do have, an adjacent concept, the logic you’d reason from, or how you’d go and find out. Then let it go and answer the next question well, because carrying the last one around with you costs more than the gap ever did.

cards.q: You’ve been invited to a superday: five back-to-back thirty-minute interviews with people at different levels. What does that format change about how you prepare?
cards.takeaway: Five interviewers compare notes afterwards, so it has to be the same story every time.
cards.a: A superday is a run of short interviews on one day, and afterwards those people sit in a room and compare impressions before anyone gets a call. That makes consistency matter more than polish: if your reason for wanting banking shifts between the second conversation and the fourth, someone will notice it in the debrief. It also means each conversation starts from nothing, so repeating your best material is expected rather than lazy, and the energy you bring to the fifth counts as much as the first. Treat the repetition as an advantage, you get several attempts at landing the same point.

cards.q: You’re two sentences into an answer when the interviewer cuts across you and says flatly, “I don’t think that’s right.” What’s happening, and how do you handle it?
cards.takeaway: Pushback tests composure, so answer the challenge itself and ignore the tone it arrived in.
cards.a: Sometimes the interviewer genuinely disagrees, sometimes they’re testing whether you collapse or dig in irrationally when someone senior pushes back, which happens constantly in the real job. Either way the move is the same: don’t rush to agree, and don’t defend by talking louder. Ask which part they’re questioning, restate your reasoning in a single sentence, and change your answer if their point is better than yours, saying so plainly. Being persuaded is a good outcome, and so is holding a position calmly with a reason attached. What reads badly is instant collapse, or visible irritation.

cards.q: Two candidates handle the technical questions equally well and only one gets the offer. What tends to separate them, and why does the other one usually never find out?
cards.takeaway: Most close rejections turn on whether people wanted you next to them at 1am, not a missed question.
cards.a: Underneath the structure, interviewers are answering something unglamorous: would I want this person on my team at one in the morning on a Sunday. The things that quietly cost people offers are rarely technical, they’re being hard to talk to, treating a junior interviewer or a recruiter differently from a senior one, sounding so rehearsed that nothing about you is readable, showing no curiosity about the work, or being unable to say anything specific about why you’re there. Almost none of it gets fed back, because recruiting feedback is thin and the honest version is awkward to give. It’s also the most fixable part.

name: Case Interview Structuring
description: How to build, communicate, and adapt a live case structure under interview pressure, not just which frameworks to memorize.
intro: Case interviews aren't won by memorizing a list of frameworks, they're won by how you structure, communicate, and adapt your thinking live, in real time, in front of an interviewer. This deck focuses on the process itself: breaking a broad prompt into a MECE issue tree, framing your structure out loud in the first few minutes, leading with a hypothesis instead of exploring everything equally, and recovering cleanly when new information proves your first structure wrong. If you already know your frameworks and want to sharpen how you actually run a case, this is built for that.

cards.q: You keep hearing that consulting firms interview you with something called a case. What actually is a case interview, and why do firms run one instead of just asking about your résumé?
cards.takeaway: A case interview is a short business problem you solve out loud, with the interviewer, in real time.
cards.a: The interviewer describes a client situation, say a food company whose profits have slipped, and you work it through out loud over roughly twenty to forty minutes: asking for data, doing arithmetic on paper, and finishing with a recommendation. Firms run cases because the job itself is being handed a messy problem, often in an industry you know nothing about, and having to break it apart quickly. A résumé shows what you have already done, while a case shows how you think when you don’t yet know the answer.

cards.q: A friend tells you the case is a test of business knowledge, so you should spend the week memorizing industry facts. Is that right, and what is the interviewer actually scoring?
cards.takeaway: They score how you break the problem down, handle numbers, judge, and explain, not what you already know.
cards.a: Interviewers are watching four things: whether you split the problem into sensible parts, whether you’re comfortable doing arithmetic out loud and saying what the number means, whether your judgement about the business is sensible, and whether you communicate clearly enough to sit in front of a client. Industry knowledge isn’t on that list. The interviewer will hand you every fact you need, because in the actual job consultants get staffed on industries they have never touched and are expected to get up to speed from the data in front of them.

cards.q: It’s the morning of your first consulting interview and you have no idea how the next forty minutes are meant to go. What are the phases of a case, and roughly how long does each one take?
cards.takeaway: Prompt, clarify, structure, analysis, recommendation, with the analysis taking most of the clock.
cards.a: The interviewer reads the prompt while you take notes, about a minute or two. You ask a couple of clarifying questions, take a short silence to build your structure, and present it, three or four minutes in total. Then comes the analysis, the long stretch at roughly fifteen to twenty-five minutes, usually including a chart to read and some arithmetic. You close with a recommendation in a minute or two. Timings vary by firm and by round, but the shape rarely does, and knowing it stops you from spending ten minutes on a structure meant to take three.

cards.q: You’ve just been given the prompt: Calder Foods is thinking about buying a smaller rival. Before you start structuring, what should you ask, and which questions are actually worth the interviewer’s time?
cards.takeaway: Ask only what would change the shape of your structure, then repeat the objective back and go quiet.
cards.a: Ask two or three questions, and only ones whose answers would change how you structure. The three that usually earn their place are what success looks like in numbers, how the client actually makes money, and whether there’s a hard constraint like a budget, a deadline, or a brand they won’t give up. Questions that wouldn’t move your structure, industry trivia or data you’d be handed anyway, read as stalling. Restate the objective in your own words before you take your silent structuring time, so you and the interviewer are solving the same problem.

cards.q: What does MECE actually mean, and why does it matter for how you structure a case?
cards.takeaway: MECE means your buckets don't overlap and together cover the whole problem, so nothing's double-counted or missing.
cards.a: MECE stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: each branch of your structure shouldn't overlap with another, and together the branches should cover the entire problem. In a case, that keeps you from counting the same driver twice under two different buckets, and from leaving an entire category of the problem unexamined. The practical test isn't reciting the acronym, it's asking yourself, before you speak, whether a given fact could plausibly belong to two of your buckets at once, or whether there's a whole area your structure doesn't touch. Real interview structures are rarely perfectly MECE, but they should be close enough that the interviewer never has to ask "where would that go?"

cards.q: NorthPeak Airlines, a regional airline, comes to you because profits fell 20% last year and the CEO wants to know why. How do you build an issue tree to break that question down?
cards.takeaway: Split the driving question into MECE branches, then keep splitting until each branch is a fact you could go verify.
cards.a: Start with the driving question at the top of the page, why did NorthPeak's profit fall 20%, and split it into its first MECE layer: since profit equals revenue minus cost, one branch is revenue and the other is cost. Each branch then splits again, revenue into price and volume, cost into fixed and variable, and volume can split further into individual routes or ticket classes if that's where the real story lives. Keep branching until each end node is something you could actually go check with a number, like "average fare on the Denver-Boise route," not a vague theme like "market conditions." The finished tree becomes your map for deciding which branches are worth digging into first, not just a diagram you draw and set aside.

cards.q: You've just heard the prompt and taken your silent structuring time. How should you actually lay out and walk the interviewer through your structure in the next few minutes?
cards.takeaway: State the objective, name your buckets top-down, then say which branch you'd start with and why.
cards.a: Open by restating the objective in your own words so the interviewer knows you understood the question, then walk through your structure top-down: name the two or three main buckets before diving into any sub-branch, so the interviewer can follow the shape of your thinking before the detail. Say each bucket out loud as a short label, not a paragraph, drawing it on paper as you talk if you have one in front of you. Close by telling the interviewer which branch you'd want to start with and why, since a structure that never turns into a starting point is just a list. The whole moment should take well under two minutes, structure is meant to set up the conversation, not replace it.

cards.q: Someone hands you a list of case frameworks: profitability, the 3Cs, the 4Ps, Porter’s Five Forces. What is each one actually for?
cards.takeaway: Each named framework is a checklist for one kind of question, not a general purpose case answer.
cards.a: A profitability tree splits profit into revenue and cost and keeps splitting to find which piece moved. The 3Cs, customer, competition and company, size up where a client stands in a market. The 4Ps, product, price, place and promotion, cover how a product gets taken to market. Porter’s Five Forces, rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power, judge how structurally attractive an industry is. Treat them the way a pilot treats a checklist, as a quick test of whether your own structure has a hole in it, rather than as the structure itself.

cards.q: What's the essential difference between a profitability case and a market-entry case, and how does it change the driving question you're answering?
cards.takeaway: Profitability cases diagnose why a number moved; market-entry cases decide whether to make a move at all.
cards.a: A profitability case starts from a problem that's already happened, profit or margin has moved in the wrong direction, and the driving question is diagnostic: which specific lever, price, volume, fixed cost, or variable cost, actually caused the change, and what should the client do about it. A market-entry case starts from a decision the client hasn't made yet, whether to enter a new market, launch a product, or make an acquisition, and the driving question is evaluative: is this worth doing, compared to the alternative of not doing it. That distinction should reshape your structure, not just your opening line: a profitability tree branches through revenue and cost hunting for the delta, while a market-entry tree branches through market attractiveness, the client's ability to win in it, and the financial return, because you're building a case for or against a decision rather than diagnosing what already broke.

cards.q: What's the difference between reciting a memorized framework and building a structure live for the prompt in front of you, and why can interviewers usually tell?
cards.takeaway: A memorized framework ignores the specific prompt; a live structure is built from the actual facts you were given.
cards.a: A scripted framework is a generic template, the classic profitability tree or 4Ps, recited the same way regardless of what the prompt actually said, and it shows up as buckets that don't quite fit: a market-entry structure applied to a cost problem, or category names that don't match the client in the prompt. A structure built live starts from the specific facts and objective you were just given and only borrows the shape of a familiar framework where it genuinely applies, which is why it sounds tailored, using the client's actual situation, numbers, and constraints instead of generic labels. Interviewers can tell the difference almost immediately because a scripted structure tends to arrive too fast, sound identical to the last several candidates, and fall apart the moment a follow-up question pushes on a branch that doesn't actually apply here. The fix isn't memorizing more frameworks, it's practicing the underlying skill, breaking a novel question into MECE parts, so you can build the right structure for whatever prompt shows up.

cards.q: Your first interview was a back-and-forth where the interviewer drove every step, and your second let you run the case yourself. What’s the difference between those two styles, and what changes for you?
cards.takeaway: Interviewer-led cases hand you one question at a time, candidate-led ones make you pick the next move.
cards.a: In an interviewer-led case the interviewer sets the sequence and hands you one question at a time, so the skill is answering each one crisply and completely, then stopping rather than wandering ahead. In a candidate-led case you drive: after your structure you decide what to ask for next, when a branch is settled, and when to move on, so the risk is stalling or drifting. Firms differ, some lean consistently one way and many sit in between, and the style can change between rounds. Your structure has to be just as good either way, what changes is who chooses the next step.

cards.q: What does it mean to be "hypothesis-driven" in a case, and how is it different from just working through your structure branch by branch in order?
cards.takeaway: Lead with your best guess at the answer, then test it first, instead of exploring every branch equally.
cards.a: Being hypothesis-driven means forming an early, informed guess about what the answer probably is, based on the prompt and the first facts you're given, and then using your structure to go test that guess first rather than working through every branch in the order you listed them. It's different from exhaustive branch-by-branch exploration, which treats every part of the tree as equally likely to hold the answer and burns limited case time confirming things that were never really in question. A hypothesis isn't a guess you're married to, if the data doesn't support it, you drop it and form a new one, but leading with one gives you a reason to ask for the data that actually matters instead of every data point available. It mirrors how real consulting engagements run: you rarely have time to check everything, so you prioritize based on what's most likely to be true and most valuable to confirm.

cards.q: You’ve laid out four branches for Northbay Logistics and the interviewer says, “where would you like to start?” How do you choose, and what do you actually say?
cards.takeaway: Start where the money is biggest and the answer is quickest to check, and say that reason out loud.
cards.a: Two tests settle it: which branch could plausibly account for most of the gap, and which one you could close fastest with data the interviewer is likely holding. Then say the reason aloud, for example “labor is roughly seventy per cent of Northbay’s cost base, so a small move there outweighs anything on price, I’d start there.” Naming the criterion is half of what’s being graded, and it gives the interviewer a cheap way to redirect you if they’d rather begin elsewhere. Picking a branch silently looks like guessing, even when the pick is right.

cards.q: Fifteen minutes into a case for Bramwell & Co., new data makes it clear your original structure is aimed at the wrong problem. What do you do?
cards.takeaway: Name the mismatch out loud, adjust the structure on the spot, and keep going, don't pretend nothing changed.
cards.a: The worst move is plowing ahead on a structure you already know doesn't fit, or quietly abandoning it without saying anything, both leave the interviewer unsure whether you've noticed the problem at all. Instead, name it directly: "this new data suggests the issue is really about X, not Y, let me adjust my structure," then briefly restate the one or two branches that change. You don't need to rebuild the whole tree from scratch, usually only the branch that's now wrong needs to move, the rest of your structure often still holds. Interviewers read a clean recovery as a strong signal, real client work is full of information that overturns your first hypothesis, and handling it calmly is closer to the actual job than never being wrong in the first place.

cards.q: You've spent 25 minutes working through Ferrow Retail Group's declining store profitability and found the real driver is rising labor cost at a handful of underperforming stores, not weak sales. How do you wrap up the case?
cards.takeaway: Lead with the recommendation, back it with your top two or three findings, then flag the key risk.
cards.a: Synthesis means answering the original question directly, not narrating everything you did to get there, so lead with the recommendation itself: Ferrow should address labor cost at the specific underperforming stores rather than launch a broad sales initiative. Back it up with the two or three findings that actually drove that answer, in this case that labor cost per store rose faster than revenue at a specific subset of locations while sales held roughly flat elsewhere, skipping the dead ends you explored along the way. Name the biggest risk or open question, for example whether the labor cost spike is a one-off staffing issue or a structural wage trend, and what you'd want to check next to be sure. A good close takes well under a minute and could stand alone as the answer, even if the interviewer heard nothing else you said.

cards.q: The prompt is about falling margins at a specialty chemicals distributor and you have never heard of that industry in your life. How do you structure it without faking knowledge you don’t have?
cards.takeaway: Every business buys something, adds something, and sells it, so structure the economics, not the industry.
cards.a: Say plainly that you’re not familiar with the industry and ask one or two questions about how the client makes money: what it sells, who buys it, and what its largest costs are. Then structure the economics rather than the sector, revenue as price times volume, cost as what the client buys plus what it costs to operate, and only add industry-specific branches once the interviewer has given you the background. Interviewers expect this and volunteer the context, because their own consultants land on unfamiliar industries constantly. Guessing at jargon you don’t understand costs far more than admitting the gap in one sentence.

cards.q: Meridian Health, a hospital group, wants to cut the time patients wait in its emergency department. There’s no profit in the objective at all. How do you structure a case like that?
cards.takeaway: When profit isn’t the goal, structure the process the metric travels through, step by step.
cards.a: A profit tree is one shape of structure, not the only one. Turn the goal into a measurable number first, here the average minutes between a patient arriving and being seen, then break the problem along the path that number travels: arrival, triage, waiting for a bed, treatment, and discharge, asking at each step where the queue builds. Splitting demand against capacity is a second workable cut. Public sector, non-profit and operations cases come up regularly, and they are exactly where a memorized profit framework falls apart while a structure built from the objective still holds.

cards.q: Halverson Industries is losing money on its core manufacturing business and separately weighing whether to enter a new overseas market. How do you build a structure that handles both a profitability problem and a market-entry decision in the same case?
cards.takeaway: Treat it as two connected trees: diagnose the core problem first, then use that answer to inform the entry decision.
cards.a: Resist the urge to mash both prompts into one tree, build two separate MECE structures, a profitability tree for the manufacturing decline and a market-entry tree for the overseas decision, and connect them explicitly rather than blending their branches together. Sequence matters: diagnosing the core profitability problem first usually matters more, since a company bleeding cash domestically has a weaker case for funding an expansion, and what you learn there, for instance whether the problem is temporary or structural, directly changes how attractive the new market decision looks. State that sequencing out loud to the interviewer before you start, for example "I'd want to understand the manufacturing issue first, since it affects how much capacity Halverson has to fund entering a new market," so the connection between the two trees is clear rather than left implicit. The goal isn't a single unified diagram, it's showing you can hold two structures in mind at once and reason about how the answer to one changes the other.

name: Market Sizing & Guesstimates
description: How to structure a defensible estimate under uncertainty when an interviewer asks you to size something with no data given.
intro: Market sizing questions, how many piano tuners are in a city, how big is the market for a new product, are a consulting-interview staple precisely because there's no dataset to recall, only a structure to build live. This deck breaks down the toolkit: top-down versus bottom-up thinking, clean population segmentation, sanity-checking your own numbers, and the habits that separate a defensible estimate from a guess. Work through it and the next guesstimate question won't feel like a trick, it'll feel like a format you already know.

cards.q: When an interviewer asks you to estimate something like the number of piano tuners in a city, what are they actually evaluating?
cards.takeaway: They're grading your structure and logic under uncertainty, not whether you nail the exact number.
cards.a: Market sizing questions test whether you can build a clear, logical structure to estimate an unknown quantity when you don't have the data memorized. Interviewers care about how you break the problem down, state your assumptions out loud, and adjust when something seems off, not whether your final number matches a figure sitting in a database somewhere. A well-reasoned estimate that lands in a plausible range beats a lucky guess with no visible logic every time. The real skill being tested is comfort with ambiguity, can you make steady progress on a problem that hands you no clean, given inputs.

cards.q: What's the difference between a top-down and a bottom-up approach to market sizing, and when should you use each?
cards.takeaway: Top-down starts from a big number and narrows it down; bottom-up builds the estimate up from a single unit.
cards.a: A top-down approach starts with a large, known or estimable figure, like a country's population, and narrows it step by step by applying percentages until you reach the answer. A bottom-up approach does the opposite, it starts from a small, concrete unit, like one store's average daily customers, and multiplies up to the whole market. Top-down tends to work well when you have a solid anchor number to start from, while bottom-up is often more defensible when the top-line figure is fuzzy but a single unit of the business is easy to picture. Strong answers sometimes use both directions on the same question, as a way of cross-checking that the two paths land in the same neighborhood.

cards.q: Your interviewer says there’s no data and no calculator, then asks you to size a market. Which handful of numbers is worth carrying into every interview, and how do you use them honestly?
cards.takeaway: Carry a few rough anchors like population, household size and life expectancy, and label them as estimates.
cards.a: A small set of figures does most of the work: world population is roughly 8 billion, a large developed country runs somewhere around 300 to 350 million people, an average household in a wealthy country holds about 2.5 people, and life expectancy sits near 80 years. Carry them as approximations rather than facts, say out loud that you’re approximating, and round them to whatever makes the arithmetic clean. Nobody expects memorized statistics, but the candidate who reaches for a sensible anchor instead of freezing gets moving in seconds rather than minutes.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail's interviewer asks you to estimate how many people in Corvale, a fictional city of 900,000, buy a birthday cake in a given year. How do you segment the population without double-counting or leaving gaps?
cards.takeaway: Split the population into buckets that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, no overlaps, no gaps.
cards.a: The core discipline is MECE: every person in Corvale should fall into exactly one segment, and every segment together should cover the whole population. For a birthday-cake question, splitting by age band, say under 10, 10 to 64, and 65-plus, works cleanly because everyone has exactly one age; splitting by categories like 'families' and 'young professionals' instead risks double-counting a young professional who is also a parent. Once the segments are clean, you can apply a different purchase-rate assumption to each, for instance a different bakery-purchase rate for a young child's party versus an adult birthday, and add the pieces back up knowing nothing was counted twice or missed entirely.

cards.q: An interviewer wants the number of people aged 30 to 44 in Corvale, a fictional city of 900,000, and gives you nothing else. How do you get an age band out of a single population number?
cards.takeaway: Spread the population evenly across a lifespan, then shave the top bands because fewer people reach old age.
cards.a: Start by assuming people are spread roughly evenly across a normal lifespan. If life expectancy is around 80 years, each single year of age holds about one eightieth of the population, so Corvale’s 900,000 people give roughly 11,000 per year of age and a 15-year band comes to about 170,000. Then correct for reality, since the top of the distribution tapers as fewer people reach old age, so trim the bands above 65 and nudge the younger ones up. Stating the flat assumption first and adjusting it afterwards is faster and far more transparent than pretending you know the real age curve.

cards.q: You’ve broken a market into eleven customer segments and the interviewer is starting to look impatient. How do you know when segmenting has stopped adding accuracy?
cards.takeaway: Split a population only where the buying rate genuinely differs, since extra buckets add work, not accuracy.
cards.a: Segmentation earns its keep when two groups would get meaningfully different assumptions, the way under-tens and adults buy birthday cakes at genuinely different rates. If you’d apply the same rate to two buckets, merging them costs you nothing but saves you time. Two to four segments is usually plenty in an interview, and a long list of thin slices tends to manufacture false precision, a number that looks carefully built but now rests on ten guesses instead of three. The interviewer is judging what you chose to care about, not counting your boxes.

cards.q: As you work through a multi-step estimate, how should you handle rounding along the way?
cards.takeaway: Round to clean numbers on purpose, say it out loud, and track which direction each round pushes your answer.
cards.a: Pick simple, round inputs at each step, for example treating a population of 4.3 million as 4 million, and state clearly that you're doing it. This keeps your mental math fast and keeps the interviewer able to follow your logic in real time instead of getting lost in decimals. It also helps to notice whether you're consistently rounding up or down across several steps; if most of your rounds went down to make the math easy, your final number is probably a slight underestimate, and flagging that directly reads as more rigorous than presenting a rounded chain of assumptions as if it were precise.

cards.q: A candidate sizing the annual market for replacement bicycle tires counts every adult in the country and stops there. Which two multipliers did they forget, and how much do they matter?
cards.takeaway: Not everyone in the pool buys, and buyers buy more than once, so multiply by penetration and frequency.
cards.a: Penetration rate is the share of your starting pool who actually own or buy the thing, and frequency is how many times each of those people buys it in a year. Leaving either one out quietly sets it to 100% or to once, which is how estimates end up off by a factor of five. For tires you might start with 40 million adults, assume 20% ride often enough to wear tires out, giving 8 million riders, then assume each replaces about two a year, landing near 16 million tires. Say both multipliers out loud, since they’re usually the two an interviewer pushes on.

cards.q: Walk through how you'd structure an estimate for the number of independent coffee shops in Dunmoor, a fictional mid-size city of 500,000 people.
cards.takeaway: Anchor on population, narrow to regular buyers, then divide by what one shop can realistically serve.
cards.a: Start from Dunmoor's population of 500,000 and estimate the share who buy coffee from a shop a few times a week or more, say 30%, giving roughly 150,000 regular customers. Next estimate how often each of them visits per week, maybe 3 times, and what fraction of those visits go to an independent shop rather than a chain, say half, which works out to about 225,000 independent-shop visits per week. Finally, estimate how many customers one independent shop can realistically serve in a week, perhaps 1,500, and divide, 225,000 divided by 1,500 lands you at roughly 150 independent coffee shops in Dunmoor. Each step used one clean, stated assumption, which is exactly what makes the answer defensible even though none of the inputs were 'known' facts.

cards.q: Partway through an estimate you land on a number, say 40,000 hospital beds in Aldmere, a fictional mid-size country. How do you sanity-check that against something you already know?
cards.takeaway: Convert your estimate to a per-capita rate and compare it to a number you already trust.
cards.a: Raw totals are hard to judge, but rates are easy to sanity check. Take your estimate, divide it by population to get something like 'beds per 1,000 people,' and compare that to a rough figure you're confident is roughly right, such as knowing a typical developed country sits somewhere around three to five hospital beds per 1,000 people. Hold that loosely, because the spread is wide: roughly 2.5 in the US and UK, nearer 8 in Germany, above 12 in Japan and Korea. The check is for order-of-magnitude errors, not small ones. If your derived rate is wildly outside that plausible range, some step upstream is probably off, and it's far easier to catch that with a familiar per-capita ratio than by staring at a seven-digit total. This kind of check is also worth narrating out loud, since it shows the interviewer you're pressure-testing your own math rather than trusting it blindly.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics asks how big the market for delivery vans is. Do they mean how many are on the road or how many get bought each year, and how do you get from one to the other?
cards.takeaway: The installed base is a stock, annual sales are a flow, and the replacement cycle converts between them.
cards.a: A stock is how many exist right now, the installed base, while a flow is how many are bought or replaced over a period. The two can differ by a factor of ten, so ask which one the question means before you calculate anything. The bridge between them is how long the product lasts: if there are roughly 200,000 delivery vans on the road and a van lasts about ten years, then around 20,000 need replacing each year, plus whatever the fleet is growing by. A parts supplier cares about that annual flow, while a fleet software vendor cares about the stock.

cards.q: Your interviewer says a market size should come back in dollars, but everything you’ve built so far is counted in users. How do you convert without inventing a price out of thin air?
cards.takeaway: Chain users to transactions to dollars one multiplier at a time, and name the unit at every step.
cards.a: Treat it as a chain and keep the unit written beside every number so you can see what each multiplication actually does. Users times visits per user per year gives transactions per year, and transactions times the average spend per transaction gives revenue per year. For a coffee app that might be 150,000 users, 40 visits a year each for 6 million transactions, at 8 dollars a visit, which is about 48 million dollars. Price is the input people invent most carelessly, so anchor it on what you’d genuinely expect to pay and tell the interviewer that’s what you did.

cards.q: An interviewer asks you to estimate the number of accordion repair technicians in Velmara, a small fictional country you know almost nothing about. What do you do when you have no anchor data at all?
cards.takeaway: When you lack a direct anchor, build one from a related number you're more confident estimating.
cards.a: Start with whatever you're most confident about, usually total population, then work through a chain of plausible ratios to get closer to the target: how many households might own an accordion, how often an owned instrument needs professional repair, and how many repairs one technician can realistically handle in a year. Say each assumption out loud and flag which ones you're least sure of, since the interviewer usually cares more about watching you reason through genuine uncertainty than about a lucky guess. It's also completely fair to state a reasonable working assumption about Velmara, like an approximate population, if the interviewer hasn't given you one, that's a normal, expected part of the exercise, not a sign that you're stuck.

cards.q: A candidate estimates that Bramwell Fitness's target city has 1.2 million gym memberships in a population of 400,000. What went wrong, and what other mistakes commonly wreck an estimate like this?
cards.takeaway: Watch for nesting errors, unstated assumptions, and any input that's implausible on its face.
cards.a: That example fails a basic plausibility check, it implies each person holds three memberships, which points to a nesting error, some rate probably got applied twice, or applied to the wrong base, like visits per week mistaken for total members. Other common breakdowns include quietly changing an assumption partway through without saying so, stacking several unstated guesses on top of each other until the interviewer can no longer follow the logic, and feeding in an input that's implausible on its own, like assuming 90% of adults belong to a gym. The fix for all of them is the same habit, say every assumption out loud as you make it, and pause to ask whether the resulting number still sounds like something that could be true in the real world.

cards.q: You give your number and the interviewer asks which of your assumptions you’d most want to check before showing it to a client. How do you answer that well?
cards.takeaway: Name the assumption whose plausible range moves the answer most, not the one you happen to like least.
cards.a: Because the estimate is a chain of multiplications, an input that’s off by a factor of two moves the final answer by a factor of two no matter where in the chain it sits. So rank your assumptions by how wide their plausible range is rather than by how uneasy they made you feel. Penetration rates are usually the worst offender, since 10% and 40% are both arguable and that alone swings the answer four-fold, whereas average household size only runs from about 2.2 to 2.8. Naming that one input, and which way it would move things, is the conversation a real team has around a client model.

cards.q: You've landed on a final number, say 60,000 gym memberships in Aldmere. What's the last thing you should do before giving that answer to the interviewer?
cards.takeaway: Zoom out and ask whether the number would surprise a reasonably informed adult, then explain why or adjust.
cards.a: Before saying the number out loud, translate it into something intuitive, like memberships per adult or per household, and ask yourself whether that rate feels plausible given everyday experience. It also helps to briefly restate the chain of assumptions that produced it, since walking back through the logic often surfaces one step that quietly went too high or too low. If the number still feels off, it's better to flag that honestly, something like 'this feels a bit high, and I think it's because of X,' than to present a suspicious number with total confidence, interviewers consistently rate that kind of self-awareness higher than a falsely confident wrong answer.

cards.q: Calder Foods is weighing entry into meal kits in Aldmere, a fictional country of 30 million. Size the annual revenue of that market out loud, then tell the interviewer whether you believe it.
cards.takeaway: Chain households, penetration, frequency and price, then check the total as a per-person number.
cards.a: Thirty million people at roughly 2.5 per household gives 12 million households. Say 30% are urban and affluent enough to be plausible buyers, and that 10% of those actually subscribe, leaving about 360,000 subscribing households. Each takes two kits a week for 50 weeks, so roughly 36 million kits a year, and at 30 dollars a kit the market is a little over a billion dollars. Then check it before you stop: that’s about 35 dollars per person per year against maybe 3,000 dollars of annual grocery spend, close to 1% of the food budget, which is plausible for a category that’s still a niche.

name: Case Maths & Mental Arithmetic
description: The arithmetic cases actually ask for, done quickly, out loud and without a calculator.
intro: Most case interviews contain three or four calculations, none of them hard, all of them done under a stare. Candidates lose more marks on arithmetic than on frameworks, because they either go silent for a minute or come back with a number that is off by a factor of ten. This deck teaches the small set of moves that fix that: rounding sensibly, working in units that keep numbers small, percentages and growth rates, breakevens, and the habit of saying the calculation out loud as you do it. Nothing here needs more than school maths.

cards.q: Why does an interviewer care how you do arithmetic, when the job has Excel?
cards.takeaway: They are testing whether you can stay structured and calm with numbers in front of a client, not whether you can multiply.
cards.a: A consultant sits in meetings where a client says a number and expects a reaction within seconds: is that big, is that plausible, what does it imply? Nobody opens a spreadsheet. The interviewer wants to see that you can take a number, decide what to do with it, do it roughly right, and say what it means, all while talking. Silence and panic are the failures, not being 3% out. So the skills are narration, sensible rounding, and sanity-checking, and a candidate who rounds 47 to 50, says so, and lands close is rated higher than one who gets 47 exactly after a long pause.

cards.q: How should you round in a case, and when should you not?
cards.takeaway: Round to one or two significant figures, say that you are doing it, and keep the direction of the error in mind.
cards.a: Round aggressively but honestly. 47 million customers becomes 50 million; £3.8 becomes £4; 23% becomes a quarter. Say it as you do it, so the interviewer knows the final figure is an estimate, and note which way you rounded, so you can say the true answer is slightly lower. Do not round when the answer hinges on a small difference, such as whether a margin is 4% or 6%, or when the interviewer has given exact figures and clearly wants an exact result. If a rounded answer comes out close to a decision threshold, go back and redo it precisely.

cards.q: What is the fastest way to multiply two awkward numbers, like 340 × 25?
cards.takeaway: Break one number into pieces that are easy to multiply, or swap in a friendlier equivalent like 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
cards.a: Two moves cover most cases. Decompose: 340 × 25 is 300 × 25 plus 40 × 25, which is 7,500 plus 1,000, so 8,500. Or substitute: multiplying by 25 is the same as multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4, so 34,000 ÷ 4 is 8,500. The same trick works for 50 (× 100 ÷ 2), 125 (× 1,000 ÷ 8), and 75 (× 100 × 3 ÷ 4). For something like 18 × 22, use the near-square: 20² minus 2², which is 400 minus 4, so 396. Practise these until they are reflexes and multiplication stops being where you slow down.

cards.q: How do you keep units under control when a case moves between thousands, millions and billions?
cards.takeaway: Pick one unit for the whole calculation, write it down, and convert everything into it before you multiply anything.
cards.a: Most factor-of-a-thousand errors come from mixing units mid-calculation. Before you start, decide: this case is in millions of pounds. Convert every input into that unit and say so. 40 million customers times £15 a year is then 40 × 15 = £600 million, not 600 of something. When you multiply two big numbers, count the zeros separately from the digits: 300,000 × 20,000 is 3 × 2 = 6 followed by five plus four zeros, so 6 billion. Writing the unit at the top of your page and checking each result against it catches nearly every slip.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail's revenue was £820m last year and £900m this year. What is the growth rate, and how do you get it quickly?
cards.takeaway: Growth is the change divided by the starting value: £80m on £820m is a little under 10%.
cards.a: Growth rate is the increase divided by the original figure. The increase is £900m minus £820m, which is £80m. Divided by £820m: 80 ÷ 820 is a bit less than 80 ÷ 800, which would be exactly 10%, so call it just under 10%, about 9.8%. Say the reasoning, because it shows you know the exact answer is slightly below the round one. The classic mistake is dividing by the new figure, 80 ÷ 900, which gives 8.9% and is the wrong ratio. Always divide by where you started.

cards.q: What is the rule of 72, and how do you use it in a case?
cards.takeaway: Divide 72 by the growth rate to get the years it takes something to double; divide by the years to get the rate.
cards.a: At a steady growth rate, a quantity doubles in roughly 72 divided by the rate in years. Growing at 8% a year, revenue doubles in about nine years; at 12%, in six. It works backwards too: if a market doubled in four years, it grew at about 18% a year. In a case this lets you answer questions like what revenue will be in ten years at 7% without compounding by hand: 72 ÷ 7 is about ten, so it doubles. It is an approximation, accurate enough for rates under about 20%, and interviewers know and respect it.

cards.q: How do you calculate a percentage of a number quickly, like 17% of £340m?
cards.takeaway: Build it from 10% and 1%, or from a nearby friendly percentage, and adjust.
cards.a: Ten per cent of £340m is £34m. One per cent is £3.4m, so 7% is about £24m. Add them: £58m. Or go from a friendly number: 20% is £68m, and 3% is about £10m, so 17% is about £58m. Either route takes a few seconds and can be said aloud. The same building blocks handle almost any percentage, and 5% (half of 10%), 25% (a quarter) and 33% (a third) are worth having as reflexes. If the interviewer gives you 17.3%, round to 17% first and mention it.

cards.q: What is breakeven, and how do you calculate it in a case?
cards.takeaway: Fixed costs divided by contribution per unit: the number of units you must sell to cover the costs that do not change with volume.
cards.a: Breakeven is the volume at which revenue exactly covers all costs. Split costs into fixed, which do not change with volume, like rent and salaries, and variable, which do, like materials. Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost per unit, the amount each sale puts toward fixed costs. Breakeven units are fixed costs divided by contribution. If Calder Foods' new bakery costs £2m a year to run, sells loaves at £2 with £1.20 of ingredients, contribution is 80p, and breakeven is £2m ÷ £0.80, which is 2.5 million loaves. Then ask whether that is plausible against the market.

cards.q: How do you estimate a payback period, and why do clients ask for it?
cards.takeaway: Investment divided by the annual cash it generates: the years until the money is back, which is the number a nervous client wants.
cards.a: Payback is the upfront cost of an investment divided by the cash it returns each year. A £6m warehouse for Northbay Logistics that saves £2m a year pays back in three years. It ignores what happens after payback and ignores the time value of money, so it is cruder than NPV, but it answers the question a client actually asks, which is how long they are exposed. In a case, calculate it, say whether three years is fast or slow for the industry, and mention that a full analysis would discount the cash flows. If savings ramp up over time, add year by year until the total passes the investment.

cards.q: Sales went from 100 to 120, then from 120 to 100. Why is the second change not the same percentage as the first?
cards.takeaway: A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not get you back to where you started, because the base changed.
cards.a: The rise is 20 on a base of 100, which is 20%. The fall is 20 on a base of 120, which is 16.7%. Percentages are always relative to the starting point, so the same absolute move is a different percentage going up and coming down. This matters in cases about recoveries: a market that fell 50% needs to rise 100% to recover, not 50%. Interviewers use it to check whether you think about bases. When you calculate any percentage change, say the base you are using out loud.

cards.q: How do you sanity-check an answer before you say it?
cards.takeaway: Compare it with something you already know: population, GDP, a big company's revenue, a typical price.
cards.a: Before you deliver a number, hold it against a benchmark. If your estimate of the UK coffee-shop market comes out at £200 billion, that is about a tenth of GDP, so something is wrong. If it comes to £5 billion, that is roughly £75 per person per year, which is plausible. Keep a few anchors in your head: the UK has about 68 million people and 28 million households; UK GDP is around £2.5 trillion; a large supermarket chain has revenue in the tens of billions. Saying the check aloud is itself impressive, and catching your own error is far better than the interviewer catching it.

cards.q: The interviewer gives you a table with revenue by product line and asks what share the top product is. How do you avoid getting lost?
cards.takeaway: Total first, then the one line you need, then divide, narrating each step.
cards.a: Add the column to get the total, rounding each line as you go and saying the running sum. Then take the top line and divide it by the total. If the top product is £340m of a £1.2bn total, 340 ÷ 1,200 is a bit over a quarter, about 28%. Say what it means: one product is over a quarter of the business, so it is a concentration risk or the core to protect, depending on the case. The failure mode is trying to hold six numbers in your head; write the total down and work from the page.

cards.q: How do you handle a calculation where you realise halfway through that you made a mistake?
cards.takeaway: Say so immediately, fix it, and carry on; the recovery counts for more than the slip cost.
cards.a: Interviewers expect errors, and they are watching how you handle them. The right move is to stop, say that you think you have made a mistake, identify it, and redo that step. Do not try to hide it or fudge the final number to match. A candidate who says 'that should be 60 not 600, let me correct it' has shown exactly the self-checking a firm wants. The wrong move is to carry a number you doubt through three more steps and present it. If you are unsure whether it is wrong, do the sanity check and let that decide.

cards.q: A client asks whether a 3% price rise or a 3% cost cut adds more profit. How do you answer without knowing the numbers?
cards.takeaway: Price rises usually add more, because they go straight to profit while cost cuts only apply to the cost base, which is smaller than revenue.
cards.a: A 3% price rise, if volume holds, adds 3% of revenue to profit, because there is no extra cost. A 3% cut in costs adds 3% of costs to profit. Since costs are less than revenue for any profitable company, the price rise is worth more. If Bramwell & Co. has revenue of £1bn and costs of £900m, the price rise adds £30m and the cost cut adds £27m. The catch is the phrase if volume holds: price rises can lose customers, cost cuts usually do not. So the honest answer is that price is the bigger lever but the riskier one.

cards.q: How do you structure a calculation out loud so the interviewer can follow it?
cards.takeaway: Say the formula first, then the inputs, then each step, then the answer, then what it means.
cards.a: Announce what you are going to calculate and how: 'Breakeven is fixed costs over contribution per unit.' State the inputs and any rounding: 'Fixed costs are £2m; contribution is £2 minus £1.20, so 80p.' Do the arithmetic in steps, each spoken: '£2m over 80p is 2.5 million units.' Give the answer with its unit, and then the implication: 'That is 2.5 million loaves a year, about 7,000 a day, which seems high for one bakery.' Five beats, always in that order. The interviewer can correct an input early, and never has to wonder what you are doing.

cards.q: What are the numbers every candidate should know cold before a case interview?
cards.takeaway: Population and households for your country, a rough GDP, working days in a year, hours in a working week, and a few everyday prices.
cards.a: Have these ready: UK population about 68 million, roughly 28 million households, GDP around £2.5 trillion; US population about 335 million; the world about 8 billion. A working year is about 250 days or 2,000 hours; a year is 52 weeks and 8,760 hours. A typical UK salary is in the low £30,000s. Everyday prices for a coffee, a meal out, a phone contract, a car. Fractions as decimals: 1/8 is 12.5%, 1/6 about 17%, 1/7 about 14%, 1/3 33%. With these you can start any market-sizing or sanity check without having to guess the foundations.

name: Microeconomics & Market Structures
description: Supply, demand, and how competition shapes a market.
intro: Interviewers in business, strategy, and even product roles often lean on basic economic reasoning: supply and demand, how competition shapes pricing, what happens when a market has only a few players instead of many. This deck builds those ideas up from first principles, so if the words "market structure" currently mean nothing to you, that is exactly who this is for. The goal is to be able to reason through an economic scenario out loud, not recite a textbook definition.

cards.q: Before we get to curves and prices: what is a market, and what do economists actually mean by the words supply and demand?
cards.takeaway: Demand is what buyers would buy at every price, supply is what sellers would offer at every price.
cards.a: A market is any arrangement where buyers and sellers come together to trade something, whether that's a weekend produce stall, an online marketplace, or the worldwide market for copper. Demand isn't a single quantity, it's the whole picture of how much buyers would purchase at each possible price, and supply is the mirror image, how much sellers would be willing to produce and offer at each possible price. Because both are lists of price and quantity pairs, they get drawn as curves. Nearly every case that touches pricing, volume, or competition is really a question about one of those two curves.

cards.q: What does the law of demand state?
cards.takeaway: Higher prices mean people buy less; lower prices mean they buy more.
cards.a: The law of demand says that, all else equal, a higher price leads people to buy less of a good, and a lower price leads them to buy more, which is what gives the demand curve its downward slope. It happens because as something gets relatively more expensive, buyers shift toward substitutes that meet the same need for less — the same substitution logic that shows up whenever a case turns on a proposed price change.

cards.q: The demand curve slopes down. Why does the supply curve slope up?
cards.takeaway: A higher price makes production worth it for more sellers, so more units get offered.
cards.a: As price rises, each unit sold becomes more profitable, so existing producers add shifts and new producers decide it's worth entering, and the total quantity offered goes up. Underneath that is a cost story: the cheapest and easiest units get made first, and squeezing out additional units usually costs more per unit, so sellers only go there when the price justifies it. That upward slope is why a burst of demand lifts price in the short run, and why the higher price eventually pulls in the extra supply that cools it back down.

cards.q: What is equilibrium price?
cards.takeaway: Equilibrium is the one price where what buyers want to buy matches what sellers want to sell.
cards.a: Equilibrium price is the price where the quantity buyers want to purchase exactly matches the quantity sellers want to offer, so there’s no leftover surplus and no shortage. Graphically, it’s the point where the supply and demand curves cross, and real markets tend to drift toward this price naturally over time — useful as a baseline anytime a case asks you to reason about where a market's price should settle.

cards.q: A city regulator caps the rent on Halden Square apartments well below what the market would charge. What happens to the number of apartments available, and why?
cards.takeaway: A price held below equilibrium creates a shortage and one held above it creates a surplus.
cards.a: At the capped price, the quantity renters want is larger than the quantity landlords are willing to supply, and that gap is a shortage: waiting lists, units pulled off the market, and rationing by something other than price. The mirror case is a price held above equilibrium, say a legal minimum price on a crop, where sellers offer more than buyers will take and the leftover is a surplus. Equilibrium is the only price that clears both sides, so any price fixed away from it has to show up as one of those two gaps.

cards.q: An interviewer asks whether demand for coffee has fallen when the price of coffee rises and people buy less of it. How do you answer, and why is this the classic trap?
cards.takeaway: A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve, anything else moves the whole curve.
cards.a: Demand hasn't fallen, quantity demanded has. A change in the good's own price just moves you along the existing demand curve, because that curve already tells you what buyers do at every price. The curve itself only shifts when something other than that price changes, like incomes, tastes, the number of buyers, or the price of a substitute, meaning a different product that meets the same need. The same split holds on the supply side, where input costs, technology, and taxes shift the curve while the product's own price moves you along it.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group sells a mid-range kitchen gadget. A viral video sends its customer base sharply higher overnight, while nothing has changed about its costs or supply conditions. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
cards.takeaway: More demand at every price pushes both the price and the quantity sold higher.
cards.a: Demand has risen while supply stayed put, so the entire demand curve shifts to the right, and the new equilibrium sits at both a higher price and a higher quantity. More shoppers now want Ferrow's gadget at every price level, so Ferrow can charge more and still sell more units — at least until supply catches up.

cards.q: What is price elasticity of demand?
cards.takeaway: Elasticity measures how sharply quantity demanded reacts when price moves.
cards.a: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. Demand is “elastic” when a small price move causes a big swing in quantity, typical for goods with close substitutes, and “inelastic” when quantity barely budges even as price changes a lot, typical for necessities with few substitutes. It's a fast gut-check in any pricing case: the more substitutes a product has, the less room there is to raise price without losing volume.

cards.q: What is consumer surplus?
cards.takeaway: Consumer surplus is the extra value buyers get for paying less than they'd have accepted.
cards.a: Consumer surplus is the gap between what consumers were willing to pay for a good and what they actually paid, added up across every buyer in the market. It represents the bonus value consumers walk away with, and on a graph, it’s the area between the demand curve and the market price line — worth having on hand whenever a case asks you to weigh a pricing decision's impact on customers, not just on the firm.

cards.q: What's the difference between fixed costs, variable costs, and marginal cost?
cards.takeaway: Fixed costs ignore volume, variable costs track it, and marginal cost is the cost of one more unit.
cards.a: Fixed costs stay the same no matter how much you produce, like the lease on a factory or the plant manager's salary. Variable costs move with output, like raw materials, packaging, and the hours worked on the line. Marginal cost is what it costs to make one additional unit, which in the short run is essentially that unit's variable cost, since the fixed costs are already paid either way. That distinction is why a plant running below capacity will often take an order priced under its full average cost: as long as the price clears marginal cost, the order still adds something.

cards.q: The CEO of Bramwell & Co. asks you how many units of a new product line the company should manufacture to maximize profit. How would you use marginal cost and marginal revenue to find that point?
cards.takeaway: Keep producing while extra revenue beats extra cost; stop right where they meet.
cards.a: Marginal cost is what it costs Bramwell to produce one more unit, and marginal revenue is what that extra unit brings in. The profit-maximizing move is to keep producing as long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, and stop right at the point where the two are equal, since pushing past that point would only shrink total profit.

cards.q: What are economies of scale, and how can a company get too big for its own good?
cards.takeaway: Cost per unit falls as volume grows, until size adds enough complexity that it starts rising again.
cards.a: Economies of scale means that as a firm produces more, the cost of each unit falls, because fixed costs like a plant or a software platform get spread across more units and inputs get cheaper in bulk. That's much of why scale is a genuine advantage and why large incumbents are hard to unseat. Past some point diseconomies of scale set in, as coordination slows, management layers pile up, and cost per unit climbs again. Plotting average cost against volume gives the familiar U shape, and knowing where a client sits on it decides whether growth actually helps margins.

cards.q: A private equity client is comparing two possible investments: one in an industry where hundreds of small farms sell an identical commodity grain, and one in an industry where a single firm, Bramwell & Co., owns the only patented process for a specialized industrial coating. How would you characterize each market structure, and what does that imply for pricing power?
cards.takeaway: Perfect competition has many price takers; a monopoly has one price setter.
cards.a: The grain market looks like perfect competition: many firms sell identical products and no single one is big enough to move the market price, so each just accepts, or “takes,” the going price. Bramwell & Co. looks like a monopoly: it is effectively the entire market for that coating, giving it real control over price, which typically means higher prices and less output than a competitive market would deliver — and, for the PE client, a very different pricing-power story.

cards.q: NorthPeak Airlines is one of four carriers controlling nearly all the traffic on a regional route. When NorthPeak cuts fares 10%, the other three match the cut within days. What market structure is this, and why does it produce that reactive behavior?
cards.takeaway: A few big firms dominate the market, and each one watches the others' every move.
cards.a: This is an oligopoly: a market controlled by a small number of large firms, where one firm’s decisions, on pricing especially, directly affect the others and usually provoke a response. Airlines are a classic real-world example of this dynamic — a handful of players control most of a route, so a fare cut by one carrier squeezes the others' volume enough that matching it is the safer move.

cards.q: A client runs one of forty coffee shops in a city, each with its own menu and its own regulars. Where does that sit among the four market structures, and how do the four compare?
cards.takeaway: The four structures run from many identical sellers to one, and pricing power grows along that line.
cards.a: That's monopolistic competition: many firms competing, but each selling a slightly differentiated product, which buys a little pricing power and no more, since a rival is always a block away. Lined up, the four structures are a spectrum set by how many firms there are and how different their products are. Perfect competition has many firms selling an identical good and no pricing power, monopolistic competition many firms with differentiated goods and a little, oligopoly a handful of large firms that must watch each other, and monopoly a single firm setting price on its own.
