cards.q: A client is weighing whether to enter the industrial water-filtration market, currently held by three incumbents with long-standing patents and multi-year supplier contracts. What would you tell them about barriers to entry here, and how should that shape their entry strategy?
cards.takeaway: Barriers to entry are whatever keeps new competitors from entering and challenging incumbents.
cards.a: A barrier to entry is anything that makes it hard for a new firm to break into a market and compete with the companies already there — think high startup costs, patents, strong brand loyalty, or economies of scale that let incumbents produce more cheaply than a newcomer could. Here, the patents and locked-in supplier contracts are both real barriers, so the client should expect a slow, capital-intensive entry, or consider a partnership or acquisition instead of competing head-on from day one.

cards.q: Calder Foods has earned 30% margins in a plant-based snack niche for three years, and the CEO wants to assume those margins hold for another five. How would you pressure-test that?
cards.takeaway: Unusually high profits attract entrants, and without barriers new supply competes those profits away.
cards.a: High margins are a signal to everyone else in the industry, so the first question is what stops a competitor from copying Calder. If entry is easy, new firms pile in, supply shifts right, price falls, and margins drift toward the level that merely compensates investors for their capital, what economists call zero economic profit. The margins hold only if something protects them: a patent, a brand that's hard to copy, a scale cost advantage, locked-up distribution, or real cost and hassle for a customer who switches. So I'd size those protections first, then stress the plan against two funded entrants arriving in year two.

name: Profitability & Cost Analysis
description: Why profits fall, and how to find the line that actually moved.
intro: Profitability cases are the single most common thing you will meet in a consulting interview, and they all start from one small equation: profit is what a business keeps after paying for everything it needed to earn that money. This deck builds from there, assuming you have never opened a financial statement and would rather not pretend otherwise. You will learn to split a profit decline into revenue and cost, narrow it down to a product, a region or a customer segment, and put real numbers behind ideas like contribution margin, break-even and mix. By the end, a client saying profits are down twelve percent should feel like the opening of a conversation rather than a trap.

cards.q: Before anything else: what is profit, and why is a company with enormous revenue not automatically a profitable one?
cards.takeaway: Profit is what is left of revenue once every cost of running the business is paid.
cards.a: Revenue is all the money customers hand over during a period, usually a year. Costs are everything the business spends to earn that money, so materials, wages, rent, marketing, interest and tax. Profit is simply revenue minus costs, which means a company can sell a billion dollars of product and still lose money if it spent more than a billion getting there. That subtraction is the whole game, and it is why an interviewer who says profits are down is never really asking about sales, but about which side of it moved.

cards.q: Your interviewer says Calder Foods lost 12% of its profit last year and asks how you would break the problem apart. What does the profit equation look like drawn as a tree?
cards.takeaway: Profit = (price x quantity) - (fixed + variable costs), and every driver hangs off one of those four boxes.
cards.a: Revenue is price times quantity: what you charge per unit and how many units you sell. Costs split into fixed costs, which do not move with volume, such as rent and salaried staff, and variable costs, which rise with every extra unit, such as ingredients and packaging. So profit equals price times quantity, minus fixed plus variable costs, and any explanation for Calder’s 12% drop has to land in one of those four boxes. Drawing that tree out loud early gives you a map, and it shows the interviewer where you intend to look first.

cards.q: What is a profit margin, and how can a company’s profit go up in a year when its margin goes down?
cards.takeaway: Margin is profit as a percentage of revenue, so it can fall even while total profit rises.
cards.a: Margin is profit divided by revenue, written as a percentage: earn 8 million of profit on 100 million of revenue and the margin is 8%. It answers a different question from absolute profit, which is the raw dollar amount, because margin tells you how much of every sales dollar the business actually keeps. If revenue doubles to 200 million while profit reaches 12 million, profit is up but the margin is now 6%, so each dollar of sales is worth less than before. Always ask which one the client cares about, because a growth story and a margin story lead to different recommendations.

cards.q: A partner drops you into a case with one line: Northbay Logistics says profits are down and wants help. What do you establish before you touch a single number?
cards.takeaway: Pin down how much, over what period, measured against what, and what the client actually wants to achieve.
cards.a: Profits are down is a symptom, not a question. Ask how large the decline is, since 2% and 30% call for very different responses, and over what period, since one weak quarter and a five-year slide are different problems. Ask what the comparison is: down against last year, against budget, or against competitors. Then ask what success would look like, because a client that wants last year’s profit back within twelve months needs different advice from one willing to spend three years rebuilding. Interviewers leave this deliberately vague to see whether you scope a problem before you start solving it.

cards.q: How do you work out whether a profit decline is a revenue problem or a cost problem, and what is the first data you ask for?
cards.takeaway: Ask for revenue and total cost separately over the same years and see which line actually moved.
cards.a: Since profit is revenue minus cost, only three things can have happened: revenue fell, cost rose, or both. So ask for both lines over the same several years and look at which one moved and by how much. If revenue held flat at 400 million while total cost climbed from 360 to 390, you have a cost problem, and the rest of the case belongs on the cost branch of your tree. Making this split early is what stops you spending fifteen minutes exploring pricing in a case that was always about warehouse expense.

cards.q: You have established that Ferrow Retail’s revenue fell from 500 million to 450 million. Your interviewer asks whether that is a price story or a volume story. How do you separate the two?
cards.takeaway: Hold one lever still at a time to see how much of the drop came from price and how much from volume.
cards.a: Revenue is price times quantity, so a 50 million shortfall has to come from a lower average price, fewer units, or some blend of both. Ask for units sold and average price in each year. If Ferrow sold 10 million units at 50 dollars and now sells 10 million at 45, the entire decline is price. If price held at 50 and units fell to 9 million, it is entirely volume. When both move, value one effect at a time, the volume effect at the old price and then the price effect on the new volume, so the two pieces add back to 50.

cards.q: Northbay’s total cost line looks unremarkable, and then the interviewer slides over a table of profit by region. What are you looking for, and how do you decide where to dig?
cards.takeaway: Averages hide problems, so cut profit by product, region, customer and channel until one piece stands out.
cards.a: A company total is an average of many smaller businesses, and averages hide things. So cut the profit number every way the data allows: by product line, by region, by customer segment, by sales channel and by time period. Usually one slice is dragging the total down while the rest is perfectly healthy, and that changes the answer entirely, since repairing one bad region is a very different project from fixing a company-wide margin. Name the cuts you want before the data appears, so the interviewer sees that you went looking for the outlier rather than stumbling onto it.

cards.q: You have found where the profit is leaking. How do you tell whether the cause is something the client did to itself or something the whole industry is living through?
cards.takeaway: Check whether competitors show the same pattern, because an industry-wide problem needs a different answer.
cards.a: Ask whether rivals in the same market are seeing the same squeeze. If every regional grocer’s food cost jumped in the same year, the cause is external, an input price shock or a shift in demand, and the useful question becomes how the client responds faster than its peers rather than what it did wrong. If the client alone is deteriorating while competitors hold steady, the cause is internal, and you look hard at its own pricing, contracts and operations. Recommending an internal fix for an industry-wide problem is one of the most common ways candidates get a case backwards.

cards.q: What is contribution margin, and what does it tell you that the headline profit number does not?
cards.takeaway: Contribution margin is what one extra sale leaves behind after its own variable cost, before any fixed costs.
cards.a: Take a single unit. Calder Foods sells a jar of sauce for 6.00 and spends 2.20 on the ingredients, packaging and line labour for that jar. The 3.80 left over is the contribution margin: the amount that jar contributes toward covering fixed costs such as the factory lease, and toward profit once those costs are covered. It matters because headline profit folds fixed and variable costs together, while contribution tells you what one more sale is genuinely worth. That is the number behind almost every decision about volume, pricing, or whether a product deserves to stay.

cards.q: Calder Foods is weighing up a new sauce line, and the plant it would need costs 1.9 million a year to run whether it makes one jar or a million. How do you find the break-even volume?
cards.takeaway: Break-even quantity is fixed costs divided by the contribution margin on one unit.
cards.a: Break-even is the sales volume at which profit is exactly zero, the point where the contribution from every jar sold has just finished paying off the fixed costs. Each jar contributes 3.80 and fixed costs are 1.9 million, so you need 1.9 million divided by 3.80, which is 500,000 jars, before Calder earns a cent. Every jar after that adds 3.80 straight to profit. The calculation earns its keep in an interview because it turns a vague question, is this worth doing, into one the client can actually judge: can we realistically sell more than 500,000 jars a year?

cards.q: Two rivals each lose 10% of their volume in the same year. One owns a large factory, the other pays an outside supplier to make everything. Why does the identical volume drop hurt one far more?
cards.takeaway: High fixed costs do not shrink when volume falls, so every lost unit takes its full contribution with it.
cards.a: Variable costs fall automatically when you make less, so the outsourcer’s costs drop roughly in step with its sales and its margin barely moves. The factory owner still pays the same lease, depreciation and salaried crew whether the line runs full or half empty, so those fixed costs now spread across fewer units and the cost per unit climbs. That sensitivity is called operating leverage: heavy fixed costs magnify profit in good years and magnify losses in bad ones. It is why a case about a manufacturer, an airline or a hotel chain usually turns into a question about volume and how full the capacity is.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co sold the same number of units this year as last, and has not cut a single price, yet profit fell 9%. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.takeaway: The mix shifted, so customers bought more of the low-margin products and fewer of the high-margin ones.
cards.a: Mix is the split of your sales across products that carry different margins, and it moves profit even when price and volume look untouched. If Bramwell sells a premium line contributing 40 per unit and a budget line contributing 10, and the split slides from half and half to 30/70, average contribution falls from 25 to 19 without a single price change. You find it by comparing contribution by product across the two periods rather than staring at total units. Interviewers like this one because candidates who check only price and volume tend to declare the case impossible.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail launched a cheaper own-brand cereal that sold 400,000 boxes in year one, and total profit in the cereal aisle still went down. What happened?
cards.takeaway: Sales that come out of your own existing products are cannibalised, not incremental.
cards.a: Cannibalisation is when a new product’s sales are taken from the company’s other products rather than from competitors or from genuinely new demand. If 300,000 of those boxes went to shoppers who would otherwise have bought Ferrow’s higher-margin branded cereal, the company traded high-contribution sales for low-contribution ones, and only 100,000 boxes were truly new. The test is always incremental contribution: total contribution with the launch, against what it would have been without it. Any new product, price cut or extra store deserves that check before anyone calls the volume number a success.

cards.q: Your team wants to know whether Northbay’s warehousing cost is genuinely too high. How do you benchmark a single cost line against competitors, and why convert everything to a per-unit basis first?
cards.takeaway: Compare cost per unit against peers to find the line that is out of step rather than merely large.
cards.a: Benchmarking means setting the client’s cost beside what comparable companies spend on the same thing. Raw totals are useless for that, because a rival twice the size spends twice as much on almost everything, so first convert to a common basis: cost per unit shipped, per store, per employee, or as a share of revenue. If Northbay spends 14% of revenue on warehousing while peers spend 9%, you have isolated a real gap worth roughly five points of margin. Then ask why, since the gap may be a deliberate choice, faster delivery for example, rather than waste to be stripped out.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail’s CFO wants 15% taken out of every cost line by year end and asks you to bless the plan. What is your concern?
cards.takeaway: Some costs buy future revenue, so a blanket cut can lift this year’s profit and shrink next year’s.
cards.a: An across-the-board cut treats every cost as equally wasteful, and they are not. Renegotiating rent or removing duplicated back-office work takes cost out without a customer ever noticing. Cutting store staff, maintenance, product quality or marketing lowers cost immediately but erodes the revenue line over the following year or two, so profit improves briefly and then falls below where it started. The honest answer separates costs that buy future revenue from costs that simply exist, and tells the client plainly which lever they are pulling, because a one-year margin win that costs three years of growth is not a win.

cards.q: One of Northbay’s twelve depots reports a 200,000 loss once its share of head-office cost is charged against it. Should the client close it?
cards.takeaway: Close it only if its own revenue fails to cover the costs that would genuinely disappear on closure.
cards.a: A reported loss usually includes allocated overhead, a slice of head-office and central cost pushed onto each site whether or not closing that site removes any of it. Suppose the depot brings in 1.4 million, spends 1.3 million on costs that really would vanish on closure, and carries 300,000 of allocated overhead. It is contributing 100,000 toward central costs that the other eleven depots would otherwise have to absorb, so closing it makes the company worse off, not better. Ask for contribution before overhead allocation, and ask exactly which costs go away.

cards.q: The interviewer adds that Northbay spent 4 million fitting out that same depot two years ago, and the CEO keeps mentioning the figure. How should it affect the decision to close?
cards.takeaway: It should not, because money already spent and unrecoverable belongs nowhere in a forward-looking decision.
cards.a: A sunk cost is money already spent that you cannot recover no matter what you choose next. The 4 million is gone whether the depot stays open or shuts tomorrow, so it cannot change which option leaves Northbay better off from today onward. The only figures that belong in the decision are future ones: the contribution the depot will earn if it keeps running, set against closure costs and whatever the site would fetch if sold. People resist this because walking away from a large investment feels like admitting a mistake, and that bias is exactly what the interviewer is testing by mentioning the number at all.

cards.q: Calder Foods’ profit fell from 40 million to 28 million. Revenue is flat, units are flat, no price changed, and no single cost line looks unusual. Walk me through how you would hunt down the missing 12 million.
cards.takeaway: When price, volume and totals all look flat, the answer is nearly always hiding in mix or in one segment.
cards.a: Start by checking that the flat totals are really flat rather than two offsetting moves, since a growing premium line and a collapsing budget line can net to zero. Then cut the business apart, contribution by product, region, channel and customer size, hunting for the slice that shifted. Test mix explicitly, because steady units at a worse blend of products drags contribution down without disturbing any headline number. If every cut looks clean, ask whether volume was held by heavier discounting, or whether fixed costs are now spread over fewer production runs. Finally benchmark against peers to see whether the cause sits inside Calder or across the industry.

name: Business Models & Unit Economics
description: How different kinds of company actually make money, and the numbers that decide whether they do.
intro: A case is easier when you already know how the client's kind of business works: what it sells, what it costs, where the margin comes from and what can go wrong. This deck walks through the models that come up most, from retailers and subscription businesses to marketplaces, airlines and banks, and the unit economics behind each one: the profit on a single customer, a single seat, a single store. With that in your head you ask better questions in the first two minutes of a case and spot the problem faster in the last ten.

cards.q: What is a business model, and why does a consultant start by asking about it?
cards.takeaway: How a company creates value for customers and captures some of it as profit; every case problem sits somewhere in that chain.
cards.a: A business model is the answer to four questions: who the customer is, what they get, how the company delivers it, and how it gets paid. Ferrow Retail sells clothes to shoppers through stores and a website and earns the gap between what it pays suppliers and what customers pay. A subscription software firm sells access to a tool to businesses through a sales team and earns recurring monthly fees. Consultants ask first because the diagnosis depends on it: falling profit means something different at a retailer, where it is usually margin or footfall, than at a software company, where it is usually churn or sales cost.

cards.q: What are unit economics, and why do investors and consultants obsess over them?
cards.takeaway: The profit or loss on one unit of the business, a customer, an order, a store, which tells you whether growth helps or hurts.
cards.a: Unit economics are the revenue and cost of one unit: one customer over their lifetime, one delivery, one seat on one flight, one shop. If a unit makes money, the company can grow by adding units and each one adds profit. If a unit loses money, growth makes the losses bigger, and the company is buying revenue. Total profit can hide this, because a business can show growing revenue and shrinking losses while each new customer still costs more to win than they ever pay. Asking for the numbers on one unit is the fastest way to see whether a business is fundamentally sound.

cards.q: What are customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, and what ratio between them is healthy?
cards.takeaway: CAC is what it costs to win a customer; LTV is the profit they generate before they leave; LTV should be about three times CAC.
cards.a: Customer acquisition cost is total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers won. Lifetime value is the profit a customer generates over their time with the company: contribution per period, times how long they stay. If a subscription costs £10 a month with £7 of contribution and the average customer stays 20 months, LTV is £140. If it cost £50 to win them, LTV to CAC is about 3, which is the usual benchmark for a healthy business. Below 1 the company loses money on every customer; a very high ratio suggests it is underinvesting in growth.

cards.q: What is churn, and why does a small change in it move a subscription business so much?
cards.takeaway: Churn is the share of customers who leave each period; because lifetime is one over churn, halving churn doubles lifetime value.
cards.a: Churn is the percentage of customers lost in a period. A monthly churn of 5% means one in twenty customers leaves each month, so the average customer stays about 20 months. Cut churn to 2.5% and the average customer stays 40 months, doubling revenue per customer without winning anyone new. That is why subscription companies spend so heavily on retention, and why a case about a struggling streaming service or gym is almost always about churn before it is about acquisition. Always ask for churn early in any recurring-revenue case.

cards.q: How does a retailer make money, and what are the two numbers that decide it?
cards.takeaway: Gross margin on what it sells, and sales per square foot or per store, against a largely fixed cost of stores and staff.
cards.a: A retailer buys goods and sells them for more; the gap is gross margin, typically 30% to 60% depending on the category. Against that sit costs that barely move with sales: rent, staff, energy, the website. So profit depends on pushing enough sales through each store to cover its fixed cost, which is why sales per square foot and like-for-like growth are the metrics retailers live by. A store with falling footfall goes from profitable to loss-making quickly because its costs do not fall with it. In a retail case, ask for margin and store-level sales before anything else.

cards.q: How does a marketplace like an app connecting drivers and riders make money, and what is the chicken-and-egg problem?
cards.takeaway: A marketplace takes a cut of each transaction between two sides, and it only works once both sides are big enough to attract each other.
cards.a: A marketplace does not own the product; it connects buyers and sellers and takes a percentage of each deal, the take rate, usually 10% to 30%. Its cost is mainly technology and the marketing to bring both sides in. The difficulty is that riders only come if there are drivers, and drivers only come if there are riders, so a new marketplace has to subsidise one side, often heavily, until the other arrives. Once it works, it is hard to dislodge, because everyone is where everyone else is. Cases about marketplaces are usually about take rate, subsidies, or whether a market is big enough to reach that tipping point.

cards.q: Why is software so profitable once it works, and what does that do to how the company grows?
cards.takeaway: The product costs almost nothing to copy, so gross margins are 80% or more and most spending goes on winning customers.
cards.a: Writing software is expensive; serving one more customer is nearly free, because it is the same code. That gives gross margins of 70% to 90%, compared with 30% to 50% for a company that makes physical things. So a software firm's cost base is people, mostly engineers building the product and salespeople selling it. Early on, it spends far more on sales and marketing than it earns, betting that each customer's lifetime value repays the acquisition cost many times over. A software case is usually about that bet: is CAC falling, is churn low, is the sales team productive, and when does the company stop needing outside money.

cards.q: How does an airline make money, and why are its economics so brutal?
cards.takeaway: It sells seats on flights whose cost is almost entirely fixed once they take off, so a few empty seats decide the profit.
cards.a: The cost of a flight, the aircraft, the crew, the fuel, the landing fees, is nearly the same whether the plane is full or half empty. Revenue depends on how many seats are sold and at what price. So the whole business comes down to load factor, the share of seats filled, and yield, revenue per seat. A plane that breaks even at 80% full makes all its profit from the last 20% of seats, which is why airlines cut prices at the last minute rather than fly empty. Add fuel prices they cannot control and fierce competition on every route, and you have an industry that loses money in most downturns.

cards.q: How does a bank make money?
cards.takeaway: Mostly from the gap between what it pays depositors and what it charges borrowers, plus fees; its risk is that borrowers do not pay back.
cards.a: A bank takes deposits, paying savers a low rate, and lends the money out at a higher rate. The difference is net interest income, and the gap as a percentage of assets is the net interest margin, usually one to three per cent. On top sit fees, for accounts, cards, advice and transactions. The costs are branches, staff and technology, and the big variable is credit losses: loans that are not repaid. That is why banks do well when rates rise, because the margin widens, and badly in recessions, because defaults rise. A bank case is usually about margin, cost-to-income ratio, or bad loans.

cards.q: What is a franchise model, and why do companies like fast-food chains use it?
cards.takeaway: The company licenses its brand and system to local operators who put up the capital and take the operating risk, in return for a royalty.
cards.a: In a franchise, the parent owns the brand, the recipes and the rules, and a franchisee owns the individual outlet, pays for the fit-out, hires the staff and keeps most of the profit. The parent earns an upfront fee and a royalty, typically 4% to 8% of sales, plus rent if it owns the property. The parent grows fast without spending its own capital and earns a high-margin, steady income; the franchisee gets a proven format. The tension is control: the parent cannot manage every outlet, so quality can slip. Cases about franchise chains usually turn on the split of economics between the two sides.

cards.q: What is the difference between a high-volume, low-margin business and a low-volume, high-margin one, and how does a case differ for each?
cards.takeaway: The first lives on efficiency and scale, the second on pricing and brand; the levers you pull are different.
cards.a: A supermarket makes two or three pence on every pound of sales and survives by selling enormous volumes efficiently: logistics, buying power, store productivity. A luxury brand makes fifty pence on every pound and survives by protecting the price: brand, scarcity, control of distribution. In a case about the first, look at costs, throughput and scale; in a case about the second, look at pricing, positioning and whether growth is diluting the brand. Applying the wrong lens is a common error, like recommending a luxury house cut prices to win volume, which would destroy the thing it sells.

cards.q: What is operating leverage, and why does it explain why some companies' profits swing so much more than their sales?
cards.takeaway: The higher the share of fixed costs, the more a small change in sales moves profit, up or down.
cards.a: If most of a company's costs are fixed, extra sales come with almost no extra cost, so profit rises much faster than revenue; but a fall in sales cuts profit just as sharply, because the costs stay. A cinema with 90% fixed costs might see profit double on a 10% rise in ticket sales and vanish on a 10% fall. A consultancy with mostly variable costs, its staff can be flexed, sees much smaller swings. In a case, high operating leverage means volume is everything, and a small forecast error matters enormously. It is worth naming explicitly when you see a business with big fixed costs.

cards.q: Calder Foods sells through supermarkets, which take a 35% margin, and is considering selling direct online. What changes in the economics?
cards.takeaway: Direct sales keep the retailer's margin but add the costs the retailer used to bear: marketing, delivery, returns and customer service.
cards.a: Selling direct means Calder keeps the full retail price instead of 65% of it, which looks like a huge gain. But the supermarket was doing work for that margin: putting the product in front of millions of shoppers, holding stock, handling the sale and delivery. Direct, Calder must win customers itself, which costs marketing; ship small orders, which costs more per unit than pallets to a warehouse; and handle returns and queries. For a £3 jar of sauce, delivery alone can exceed the margin gained. Direct works for high-value, repeat-purchase products and as a way to learn about customers; for cheap groceries it rarely does.

cards.q: What is a two-sided subsidy, like a free service paid for by advertisers, and what is its weakness?
cards.takeaway: Users get the product free and advertisers pay for access to them; the model depends on attention that competitors can steal.
cards.a: Many media and internet businesses charge the user nothing and sell the user's attention to advertisers. Revenue is audience size times the price advertisers pay per thousand views. The costs are content and technology. It scales well, because a bigger audience commands both more views and a higher price. The weakness is that attention is fickle and advertisers follow it; a rival with a better product takes users, and revenue follows immediately. It also ties the company's fortunes to the advertising market, which collapses in recessions. Cases here are about audience growth, engagement, and whether to add a paid tier.

cards.q: How do you work out whether a new store, route or product is worth opening, in a case?
cards.takeaway: Estimate its unit economics, revenue against its own costs, then compare the return on the investment with what the client could do instead.
cards.a: Build the case for one unit. For a new Ferrow store: expected sales, from footfall or comparable stores, times gross margin, minus the store's own costs, rent, staff, energy, gives store-level profit. Compare it with the upfront investment for a payback or return. Then ask three questions: is the forecast sales figure plausible against nearby stores; does the new store steal sales from existing ones, called cannibalisation; and could the money earn more elsewhere. A recommendation that covers those, with a number and the biggest risk named, is a complete answer.

cards.q: An interviewer asks how a company you admire makes money. How do you answer in under a minute?
cards.takeaway: Customer, product, channel, revenue model, cost structure, and the one number that drives it.
cards.a: Use a fixed order. Who buys it and why. What they get. How it reaches them. How the company is paid: per unit, subscription, commission, advertising. What its main costs are and whether they are fixed or variable. Then the single metric that decides success: load factor for an airline, churn for a subscription, sales per square foot for a retailer, net interest margin for a bank. Finish with what could go wrong. That is six sentences, it works for any company, and it shows the interviewer that you think about businesses as systems rather than brands.

name: Statistics & Data Analysis for Business
description: The core statistical concepts behind sound, defensible business analysis.
intro: Most business and data roles do not expect you to be a statistician, but they do expect you to reason clearly about numbers: what an average actually tells you, when a sample might be misleading, how confident you can really be in a conclusion. This deck focuses on the statistical concepts that come up in business contexts specifically, not abstract math theory, so the framing stays close to how you would actually use it in an interview or on the job. No statistics background required to start.

cards.q: What’s the difference between descriptive and predictive analytics?
cards.takeaway: Descriptive analytics explains what already happened; predictive analytics forecasts what's likely to happen next.
cards.a: Descriptive analytics summarizes what has already happened — like last quarter's sales broken out by region. Predictive analytics goes further, using patterns in that historical data to estimate what's likely to happen next, like forecasting next quarter's numbers. Most case analysis starts descriptive, establishing a clear picture of what happened, before it moves on to predicting or recommending what to do next.

cards.q: You're advising Ferrow Retail Group on store performance. The regional director's slide says “average weekly revenue across our 40 stores is $84K” — but one flagship store does 5x the volume of any other location. What's the risk in leaning on that number, and how do mean, median, and mode differ?
cards.takeaway: Mean is the average, median is the middle, mode is the most common — skewed data favors the median.
cards.a: The regional director's mean gets pulled upward by that one outlier store, making the “typical” store look stronger than it actually is. Mean adds up every value and divides by the count, median is the middle value once everything's sorted, and mode is whichever value shows up most often. Because the mean gets dragged around by outliers, the median holds steady and gives a better read on what a typical store is actually doing — the same logic applies to skewed data like income or home prices.

cards.q: Calder Foods' operating margin went from 4% to 5%. The associate wrote “margins up 1%” on the page and your engagement manager circled it. What's wrong with that, and what's a percentage point change?
cards.takeaway: Going from 4% to 5% is one percentage point but a 25% increase, so say which one you mean.
cards.a: When the figure you're describing is itself a percentage, there are two honest ways to describe a move and they give very different numbers. Subtract them and you get the percentage point change, usually written pp: 5 minus 4 is one percentage point. Divide the change by where you started and you get the percentage change: 1 divided by 4 is a 25% increase. Writing “margins up 1%” blurs the two, and a client reading it may think almost nothing happened when the business is actually keeping a quarter more profit on every dollar of sales.

cards.q: What does standard deviation tell you?
cards.takeaway: Standard deviation measures how tightly values cluster around the average — small means consistent, large means volatile.
cards.a: Standard deviation tells you how far values typically stray from the mean. A small standard deviation means the data clusters tightly around the average — consistent, predictable — while a large one means values swing widely in either direction. In a case, pairing it with the mean tells you not just what a client's typical store, deal, or customer looks like, but how reliable that “typical” figure actually is.

cards.q: A client tells you the average call-centre wait is 4 minutes, so service is clearly fine. You pull the raw data and the 90th percentile is 19 minutes. What's a percentile, and why does that number change the story?
cards.takeaway: A percentile says what share of cases fall below a point, and the tail is where customers get angry.
cards.a: Sort every call from shortest wait to longest, and the 90th percentile is the value that 90% of callers come in under: nine in ten wait less than 19 minutes, one in ten waits longer. The median you already know is simply the 50th percentile, the middle of the queue. A 4-minute average can sit on top of a long tail of callers stuck for twenty minutes, and those are the people who hang up and complain, which is why service targets, salary bands, and delivery promises are usually written as medians and percentiles rather than averages.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics hands your team four million delivery records and a two-day deadline. A partner asks whether you really need all of them. What is a sample, and why can a few thousand records tell you anything about four million?
cards.takeaway: Random sampling works because every record had an equal chance of being picked, not because it is huge.
cards.a: A sample is a subset of the full group, called the population, that you measure in place of measuring everything. It works when selection is random, meaning every record had an equal chance of being drawn, because a random draw tends to reproduce the population's mix of fast and slow deliveries in miniature. What matters most is how the sample was chosen rather than what fraction of the population it covers, so a clean 2,000-record sample beats a carelessly chosen 400,000-record one. Accuracy does improve as the sample grows, but slowly, which is why doubling the pull rarely doubles your confidence.

cards.q: A client's product team surveys only its loyalty-program members about a new subscription tier and reports 90% approval. Your case team should flag this before it goes in the client's board deck — why?
cards.takeaway: Sample bias means your data doesn't represent the population you're trying to understand, so conclusions don't generalize.
cards.a: That 90% is sample bias in action: loyalty-program members aren't representative of the broader customer base the client is trying to understand, so the result won't generalize. It's the classic version of surveying only your existing customers about a new idea — you'd completely miss the opinions of everyone who looked at what you offer and decided not to buy, which is often exactly the group a new subscription tier needs to win over.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail's franchising head studies the 40 franchisees still trading after ten years, finds most run a large-format store, and calls large format the winning formula. Your manager calls this survivorship bias. What did the study miss?
cards.takeaway: Studying only the survivors hides everyone who failed doing exactly the same thing.
cards.a: Survivorship bias is what happens when you analyse only the cases that made it and never see the ones that dropped out along the way. Plenty of large-format franchisees may have opened and closed over those ten years, and if they failed at the same rate as the small ones, format explains nothing at all. The fix is to rebuild the original cohort, every franchisee that ever opened, and compare survivors against closures on the same measures. It's worth spotting early, because it quietly infects fund performance tables, customer surveys, and any best-practice study built only on today's winners.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group's CEO points out that stores with an in-store café also have higher electronics sales, and concludes the café is driving people to buy more electronics. What's wrong with that conclusion, and how would you push back?
cards.takeaway: Two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — a hidden third factor might explain both.
cards.a: The CEO is treating a correlation as if it were proven causation. Two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — cafés and strong electronics sales might both simply show up in larger, higher-traffic stores, a hidden third factor driving both. Before recommending the client roll out cafés chain-wide, you'd want to isolate that store-size effect or run a controlled test, since proving causation usually takes an experiment or careful statistical work, not just an observed pattern.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group's e-commerce lead wants to know whether a redesigned checkout page increases conversion before rolling it out site-wide. How would you design a test to answer that fairly?
cards.takeaway: A/B testing randomly splits an audience into two groups to fairly compare which version performs better.
cards.a: You'd run an A/B test: randomly assign incoming visitors to either the current checkout page or the redesign, then compare conversion rates between the two. Randomization is what makes the comparison fair — it ensures the two groups of visitors are alike in every other way, so any difference in conversion can be attributed to the redesign itself rather than, say, one group happening to skew toward more loyal customers.

cards.q: What is a p-value, in plain terms?
cards.takeaway: A p-value is the odds you'd see a result this extreme if nothing real were actually going on.
cards.a: A p-value estimates the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming there's actually no real effect. The smaller the p-value, the more surprising your result would be in a world where nothing real is going on. It is not the probability that your finding is a fluke, which is the version interviewers like to probe. Below 0.05 is the common cutoff, which is why it's the usual bar for calling a client's test result “statistically significant” rather than noise.

cards.q: An A/B test across two million users shows a new banner lifting click-through from 3.00% to 3.04%, with a p-value of 0.001. The client's marketing lead wants to roll it out immediately. What would you tell her?
cards.takeaway: Statistical significance says an effect is probably real, not that it is big enough to be worth doing.
cards.a: Statistical significance only means the difference is unlikely to be a fluke of sampling, and with two million users even a microscopic gap clears that bar comfortably. It says nothing about size. A lift of 0.04 percentage points is real but tiny, so whether it's worth anything depends on the revenue behind each extra click set against the cost of building and maintaining the change. The honest answer keeps the two questions apart, is the effect real and is the effect material, and lets only the second one drive the recommendation.

cards.q: What is a confidence interval?
cards.takeaway: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values, not a single guess — it expresses how much uncertainty surrounds an estimate.
cards.a: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for something you don't know exactly — like a population average — built from your sample data, rather than one single point estimate. A 95% confidence interval means that if you repeated the same sampling process many times, about 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain the true value. It's a way of expressing uncertainty around an estimate — useful shorthand when you need to tell a client how much to trust a number, not a guarantee about any one specific interval.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co. wants to know how much of NorthPeak Airlines' recent revenue uptick came from its new marketing campaign versus other factors, like added routes or seasonal demand. What tool would you reach for, and what would it tell the client?
cards.takeaway: Regression puts a number on how much an outcome changes when an input changes.
cards.a: This is a regression problem: it estimates the relationship between an outcome (revenue) and the factors that might explain it (marketing spend, route count, seasonality), letting you put a number on how much revenue shifts as each input changes while holding the others constant. That's exactly the kind of question regression is built for in a business setting — forecasting sales, isolating what marketing spend or pricing actually does to revenue, and ranking which factors matter most.

cards.q: Calder Foods put its 20 worst-performing stores through a new training program. Six months later those stores improved more than the rest of the chain, and the client wants to roll training out everywhere. Why would you be sceptical?
cards.takeaway: Extreme results drift back toward normal on their own, making almost any intervention look like it worked.
cards.a: Any store's result in a given period is part real performance and part luck, so the worst 20 are likely to be stores having a genuinely weak run plus a dose of bad luck on top. Bad luck doesn't repeat, so on average those stores would have improved next period with no training at all. That's regression to the mean, and it's why deliberately picking the extremes for an intervention almost guarantees a flattering result. The only clean read is a control group, a comparable set of equally weak stores left untrained, so you measure the training against what would have happened anyway.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics' new routing software has a worse on-time rate than the old one overall, yet it wins on short-haul routes and wins again on long-haul routes looked at separately. How is that possible, and which number goes in the deck?
cards.takeaway: An uneven mix of easy and hard cases can flip an aggregate, so check the segments before trusting a total.
cards.a: This is Simpson's paradox: a pattern that holds inside every segment can reverse once the segments are pooled together. It happens when the groups differ in both size and difficulty. If the new software was mostly trialled on long-haul routes, where every carrier runs late more often, its overall rate gets dragged down by the harder mix rather than by worse performance. The segment numbers are the honest ones because they compare like with like, and you'd show the client both, explaining that the aggregate is really describing the route mix rather than the software.

cards.q: It's Thursday, the client readout is Monday, and your one real finding is that a segment's margin looks six points better — but it rests on nine months of data from a single region. How do you present it without overselling or burying it?
cards.takeaway: State the finding, then the evidence it rests on, then what would change your mind, in that order.
cards.a: Lead with the finding in plain language and the number behind it, then state the basis in the same breath: nine months, one region, so treat it as a signal rather than a settled result. Say what would confirm it, another region or a full year of data, and be explicit about which decisions it can carry and which it can't. Clients rarely punish a caveat that arrives with a clear next step, and they never forgive a number that quietly falls apart in a board meeting, which is why senior people scrutinise how a finding is framed as hard as they scrutinise the analysis under it.

name: Charts, Exhibits & Data Interpretation
description: Reading the chart the interviewer slides across the table: what it shows, what it hides, and the so-what.
intro: Halfway through most cases the interviewer hands you a chart or a table and waits. What they want is not a description of the axes but a reading: the one insight the exhibit contains and what it means for the client. This deck covers the exhibits that come up, from bar charts and line charts to segmented tables and waterfall charts, the traps built into each, from truncated axes to mixed units, and a repeatable way to go from looking at a page to saying something useful about it in thirty seconds.

cards.q: What is the interviewer testing when they hand you a chart?
cards.takeaway: Whether you can extract the one thing that matters and connect it to the case, quickly and out loud.
cards.a: The chart usually contains one insight the case turns on: one segment is losing money, one competitor is growing, one cost has doubled. The interviewer wants to see whether you find it, how quickly, and whether you can say why it matters for the client's question. They are also watching for discipline: do you read the title and axes before speaking, do you notice the units, do you get lost in the details. A good answer takes half a minute, names the insight, gives one number to support it, and links it to the recommendation. A bad answer describes every bar.

cards.q: What is the first thing to do with any exhibit, before saying anything?
cards.takeaway: Read the title, the axes, the units and the source, then take ten seconds of silence to find the pattern.
cards.a: Say that you would like a moment, then read in order: the title, which tells you what the chart claims to show; the axis labels and units, which tell you what the numbers are; the legend; the time period; and any footnotes, which is where the tricks hide. Only then look at the data, and look for the pattern rather than the points: what is biggest, what is growing, what stands out. Ten seconds of silence is fine and expected. Speaking before you have read the axes is how candidates confidently describe revenue when the chart shows units, or 2019 when it shows 2024.

cards.q: How do you describe what a chart shows without just listing the bars?
cards.takeaway: Lead with the headline, support it with one or two numbers, then say what it means; the details can wait for questions.
cards.a: Structure the reading in three beats. Headline: 'This shows that Ferrow's online sales have tripled since 2021 while store sales have fallen a fifth.' Evidence: 'Online has gone from £100m to £300m; stores from £900m to £720m.' Implication: 'So total revenue is flat, but the mix has shifted sharply toward the channel with lower margins, which may explain the profit decline we are investigating.' That is the whole answer. If the interviewer wants more, they will ask. Listing every data point signals that you cannot tell what matters.

cards.q: What is a truncated axis, and how does it mislead?
cards.takeaway: An axis that starts above zero exaggerates differences; check where the axis begins before judging how big a gap is.
cards.a: If a bar chart's vertical axis starts at 90 rather than 0, a bar at 95 looks twice the height of one at 92, although the real difference is 3%. Charts in company presentations do this constantly, sometimes carelessly and sometimes on purpose. The check takes one glance at the bottom of the axis. In an interview, noticing it and saying 'the axis starts at 90, so the differences are smaller than they look, about 3%' is exactly the kind of observation that earns credit, because it shows you read the chart rather than the picture.

cards.q: A chart shows revenue growing every year. What questions should you ask before concluding the business is healthy?
cards.takeaway: Growth in what units, against what, with what margin, and whether it is organic or bought.
cards.a: Revenue growing does not mean profit growing: ask about margin. It does not mean the company is winning: ask how fast the market grew, since 5% growth in a market growing 15% is losing share. It does not mean the business is doing it: ask whether growth came from acquisitions or currency. And check the units: is it nominal, so inflation is inside it; is it in a currency that moved. A candidate who sees an upward line and says the company is doing well has fallen for the chart. One who asks two of these questions has shown judgement.

cards.q: What is a waterfall chart, and how do you read one?
cards.takeaway: It walks from a starting value to an ending value through the steps that changed it; read the biggest step first.
cards.a: A waterfall starts with one bar, say last year's profit, then shows a floating bar for each factor that added or subtracted, ending with this year's profit. It answers 'what happened between then and now'. Read it by finding the largest positive and largest negative steps, since those are the story: profit fell from £50m to £30m mostly because raw material costs rose £25m, partly offset by £8m of price increases. Ignore the small steps until asked. Waterfalls are how consultants present profit bridges, so being fluent with one shows familiarity with the work.

cards.q: A table shows profit by customer segment: large accounts £40m, mid-size £25m, small £-15m. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: Small customers lose money, and the question is why and whether to fix, reprice or exit them.
cards.a: The headline is that one segment is destroying value: small customers lose £15m, which wipes out more than a third of what the other two earn. Then the questions: is it a cost-to-serve problem, where each small account costs more to handle than it generates; is it a pricing problem, where small customers get the same discounts as large ones; or is it strategic, where small customers grow into large ones and the losses are an investment. The recommendation depends on which. Saying that, rather than just reading the three numbers, is what the exhibit is for.

cards.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative numbers on a chart, and why does it matter?
cards.takeaway: A big percentage on a small base can be a small number; always ask what the base is.
cards.a: A chart showing a segment growing 80% a year looks like the story, until you learn it is £2m of a £2bn business. Conversely, a segment growing 3% might be adding £30m. Charts that show percentages hide the base; charts that show absolute values hide the rate. When you see either, ask for the other. In a case, the common trap is a fast-growing small segment presented as the answer to a big problem. The question to ask aloud is 'what is that as a share of total revenue', and the interviewer will usually tell you.

cards.q: Two lines on a chart, market size and the client's revenue, both rising. How do you tell whether the client is gaining or losing share?
cards.takeaway: Compare the growth rates, or compute the ratio at the start and end; a slower-growing line is losing share even while rising.
cards.a: Rising revenue in a rising market says nothing about share until you compare rates. If the market went from £10bn to £15bn, up 50%, and the client from £1bn to £1.2bn, up 20%, the client's share fell from 10% to 8%. Compute the share at both ends and say it. That is the insight the chart was built to test: a company can be growing and losing at the same time, and a client who is celebrating growth may need to hear that competitors are growing faster. Then ask who is taking the share and why.

cards.q: What is a stacked bar chart, and what does it tend to hide?
cards.takeaway: It shows the total and its composition, but makes it hard to read changes in the middle segments.
cards.a: A stacked bar piles segments on top of each other so the full bar is the total and each band is a part. It is good for seeing the total and the bottom segment, whose base is the axis, and bad for the segments in the middle, whose position depends on everything beneath them. A middle segment can look like it is growing when it is only being pushed up by the one below. If the case turns on a middle segment, ask for the numbers or mentally subtract. Saying 'the middle band is hard to read from a stacked chart, can I have the figures' is a legitimate and impressive request.

cards.q: An exhibit shows costs per unit falling as volume rises. What is it showing, and what is the trap?
cards.takeaway: Economies of scale: fixed costs spread over more units; the trap is assuming the curve continues forever.
cards.a: Cost per unit falls with volume because fixed costs are spread more thinly, and sometimes because buying power and learning improve. That supports a strategy of growing to cut costs. The trap is extrapolating: at some point the factory is full, the next unit needs a new factory, and cost per unit jumps. Diseconomies also appear, as coordination gets harder. So read the chart, name the mechanism, and then ask where the current capacity limit is and what the step cost of the next one would be. That turns a chart into a decision.

cards.q: The chart is in a currency and time period different from the rest of the case. What do you do?
cards.takeaway: Say so, convert or align if you can, and if you cannot, state the assumption you are making.
cards.a: Mixed units are a deliberate test. If the case has been in pounds and the exhibit is in dollars, note it and ask for or estimate an exchange rate before comparing anything. If the exhibit covers 2020 to 2023 and the case question is about 2024, say that you are assuming the trend continued, or ask for 2024. Interviewers reward the noticing more than the conversion. The failure is to compare a dollar figure with a pound figure as if they were the same, which happens surprisingly often under pressure.

cards.q: How do you go from a chart insight to a recommendation in the same breath?
cards.takeaway: Insight, cause, action: what the chart shows, why it is probably happening, and what the client should do about it.
cards.a: After the headline reading, add two sentences. First, a hypothesis for the cause: 'Store sales are falling, most likely because footfall is shifting online rather than because of pricing, given online is growing.' Second, an action: 'That suggests the client should look at closing the weakest stores and investing in fulfilment rather than discounting in-store.' You have then turned an exhibit into a piece of the answer. Even if the hypothesis is wrong, the interviewer sees you reasoning toward a decision, which is the job. Ending on a description leaves the work to them.

cards.q: What is a scatter plot with a trend line telling you, and what is the classic mistake in reading it?
cards.takeaway: It shows whether two things move together; the mistake is assuming one causes the other.
cards.a: A scatter plot puts one variable on each axis and each point is one observation, one store or one customer. A trend line shows correlation: stores with more staff have higher sales, say. The classic error is to conclude that adding staff would raise sales, when it may be that busy stores get more staff. Say what the chart shows, note the correlation, and then ask what might be driving both, or whether there is a natural experiment. Interviewers set this up deliberately, and a candidate who says 'correlation, not necessarily causation, and here is why' stands out.

cards.q: An exhibit contradicts something the interviewer said earlier in the case. What do you do?
cards.takeaway: Point it out politely and ask which to rely on; the contradiction may be the point.
cards.a: Sometimes the interviewer said the market was growing and the exhibit shows it shrinking. That is either a test or a mistake, and either way you should raise it: 'This shows the market declining 2% a year, which is different from the growth we discussed earlier; should I rely on the exhibit?' Never quietly pick one, and never pretend not to notice. Consultants are paid to catch inconsistencies in client data, and an interview is the first place to show that you will. Most interviewers will smile and tell you which is right.

cards.q: Give a complete thirty-second reading of an exhibit, in order, that would satisfy any interviewer.
cards.takeaway: Read silently, headline, two numbers, implication, hypothesis, next step.
cards.a: Take ten seconds and read the title, axes, units and footnotes. Then: 'This chart shows Ferrow's profit by channel from 2021 to 2024. The headline is that store profit has halved, from £80m to £40m, while online has gone from a £10m loss to break-even. Total profit is down £50m, almost all of it from stores. My hypothesis is that fixed store costs have not come down as sales moved online. I would like to test that by looking at store-level sales and costs next.' Headline, evidence, implication, cause, next step. Practise it on any chart in a newspaper until it is automatic.

name: Marketing Fundamentals
description: The core concepts behind how products get positioned and sold.
intro: Marketing questions show up in more interviews than people expect, not just marketing roles, but general business and case interviews that touch product or strategy. This deck covers the core vocabulary and frameworks, like the four Ps, that give you a structured way to talk about how a product actually gets positioned, priced, and sold. Written for someone starting from zero, with an emphasis on frameworks you can actually apply to a real example on the spot.

cards.q: A client's CFO tells you he wants to cut the marketing budget, and points straight at the ad spend. What would you tell him marketing actually covers?
cards.takeaway: Marketing is the whole job of matching a product to people who want it, and ads are only the last mile.
cards.a: Marketing is the work of figuring out which customers to serve, what those customers actually need, and then designing, pricing and distributing something that meets that need before a single ad runs. Advertising is just the visible end of it, the part that tells people the thing exists. Deciding to sell a smaller pack at a lower price to a different kind of shopper is a marketing decision with no advertising in it at all. That matters in a case, because a problem labelled marketing very often turns out to be about product or price, not promotion.

cards.q: What is market segmentation, and what are some common bases for it?
cards.takeaway: Segmentation splits one big, messy market into smaller groups that actually behave the same way.
cards.a: Market segmentation is the process of breaking a broad customer base into smaller groups that share similar characteristics or needs, so a company, or the team advising it, can market to each group more precisely than it could to everyone at once. Common bases include demographic (age, income), geographic (location), psychographic (lifestyle, values), and behavioral (purchase habits, brand loyalty).

cards.q: Bramwell & Co., a regional eyewear retailer, is expanding into a new market and isn't sure which customers to go after first or how to stand out once it's there. What three-step process would you walk the client through?
cards.takeaway: STP walks you from a broad, messy market down to one clear position in customers' minds.
cards.a: Walk Bramwell through STP: Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning. Segmentation splits the new market into groups that share similar needs, targeting picks which of those groups is actually worth pursuing first, and positioning defines how Bramwell should be perceived, relative to competitors, in that group's mind. Run through in order, it takes the client from 'everyone in this new market' to a specific, ownable position for a specific audience.

cards.q: What is a value proposition?
cards.takeaway: A value proposition is the one-line answer to 'why should I buy this instead of anything else?'
cards.a: A value proposition is a clear statement of the specific benefit a product delivers to its target customer, and why that beats the alternatives available to them. It's usually the first thing worth pressure-testing on an engagement — it exists to answer the customer's unspoken question up front: why choose this over everything else competing for their attention and money?

cards.q: Your client, Ferrow Retail Group, is about to launch a new private-label snack line and wants a structured way to plan the launch. What framework would you reach for, and what does it cover?
cards.takeaway: The 4 Ps are the four levers a company pulls to bring a product to market.
cards.a: Reach for the 4 Ps, or marketing mix: Product (what you're selling), Price (what it costs), Place (where and how customers can get it), and Promotion (how you tell people about it). For Ferrow's snack launch, that means nailing down what the product actually is, what it's priced at, which shelves or channels it lands in, and how shoppers hear about it. Every go-to-market decision falls under one of these four buckets, and getting them working together is what makes a launch land instead of falling flat.

cards.q: Calder Foods sells its sauces through supermarkets, and now wants to sell direct from its own website. The supermarket buyer is furious. What is going on here, and how would you frame the decision?
cards.takeaway: Channel conflict is what happens when two routes to the same customer start competing with each other.
cards.a: A distribution channel is the path a product travels to reach the buyer, either direct from the company or indirectly through wholesalers and retailers. Selling direct earns Calder the full margin and gives it customer data it never sees from a supermarket, but the supermarket delivers volume and shelf space Calder cannot replicate on its own. Channel conflict is the clash that follows, especially if the website undercuts the shelf price and the retailer responds by cutting orders or delisting. The decision comes down to whether the extra direct margin outweighs the volume the client is putting at risk.

cards.q: What's the difference between a push strategy and a pull strategy, and when would each one make sense?
cards.takeaway: Push sells the product into the channel, pull makes customers walk in and ask the channel for it.
cards.a: A push strategy aims your effort at the middle of the chain, using trade discounts, sales reps and shelf incentives so wholesalers and retailers stock the product and move it. A pull strategy aims past them at the end customer, using advertising, samples and word of mouth so people come asking for it by name, which forces retailers to carry it. A new brand nobody has heard of usually has to push first, while a brand people already trust can afford to pull. Most real programs run both at once, and the interesting question is the mix.

cards.q: What's the difference between B2B and B2C marketing?
cards.takeaway: B2B sells to a committee on ROI; B2C sells to one person on emotion and price.
cards.a: B2B (business-to-business) marketing sells to other companies, where multiple stakeholders typically weigh in and decisions hinge on ROI over a longer sales cycle — the kind of buying committee you'd map out on a client engagement. B2C (business-to-consumer) marketing sells directly to individual consumers, where decisions are usually faster and driven more by emotion and price than by a formal evaluation process.

cards.q: What is brand equity, and why does it matter in a pricing engagement?
cards.takeaway: Brand equity is the extra value a name adds on top of what the product actually does.
cards.a: Brand equity is the value a brand name adds beyond the product's raw functional benefits: the premium customers will pay, the loyalty they show, and the trust they extend before they've even used it. It's often the first thing to check when a client's product and a competitor's are functionally identical but priced far apart — two nearly identical products can sell at very different prices purely because one has a name behind it that people already believe in.

cards.q: What does AIDA stand for, and what is it used for?
cards.takeaway: AIDA maps the four stages a stranger passes through on the way to becoming a buyer.
cards.a: AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action, the stages a customer moves through before they buy: first they have to notice something exists, then care enough to learn more, then want it specifically, then actually act. Marketing teams, and anyone advising them on a campaign, use it as a checklist, making sure each piece of content moves people to the next stage instead of skipping ahead.

cards.q: Northbay Fitness is spending heavily on ads and getting plenty of website traffic, but sales are flat. How would you use a funnel to work out where the money is leaking?
cards.takeaway: A funnel turns a vague ‘sales are flat’ into one specific stage where conversion is falling short.
cards.a: A funnel counts how many people survive each step on the way to buying, so you can read the conversion rate between steps rather than the total at the end. Say 200,000 people see the ad, 20,000 visit the site, 6,000 start checkout and 600 buy: the ad to visit step converts at 10 percent and checkout to purchase at 10 percent, when a working checkout usually holds 40 percent or more. That gap says the problem is at the bottom, not the top. Fixing a late step is normally cheaper than buying more traffic, because it multiplies through every stage below it.

cards.q: Vantry Appliances says its flagship blender has gone flat after five years of strong growth, and the team wants to spend more on advertising. How would you think about where that product sits in its life?
cards.takeaway: Products run through introduction, growth, maturity and decline, and the right move changes at each stage.
cards.a: Products tend to follow a curve: a slow introduction while few people know it exists, a growth phase as adoption spreads, a long maturity where almost everyone who wants one has one, and eventually decline. Flat sales after five strong years usually means maturity, where the category has stopped growing and extra volume can only come from a competitor's share. Pouring more money into advertising rarely restarts a mature category, so the usual plays are defending margin, taking cost out, or extending the line with variants. You cannot observe the stage directly, so treat it as a hypothesis and test it against category growth.

cards.q: Larkspur Meals, a subscription meal-kit service, wants to know how much it can afford to spend acquiring a new subscriber and still turn a profit. What number would you calculate, and what does it capture?
cards.takeaway: CLV is the total profit one customer is worth over the whole relationship, not just their first order.
cards.a: Calculate customer lifetime value: the total profit, not revenue, that Larkspur can expect from a single subscriber across the entire relationship, not just their first box. Take the contribution left after the food and delivery costs of an average box, then multiply by how often they order and how long they stay. Because it captures repeat purchases over time, CLV is the number that tells Larkspur how much it can afford to spend acquiring a customer and still come out ahead. Use revenue instead and you overstate that ceiling by the entire cost of making and shipping the boxes, which is how a business ends up losing money on every subscriber it wins.

cards.q: Solenne Software's monthly revenue looks healthy and growing, but the CEO worries it's masking a deeper retention problem. What metric would you pull to check, and why can't total revenue alone tell you this?
cards.takeaway: Churn rate is the percentage of customers you're losing each period, the leak in the bucket.
cards.a: Pull churn rate: the share of customers who stop doing business with Solenne over a given period, a metric subscription businesses watch closely because it's their clearest signal of retention. A high churn rate means Solenne is losing customers faster than is sustainable, even while new signups make total revenue look fine on the surface — so growth and churn always have to be read together.

cards.q: Larkspur Meals spent nine million dollars on marketing last year and added 150,000 subscribers. Finance says a subscriber is worth 180 dollars over their life. What do you calculate, and what does it tell you?
cards.takeaway: CAC is what you pay to win one customer, and lifetime value over CAC tells you whether it was worth paying.
cards.a: Customer acquisition cost is total acquisition spend divided by the customers it won, so here nine million over 150,000 is 60 dollars a subscriber. Set that against the 180 dollar lifetime value and you get a ratio of three to one, which subscription businesses generally read as healthy: near one to one you are barely covering the cost of winning the customer, while a very high ratio can mean you are underspending and leaving growth on the table. It also matters how fast the 60 dollars comes back, since a long payback ties up cash. Cutting churn raises lifetime value and improves the ratio without spending another dollar on ads.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail runs search ads, a podcast sponsorship and an email program all at once, and sales are up 12 percent. The CMO wants to know which one worked. Why is that so hard to answer honestly?
cards.takeaway: Attribution tries to credit a sale to the marketing that caused it, and overlapping activity muddies it.
cards.a: Attribution is the set of rules for splitting credit for a sale across the touchpoints a customer saw on the way to it. Last-click attribution hands all the credit to the final touch, which flatters search and email while starving the podcast that created the demand in the first place. Multi-touch models spread the credit around, but the weights are assumptions someone chose, not measurements. The honest test is an experiment: hold spend back in a set of comparable regions and compare against the rest, which is what a good interviewer wants to hear you reach for before the dashboard.

cards.q: A discount chain undercuts Bramwell's mid-price eyewear by 30 percent, and Bramwell's CEO wants to match. Walk me through the trade-off you'd put in front of him.
cards.takeaway: Matching a discounter buys volume today by spending down the brand equity that justified your price.
cards.a: Start with the arithmetic. If a pair sells for 100 with 50 of cost in it, Bramwell keeps 50, and cutting the price 30 percent leaves 20, so it needs two and a half times the units just to stand still. Then the harder part: price tells customers where a brand sits, so matching resets what they believe the product is worth, and that belief is very hard to walk back up. Check too whether the discounter is even fishing in Bramwell's segment. Often the better answer is defending the dimension you own, or launching a cheaper second line that takes the fight without dragging the main brand down.

name: Pricing Strategy
description: How companies set prices, and why price is the sharpest profit lever.
intro: Price is the fastest lever a business has, and the one most companies handle worst. This deck starts with the simplest question, what a price has to sit between, and builds toward the tactics interviewers actually test: tiers, bundles, discounts, launch pricing, and price wars. You’ll do a little arithmetic along the way, because a pricing answer is only convincing when you can show what a few points of price do to profit. Nothing here assumes you’ve ever priced anything before. By the end you should be able to take a pricing case, find the real constraint, and defend a recommendation with a number behind it.

cards.q: What is a price actually doing for a business, and what sets the floor and the ceiling it has to sit between?
cards.takeaway: Price sits between a cost floor and a customer-value ceiling, and it decides how the gap gets split.
cards.a: Price is the mechanism that turns the value a company creates into money it actually keeps. Below your cost per unit you lose money on every sale, so cost is the floor. Above what the customer believes the product is worth to them, they simply walk away, so their perceived value is the ceiling. Everything in between is negotiable space, and where you land in it decides how much of the created value the company captures and how much the customer walks off with. Most pricing work is an argument about that split.

cards.q: Two people buy the same $4 coffee at Kestrel Roasters. Your engagement manager says one of them would happily have paid $7. What is willingness to pay, and why does it vary so much between customers?
cards.takeaway: Willingness to pay is the most a customer would hand over before walking away, and it varies by person.
cards.a: Willingness to pay is the highest price a particular customer would still say yes to. It differs from person to person because people differ in income, in how urgently they need the thing, in what alternatives they know about, and in how much they care about the brand or the convenience. A single posted price therefore leaves money on the table with the eager buyers and prices out the reluctant ones. Almost every advanced pricing tactic is an attempt to charge each customer closer to their own number.

cards.q: A client asks how you would even go about setting a price for a new product. What are the three classic approaches, and which one would you push them toward?
cards.takeaway: Cost-plus prices off your costs, competitor-based off rivals, value-based off what the buyer gains.
cards.a: Cost-plus takes your cost per unit and adds a fixed markup, so the price is really a statement about your own factory. Competitor-based sets price relative to what rivals charge, which keeps you in the running but hands your pricing decision to someone else. Value-based starts from what the product is worth to the customer, measured against the next-best alternative they would otherwise buy. Value-based is the one to defend in an interview, because it is the only approach that looks at the person actually paying.

cards.q: Cost-plus pricing is the weakest of the three approaches, yet it is everywhere. Why do so many companies use it, and what goes wrong when demand softens?
cards.takeaway: Cost-plus is easy and defensible, but it ignores the customer and can spiral once volume drops.
cards.a: Companies use it because the cost data already sits in their own systems, the markup is easy to justify to a board, and it feels fair. The trouble is that it ignores the customer entirely, so it underprices things people love and overprices things they don’t. It also feeds a spiral: when volume falls, fixed costs like rent and salaries spread over fewer units, the unit cost rises, the formula demands a higher price, and volume falls again. Interviewers like that failure mode because it tests whether you understand fixed costs.

cards.q: Your partner claims a 1% price increase beats a 1% volume increase. Ardleigh Cycles sells 100 units at $100, with $60 of variable cost a unit and $3,000 of fixed costs. Show her the math.
cards.takeaway: A point of price falls straight to profit, while a point of volume drags its variable cost along with it.
cards.a: Start with the baseline: 100 units at $100 is $10,000 of revenue, less $6,000 of variable cost, the $60 a unit you only incur when you actually make one, and less $3,000 of fixed cost, leaving $1,000 of profit. Raise price 1% and the extra $100 lands entirely in profit, which becomes $1,100, a 10% gain. Sell 1% more units instead and you collect $100 more but spend $60 more, so profit is $1,040, only a 4% gain. Price is the sharpest lever a business has, which is why it draws so much consulting attention.
