cards.q: What is price discrimination, and how does a company charge different customers different prices for essentially the same thing without causing an uproar?
cards.takeaway: Charge different buyers different prices by fencing them apart with something they cannot easily fake.
cards.a: Price discrimination means selling the same or a nearly identical product at different prices to different buyers, so each one pays closer to their own willingness to pay. It only works if you can build a fence the customer can’t simply step over: a student or senior ID, a country, an advance-purchase deadline, a midweek rather than weekend booking. The fence has to line up with willingness to pay and be hard to fake, and it has to feel fair, which is why age and timing are tolerated while obvious personal targeting usually is not.

cards.q: Talbridge Software keeps arguing about which single price is right. Someone suggests offering three plans instead. What is versioning, and what makes a good-better-best ladder actually work?
cards.takeaway: Tiers let customers sort themselves by value, so each one pays closer to their own number.
cards.a: Versioning means deliberately selling several versions of the same underlying product at different prices, so customers sort themselves instead of you guessing. It works when the differences between tiers track what different buyers genuinely value, things like seats, capacity, support speed, or warranty length. The top tier often earns its keep less by selling than by making the middle tier look reasonable, and the cheapest tier catches price-sensitive buyers who would otherwise buy nothing. Draw the lines wrong and everyone buys the cheapest plan.

cards.q: Norwood Media sells a news subscription and a puzzle app separately. Some readers care about news, others about puzzles. Why might selling both together for one price make more money than selling them apart?
cards.takeaway: Bundling smooths out differing tastes, so one price can capture both customers instead of one each.
cards.a: Suppose one reader would pay $8 for news and $2 for puzzles, while another would pay $3 for news and $7 for puzzles. Priced separately, news at $8 and puzzles at $7 each sell to only one reader, for $15 in total. Bundle the two at $10 and both readers buy, for $20, because their combined willingness to pay is similar even though their tastes point in opposite directions. Bundling wins when tastes vary that way and the extra component costs almost nothing to deliver. Unbundle when one piece is strong enough to sell alone.

cards.q: Ashcombe Devices is launching something nobody else sells yet. Should it come in low to grab the market, or start high and walk the price down? Make the case for each.
cards.takeaway: Skim high when early buyers will pay a premium, penetrate low when scale and lock-in decide the winner.
cards.a: Price skimming starts high to harvest the buyers who want the product most, then steps down over time to reach each next layer of demand. Penetration pricing starts low to win share fast, betting that volume brings lower unit costs, habit, or network effects that make the position hard to attack later. Skimming suits real differentiation, patent protection, and slow-moving rivals. Penetration suits markets where scale drives cost down or customers rarely switch once signed up. Skimming invites entrants, and penetration can leave you unable to raise price later.

cards.q: A client’s head of retail insists on ending every price in .99 and printing a crossed-out “was” price on the shelf tag. How much of that is real, and how much is folklore?
cards.takeaway: Buyers judge a price against a reference point, so framing matters, but it can’t rescue a weak offer.
cards.a: People rarely judge a price on its own. They compare it against a reference point, whatever they last paid, what sits beside it on the shelf, or the crossed-out figure on the tag, and that comparison drives whether the price feels fair. Charm pricing, the .99 ending, does show measurable effects in some categories, but the size varies a lot across products and studies, and it can cheapen a premium brand. Treat framing as a small, testable adjustment on top of a price set from customer value, not a substitute for it.

cards.q: Sales at Pallant Paper wants a 10% discount to hit the quarter-end target. Gross margin is 40%. How much extra volume does that discount have to generate just to break even on profit?
cards.takeaway: A 10% discount on a 40% margin needs 33% more volume just to stand still.
cards.a: Take a $100 sale carrying $60 of variable cost, so $40 of contribution, the money left after the costs that move with each unit. Discount 10% and you collect $90 while the cost stays $60, so contribution drops to $30, a quarter of it gone. To earn the same total contribution you now need $40 divided by $30 of volume, which is 33% more units. The thinner the margin the worse this gets, which is why pricing teams fence discounts to buyers who genuinely wouldn’t have bought otherwise.

cards.q: What’s the difference between subscription and usage-based pricing, and what does each one do to the customer’s decision and the seller's revenue?
cards.takeaway: Subscriptions buy predictability, usage pricing ties what a customer pays to what they actually consume.
cards.a: A subscription charges a recurring fee for access, so the customer pays the same whether they use the product once a month or constantly, and the seller gets revenue that is easy to forecast as long as churn stays low. Usage-based pricing charges per unit consumed, per gigabyte, per call, per hour, so the bill tracks the value the customer draws. Usage pricing lowers the barrier to starting and grows with a successful account, but it makes forecasting harder. Many companies now blend the two, a platform fee plus metered usage on top.

cards.q: Two hardware chains on the same highway keep undercutting each other until neither one makes money. Why do price wars start so easily, and why is winning one so hard?
cards.takeaway: Cutting looks smart for each rival on its own, and everyone ends up poorer with the same market shares.
cards.a: With few players and similar products, cutting price looks like the better move whichever way your rival goes: if they hold, you take volume, and if they cut, you cannot afford to be the expensive one. So both cut, both keep roughly the share they started with, and both earn less, which is the classic prisoner’s dilemma shape. Price is also the easiest move for a rival to see and copy within days, unlike a product improvement. Winning takes a durable cost advantage the other side simply can’t match.

cards.q: Riversedge Tools hasn’t raised prices in six years and its input costs are up 20%. The CEO is terrified of losing customers. How would you get an increase through, and how would you test it first?
cards.takeaway: Raise price narrowly first, give customers a reason and a cheaper option, then measure what you lose.
cards.a: Start where you have the most room: products with few substitutes, customers who buy on service rather than price, and segments where your price has drifted furthest below what the product is worth. Test rather than announce, by raising price in a few regions or accounts and watching volume against comparable ones you left alone. Give customers a reason they can repeat, a real input cost or a genuine improvement, and a cheaper stripped-down option so leaving is not the only response. Then check whether the volume lost was worth less than the margin gained.

cards.q: Your team pulls Holloway Ceramics’ invoices and finds the average customer pays 22% below list. The VP calls it a pricing leak. What is a pocket price waterfall, and what would you look for in it?
cards.takeaway: Pocket price is what’s left after every discount and term, and it is rarely close to list price.
cards.a: List price is the number on the price sheet. Subtract the negotiated discount and you get invoice price, then subtract everything that comes off after the invoice, volume rebates, early-payment terms, freight, co-op marketing allowances, returns, and what’s left is the pocket price, the cash the company genuinely keeps. The waterfall lays those steps out one at a time so you can see where the money went. Nearly every waterfall shows similar customers paying wildly different pocket prices for no defensible reason, and closing that spread is often the fastest margin win available.

cards.q: Brackwell Instruments can cut price 15% to win a distributor that would add 40% to volume, or hold price and stay a premium niche brand. Gross margin is 45%. How do you advise them?
cards.takeaway: Test whether the volume clears the margin hurdle, then ask what the low price does to everything else.
cards.a: Run the arithmetic first. On $100 with $55 of variable cost, contribution is $45, and a 15% cut leaves $85 against the same $55, or $30, so you’d need 50% more volume to break even against the 40% on offer. That alone says no, and the strategic case is worse: a price that low leaks to existing customers and resets what the market thinks the product is worth. I’d counter with a fenced offer, a stripped-down model or a volume rebate, that gives the distributor a lower price without repricing the flagship.

name: Management & Strategy Frameworks
description: The core frameworks used to analyze markets, competitors, and business decisions.
intro: Case interviews and strategy conversations lean heavily on a small set of well-known frameworks, SWOT, Porter’s five forces, the kind of tools that give structure to a messy business question. This deck introduces each one from scratch: what it is for, when it actually applies, and the trap of using it as a checklist instead of a thinking tool. If you have never used a strategy framework before, this is designed to get you comfortable enough to reach for the right one under pressure.

cards.q: A client’s CEO tells you the company’s strategy is to grow revenue 20% next year. Your engagement manager winces. Why isn’t that actually a strategy, and what would one look like?
cards.takeaway: A goal says where you want to end up, a strategy is the set of choices about how you get there.
cards.a: Growing 20% is a goal, an outcome the company wants. A strategy is the set of choices about how it intends to get there, which customers to serve, what to offer them, and just as importantly what it will deliberately not do. A quick test is whether a sensible rival could have chosen the opposite: a competitor might reasonably decide to win on service rather than on price, but no competitor would choose to shrink 20%. If a client’s strategy contains no trade-off, it’s a wish, and saying so politely is often the first real value a team adds.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a company’s mission and its strategy?
cards.takeaway: Mission is why a company exists; strategy is how it competes to get there.
cards.a: A mission statement explains why an organization exists and what it's fundamentally trying to achieve, while strategy is the specific plan for how it will compete and allocate resources to accomplish that. Mission tends to stay fixed for years or decades, while strategy adapts as markets, competitors, and client priorities change.

cards.q: What is opportunity cost?
cards.takeaway: Opportunity cost is what you give up by not choosing the next-best alternative.
cards.a: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option you give up when you make a choice. It matters in case interviews and real strategy work alike because the true cost of any decision isn't just the money spent on it, it's also whatever else that same time, money, or resource could have produced instead.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group, a mid-size apparel chain, is trying to decide whether to expand into a new region. Before the team builds a recommendation, the engagement manager asks you to lay out where the client stands today. What framework do you reach for?
cards.takeaway: SWOT sorts a company's position into internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.
cards.a: Start with a SWOT analysis, a simple four-box way to take stock of where a company stands before making a strategic call. Strengths and weaknesses are internal, things the client controls, like its brand or cost structure, while opportunities and threats come from the external environment, like market trends or new competitors. Laying all four out side by side helps the team surface what to build on, what to fix, what to chase, and what to defend against, before proposing any recommendation to expand.

cards.q: What does “economies of scale” mean?
cards.takeaway: Average cost per unit drops as production volume rises, letting big companies price lower.
cards.a: Economies of scale is the tendency for a company's average cost per unit to fall as it produces more, a lever worth flagging any time a client's advantage rests on scale. Fixed costs, like a factory or corporate overhead, get spread across a larger number of units, and higher volumes often let a company negotiate better prices from suppliers too. It's a big reason large incumbents can often compete on price in ways smaller rivals simply can't afford to match.

cards.q: What does “economies of scope” mean, and how is it different from economies of scale?
cards.takeaway: Economies of scope save money by producing different products together, not just more of one.
cards.a: Economies of scope are cost savings a company gets from producing multiple related products together rather than separately, for example by sharing R&D, distribution, or manufacturing capacity across product lines. It's a different lever from economies of scale, which comes from producing more of the same thing rather than a wider mix of things, worth distinguishing clearly if a case turns on which one is actually driving a client's costs.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co. is considering entering the packaged foods industry and has hired your firm to assess whether it's an attractive market to enter. What framework would you use to size up industry attractiveness, and what does it look at?
cards.takeaway: Five surrounding pressures, rivals, entrants, substitutes, and supplier/buyer power, decide how profitable an industry can be.
cards.a: Reach for Porter's Five Forces, which sizes up how attractive an industry actually is based on five competitive pressures bearing in from every direction: rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants like Bramwell itself, the threat of substitute products, and the bargaining power of both suppliers and buyers. If most of these forces are strong, they squeeze margins and make the industry a tougher place to make money; if they're weak, incumbents tend to enjoy healthier profits, a call the team needs to make before recommending Bramwell enter.

cards.q: Merrowfield Bakery knows its costs are too high but can’t say where the money actually goes, or what customers are really paying for. How would a value chain help you answer both questions?
cards.takeaway: A value chain splits a company into its separate activities so you can see which ones actually add value.
cards.a: A value chain cuts a company into the distinct activities it performs to get a product to a customer, from buying inputs through operations, distribution, marketing, and after-sales service, with support activities like technology and hiring running underneath all of them. For each activity you ask two things: what does it cost us, and would a customer pay more because we do it well. That separates the few steps where Merrowfield genuinely earns a premium from the ones that are just overhead, and it shows the team where a cost cut is safe and where it would quietly damage the product.

cards.q: Aldercrest Furniture, a mid-market retailer, asks your team how it should compete against both big-box discounters and boutique design brands. What are Michael Porter's three generic strategies for building a competitive advantage, and how might you frame Aldercrest's choice?
cards.takeaway: Porter's three routes to advantage: be the cheapest, be meaningfully different, or dominate a narrow niche.
cards.a: A competitive advantage is something that lets a company consistently outperform its rivals over time. Porter described three generic strategies for building one: cost leadership, becoming the lowest-cost producer and competing on price; differentiation, offering something distinctly better that customers will pay a premium for; and focus, applying either of those approaches to a narrow market segment instead of the whole industry. For Aldercrest, the team would need to help the client pick a lane rather than get stuck in the middle, competing against discounters on price while boutique brands out-differentiate them.

cards.q: Your team finds that Castellan Tools earns far higher margins than its rivals. The partner asks the obvious next question: will that still be true in five years? How do you test whether an advantage lasts?
cards.takeaway: An advantage only lasts if rivals cannot cheaply copy it, buy it, or route around it.
cards.a: An advantage shows up as returns above what rivals earn, but the real question is what stops those returns from being competed away. Name the specific thing producing the gap, then ask how a well funded competitor would copy it by next year. Barriers that tend to hold include a protected process, a cost position built on scale a smaller rival can’t reach, a brand customers genuinely trust, switching costs that make leaving painful, and network effects, where each extra user makes the product better for everyone else. A clever feature or a temporary price cut holds nothing, since it can be matched in a season.

cards.q: A consumer goods client, Cassidy Home Goods, sells six product lines and wants help deciding where to keep investing versus where to cut. What framework helps sort a portfolio like this into clear buckets?
cards.takeaway: The BCG matrix sorts products by growth and market share into stars, cash cows, question marks, and dogs.
cards.a: The BCG matrix plots each of the client's product lines on two axes, market growth and relative market share, to sort them into four categories: stars (high growth, high share) are worth continued investment, cash cows (low growth, high share) generate steady cash with little need for reinvestment, question marks (high growth, low share) are uncertain bets that need cash to prove out, and dogs (low growth, low share) are usually candidates to divest. It gives the team a quick, defensible way to recommend where Cassidy should keep investing, hold steady, or cut loose.

cards.q: Halvers Sporting Goods tells your team it wants to grow but has no view on how. How would you lay out the full set of growth options on one page, and which one carries the most risk?
cards.takeaway: Growth is old or new products sold to old or new customers, and doing both at once is riskiest.
cards.a: Ansoff’s growth matrix lays the options out on two questions: is the product one you already sell or a new one, and is the customer group one you already serve or a new one. Selling more of what you have to the customers you have, called market penetration, is the cheapest and best understood. Taking an existing product into a new market, or building a new product for existing customers, stretches Halvers in one direction each. Diversification, a new product for a new market, stretches it in both at once, which is why it fails most often and draws the hardest questions from a board.

cards.q: Denholm Coffee Roasters, a client of your firm, is weighing whether to buy its own bean farms and also open branded retail cafes. What strategic move is this, and how would you frame the options for the client?
cards.takeaway: Vertical integration means owning more of your own supply chain, upstream or downstream.
cards.a: This is vertical integration, taking ownership of additional stages of your own supply chain. Backward integration would mean Denholm acquiring bean farms, moving upstream toward raw materials; forward integration would mean opening its own retail cafes, moving downstream toward the customer. Clients pursue it to control costs, secure supply, or capture margin that would otherwise go to an outside partner, though each direction comes with its own execution risk worth flagging.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics needs a same-day delivery capability it doesn’t have today. The CEO asks whether to build it, buy a company that already has it, or partner with one. How would you frame that decision?
cards.takeaway: Build when the capability is core and you have time, buy when speed matters, partner when neither holds.
cards.a: Start by asking whether the capability is core, meaning it is central to why customers pick Northbay rather than something a competent outsider could do just as well. Core capabilities usually get built or bought, because owning them is what protects the advantage, while everything else is a fair candidate to partner or outsource. Then weigh time, price, and control. Building costs least per dollar but is slow and can fail outright, buying is fast and proven but carries a premium and an integration job, and partnering is quick and cheap while leaving Northbay dependent on someone whose interests can drift.

cards.q: A client’s CMO keeps calling a small new competitor “disruptive.” Your partner asks you to be precise about the word. What does disruption actually mean, and why does the distinction change the response?
cards.takeaway: Real disruption starts cheap and unimpressive at the low end, then improves until it takes the mainstream.
cards.a: Used precisely, disruption describes an entrant that begins by serving customers the incumbent doesn’t much want, with something cheaper and genuinely worse on the dimensions the mainstream cares about, and then improves quickly enough to pull those mainstream customers across. That is different from a rival attacking with a better, more expensive product, which is ordinary competition. The distinction changes the recommendation, because a better product can often be met head on, while a disruptor is dangerous precisely because giving up the unprofitable low end looks like sound judgement right until the entrant catches up.

cards.q: You present a strategy the client’s leadership team fully agrees with, and a year later almost none of it has happened. What usually goes wrong between a good strategy and a real result?
cards.takeaway: Strategies fail when nobody moved the budget, the owners, or the incentives to match them.
cards.a: Agreement in a room is cheap. A strategy only becomes real when money actually moves to the chosen priorities, when one named person owns each piece and is measured on it, and when the activities the company agreed to stop doing genuinely stop. Most failures trace back to one of those three: the budget stayed roughly where it was, incentives kept paying people for last year’s behavior, or the trade-off was quietly reversed the first time a large customer complained. That is why strong teams write the resource shifts and the owners into the recommendation itself, rather than leaving them for later.

cards.q: Larkmoor Instruments can double down on its premium niche or launch a cheaper line to blunt a fast-growing discounter. The partner wants your call, not another framework. Which do you pick, and what are you giving up?
cards.takeaway: Commit to the option whose downside you can survive, and say out loud what you are trading away.
cards.a: Both are defensible, so the interviewer is testing whether you can commit and then name the cost honestly. A good answer holds the premium niche, on the grounds that Larkmoor’s advantage sits in things the discounter can’t cheaply copy, while a cheap line would compete on a cost base Larkmoor loses on and would teach its own customers that the brand is negotiable. What you accept is a smaller market and real exposure if the discounter’s quality improves over time, so pair the call with a trigger, a defined loss of share among mid-tier buyers, that forces the client to revisit it.

name: Operations & Supply Chain Management
description: How companies manage inventory, production, and the flow of goods.
intro: Operations questions test a different kind of thinking than finance ones: how a business actually moves inventory, manages production, and keeps a supply chain from breaking under pressure. This deck introduces the core concepts, like the bullwhip effect, through simple explanations first, building toward the vocabulary interviewers expect you to use fluently. No operations background needed, just a willingness to think about a business as a physical system, not just a spreadsheet.

cards.q: A partner tells you your next case is “an operations case.” In plain terms, what part of a business does operations actually cover?
cards.takeaway: Operations is everything a company does to turn inputs into a product a customer actually receives.
cards.a: Operations is the machinery of the business: buying materials, making the product, moving it around, and getting it into a customer's hands. Where a marketing question asks who will buy and a pricing question asks what to charge, an operations question asks how the thing gets made and delivered, at what cost, at what speed, and how reliably. Almost every operations case comes down to one of those three levers. Interviewers like the topic because the answers are concrete and countable, so vague structure gets exposed fast.

cards.q: Calder Foods buys wheat and sells boxed cereal. Walk me through its supply chain, stage by stage, and tell me why the stages are worth naming out loud.
cards.takeaway: A supply chain is the full run of hands a product passes through from raw material to end buyer.
cards.a: A supply chain is every organization and step involved in getting a product from raw material to final buyer. For Calder that runs roughly: farms grow the wheat, a mill processes and sells it, Calder's plant turns it into cereal and packs the boxes, a distributor stores and moves the cases, a retailer stocks the shelf, and a shopper buys one. Goods move one way while orders and cash move back the other. Naming the stages first matters because each handoff adds cost and time and is a candidate location for the problem you've been asked to solve.

cards.q: What do “cycle time” and “throughput” mean on a production line, and how do the two connect?
cards.takeaway: Cycle time is the gap between finished units and throughput is how many finish per hour.
cards.a: A process is just a sequence of steps a unit passes through. Cycle time is the gap between one finished unit coming off the end and the next one, and throughput is how many units the line actually completes per hour or per day. They're two readings of the same fact: if a finished unit appears every 3 minutes, throughput is 20 an hour. Capacity is the highest throughput the line could hold if nothing went wrong. Get these three words straight early, because most operations cases are an argument about which one the client should be moving.

cards.q: At Dunmore Assembly Co.'s plant, three of four stations sit idle for stretches during the shift, yet the plant still can't hit its daily output target. Where should you start looking, and why?
cards.takeaway: A bottleneck is the slowest station in a process, and it caps what the whole system can produce.
cards.a: Start by finding Dunmore's bottleneck: the single stage in the process with the least capacity, which sets the ceiling on how much the entire line can produce no matter how efficient every other stage is. That's consistent with what the plant manager is describing, the idle stations are simply waiting on the slow one. Speeding up any other stage won't help, since output still can't exceed what the bottleneck allows, so improving the process starts with finding that constraint and fixing it first.

cards.q: Your client, NorthPeak Manufacturing, is missing its quarterly output targets even though the plant manager insists the machines are running nearly non-stop. Before diving into the process itself, what metric would you check first, and what would it tell you?
cards.takeaway: Capacity utilization shows what share of a company's maximum output it's actually using.
cards.a: Start with capacity utilization: it measures how much of NorthPeak's total production capacity is actually being used, shown as a percentage of the maximum possible output. Low utilization can point to inefficiency or weak demand pulling orders away from the plant, while very high utilization is a warning sign too: the plant is close to its ceiling and at risk of bottlenecks if demand climbs any further. Either reading points you toward a different next question, which is exactly why it's worth checking before you go any deeper.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics' CFO points at a full warehouse and asks why the company is sitting on stock that earns nothing today. Why hold inventory at all, and what does holding it cost?
cards.takeaway: Inventory buys smooth operations, paid for in tied-up cash, storage and goods going stale.
cards.a: Inventory exists because supply and demand don't run on the same clock: goods arrive in big batches, customers buy in ones and twos, and nobody knows exactly what next week looks like. Stock on the shelf lets Northbay serve a customer today instead of after the next delivery. The cost is real, though. Cash is parked in the warehouse rather than earning a return, you pay for space, handling and insurance, and goods can spoil, get damaged or go out of date. A common rule of thumb puts the total holding cost near 20 to 30 percent of the inventory's value a year, though it varies widely by industry.

cards.q: What is safety stock, and why do companies hold it? What's the cost of holding too much?
cards.takeaway: Safety stock is the buffer inventory that absorbs surprise demand spikes or supply delays.
cards.a: Safety stock is extra inventory held beyond what's expected to be needed, acting as a cushion against uncertainty, like a sudden spike in orders or a delayed shipment. It lowers the risk of running out of stock, but it isn't free: it ties up capital and storage space, so companies weigh that cost against the protection it buys them. In a case, a client with chronic stockouts and a client with bloated warehouse costs can both trace back to the same lever, just tuned in opposite directions.

cards.q: What is lead time, and why do interviewers ask about it in operations cases?
cards.takeaway: Lead time is the full clock from placing an order to actually having it in hand.
cards.a: Lead time is the total stretch between placing an order and actually receiving it, covering everything from processing and production to shipping. The shorter it is, the less safety stock a client needs to keep on hand to reliably meet customer demand, since there's less time for something to go wrong or for demand to shift in between. When a case involves a supplier switch or a new distribution route, lead time is usually the first number worth asking for.

cards.q: What is Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and why is it a useful reflex in an operations case?
cards.takeaway: EOQ finds the order size where ordering costs and holding costs balance out to the lowest total cost.
cards.a: Economic order quantity is the order size that minimizes total inventory cost, balancing two costs that pull in opposite directions: the fixed cost of placing an order, and the cost of storing the units once they've arrived. Order too little and you pay that fixed ordering cost too often; order too much and you pay more to store the excess. EOQ is simply the quantity where those two costs are lowest combined, which is why it's a handy structure to reach for whenever a case turns on 'how much should the client order at a time.'

cards.q: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management, and what's the tradeoff a case interviewer wants you to name?
cards.takeaway: JIT brings materials in only as production needs them, trading safety stock for leaner inventory.
cards.a: Just-in-time inventory management brings materials and components in right as production needs them, instead of stockpiling them in advance. That keeps holding costs and waste low, since there's little excess inventory sitting around. The tradeoff is fragility: with barely any buffer stock, a single disruption anywhere in the supply chain can quickly bring production to a halt. It's a favorite lever in operations cases: a client chasing the cost savings is also signing up for that exposure, and naming the tradeoff explicitly is what separates a strong answer from a list of definitions.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co., a mid-sized furniture maker, is debating whether to keep building sofas against a demand forecast or switch to starting production only once a customer order comes in. What are the two production models on the table, and what's the tradeoff?
cards.takeaway: Push production guesses ahead of demand; pull production only makes what's already been ordered.
cards.a: Bramwell is weighing a push system, which produces to a forecast, building up inventory ahead of actual orders in the hope demand shows up to match it, against a pull system, which flips that logic: production only kicks off once a real customer order actually appears. Pull is the thinking behind JIT and cuts the risk of building sofas nobody ends up wanting, but it generally means longer wait times for the customer and less room to smooth production volume.

cards.q: Two rival plants build the same part, one heavily automated and one mostly manual. Industry volume drops 10 percent. Which plant's profit falls further, and why?
cards.takeaway: Heavy fixed costs make profit swing much harder than volume does, in both directions.
cards.a: The automated one. Fixed costs don't move with output, machines, rent and salaried supervisors, while variable costs rise with every unit made, materials, hourly labor and packaging. Automation swaps variable cost for fixed cost, so the automated plant earns more on each unit but has a bigger base to cover before it earns anything. That sensitivity is called operating leverage: volume falls 10 percent, the fixed costs sit exactly where they were, and profit can fall 60 percent. The same leverage works in its favor on the way back up, which is the honest version of the answer.

cards.q: Vantor Appliances wants to cut a two-dollar-per-unit inspection at the end of its line to save money. How would you frame the cost of quality for them?
cards.takeaway: A defect gets roughly ten times more expensive to fix at every stage it slips past.
cards.a: Quality spending falls into two buckets: what you spend to stop defects, designing the process well and inspecting output, and what you spend once one gets through, scrapping or reworking it inside the plant, or handling a return, warranty claim or recall after a customer has it. The widely used rule of thumb is that a defect costs about ten times more at each stage it escapes, so a dollar of prevention saves ten in rework and a hundred in warranty. It's a rule of thumb rather than a law, but the shape holds: Vantor is trading a small known saving for a large unknown cost.

cards.q: What is Six Sigma, and how can its framework help structure a case answer?
cards.takeaway: Six Sigma hunts down process defects using data, aiming for near-flawless, 3.4-in-a-million quality.
cards.a: Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology for shrinking defects and variability in a process, aiming for a quality level where only about 3.4 defects occur per million opportunities. Teams typically work through it using DMAIC, a five-step cycle: Define the problem, Measure current performance, Analyze the root cause, Improve the process, and Control it so the gains stick. That same define-measure-analyze arc is a useful skeleton for walking an interviewer through any client process problem, not just a formal Six Sigma engagement.

cards.q: A client wants to move final assembly to a lower-cost country and shows you the wage saving. Beyond that number, what would you check before calling it a good idea?
cards.takeaway: Offshoring trades a visible wage saving against longer lead times, thinner control and more risk.
cards.a: First get the words straight: outsourcing means paying an outside firm to do a step you used to do yourself, offshoring means moving the work to another country, and a client can do either, both or neither. The wage saving is the easy number, so your value is the rest of the landed cost, freight and duties, tighter quality oversight, currency swings, and the extra inventory needed to cover a lead time that just went from days to weeks. There's a strategic filter too: don't hand out the step you actually compete on, since a cheaper version of the thing customers choose you for is rarely a saving.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group's category buyers see it every quarter: a small uptick in weekend foot traffic at stores turns into wildly swinging order quantities from their manufacturers a few weeks later. What's happening, and what's it called?
cards.takeaway: Small demand blips get amplified into big order swings the further upstream you look.
cards.a: This is the bullwhip effect: a small shift in real customer demand gets amplified as it passes upstream, from retailer to distributor to manufacturer, because each link tends to over-adjust its own orders instead of passing the true signal along unchanged. Those small overreactions stack at every step, so by the time the signal reaches Ferrow's manufacturers, a minor blip in weekend traffic looks like a huge swing in orders, distorting what's actually happening at the register.

cards.q: Grenwood Instruments' on-time delivery has slipped from 96 percent to 74 percent over two quarters with no change in total demand. Walk me through how you'd diagnose it end to end.
cards.takeaway: Walk one order from entry to shipment and find the first stage where planned and actual come apart.
cards.a: Take one order and walk it from the moment it's placed to the moment it ships, comparing what each stage is supposed to take against what it now takes. With demand flat, the lost time sits in one of three places: capacity, where a stage is running above the utilization it can sustain, process, where a stage's cycle time got longer through a new part, new staff or more rework, or supply, where a supplier's lead time has quietly stretched and starves a stage. Confirm the bottleneck with data before recommending anything, since fixing a stage that isn't the constraint moves nothing at all.

name: Growth Strategy & Market Entry
description: How to judge a new market, pick a way in, and commit to an answer.
intro: Market entry is one of the two or three case types you are most likely to actually get, and it is really three questions stacked on top of each other: is this market worth being in, could this client win in it, and does the money work. This deck takes you from what the prompt is asking through the tools you need to answer it, market attractiveness, TAM, SAM and SOM, the entry modes from building to franchising, and how incumbents fight back when you show up. It leans on the sizing, profitability and strategy work you have already done, so you can spend your effort on the entry decision itself. By the end you should be able to take a cold prompt and land a real go or no-go.

cards.q: What is a market-entry case, and what does your answer actually have to end in?
cards.takeaway: A market-entry case asks whether a client should go into a new market, and it ends in yes or no.
cards.a: A market-entry case hands you a client and a market they are not in yet, a new country, a new customer segment, a new product category, and asks whether they should go in. It is one of the most common case types in consulting interviews because it forces you to do several things at once: size a market, judge the competition, and check whether the client could actually pull it off. What it is not is an essay. The interviewer wants to hear enter or don’t enter, plus the two or three reasons that drove it, said out loud in under a minute.

cards.q: Your interviewer opens with: Halden Dairy, a regional milk producer, is thinking about entering the plant-based drinks category. How would you structure this?
cards.takeaway: Three tests in order: is the market attractive, can we win in it, and is the prize worth it to us.
cards.a: Lay out three buckets, in that order. First, is the market attractive: how big is it, how fast is it growing, and how profitable are the companies already in it. Second, can Halden win: does it have the brand, the plants, the shelf space and the cost position to take share from people who got there first. Third, is it worth it: what does entry cost, what does it return, and is that better than anything else Halden could do with the same money. Say all three out loud before you dig into any one of them.

cards.q: What makes a market attractive to enter, beyond simply being big?
cards.takeaway: Attractiveness is size, growth, profitability, and how concentrated the competition already is.
cards.a: Size tells you the ceiling, but a large market that is barely growing and already carved up between three players earning thin margins is a bad place to arrive. Growth matters because in a fast-growing market you can win volume without taking it off anyone, which incumbents fight far less hard. Profitability, meaning the margin the existing players actually earn, tells you whether the economics survive the trip. Concentration, meaning how much share sits with the top few, tells you how much of the market is genuinely available. A market can pass on size and fail on the other three.

cards.q: An interviewer stops you and asks for the size of the prize for Verrow Fitness in TAM, SAM and SOM terms. What are those three, in plain language?
cards.takeaway: TAM is everyone, SAM is everyone you could serve, SOM is the slice you could realistically win.
cards.a: TAM, the total addressable market, is every dollar spent on the thing anywhere, with no constraints at all. SAM, the serviceable addressable market, narrows that to the part Verrow could actually reach given its product, its channels and the places it operates. SOM, the serviceable obtainable market, narrows again to what it could plausibly capture within a few years against competitors already sitting there. If the category is $4 billion, Verrow only sells in regions worth $900 million, and 8 percent share there is credible, the number that belongs in your recommendation is about $70 million, not $4 billion.

cards.q: Your engagement manager agrees the market looks great, then asks the harder question: does the client have a right to win here? What does that mean, and how do you test it?
cards.takeaway: A right to win is a specific reason this client beats incumbents, not just a wish to be in the market.
cards.a: A right to win is a concrete answer to why this client, rather than anyone else with money, takes share in a market where competitors are already established and already know the customers. You test it by listing what the market actually rewards, low cost, a trusted brand, distribution reach, technical skill, then checking honestly which of those the client already owns and which it would have to buy or build from scratch. Enthusiasm is not a capability. If every advantage on the list has to be acquired, the client is just another new entrant, and interviewers listen closely for whether you will say that.

cards.q: Calder Foods has decided the market is worth entering. What are its options for how to actually get in, and what is the trade-off between them?
cards.takeaway: Build, acquire, joint venture, license or franchise, trading speed and cost against control.
cards.a: Building organically means starting from nothing, the slowest and most capital-hungry route up front, but you keep all the economics and all the control. Acquiring buys a business that already works, so you arrive with customers and staff on day one, at a price. A joint venture pairs you with a local partner who brings market knowledge or distribution and takes a share of both the profits and the decisions. Licensing and franchising let someone else run the operation using your brand or technology for a fee, the fastest and cheapest way in and the one where you control quality least.

cards.q: Northbay Logistics could build a warehouse network in the new region or buy a mid-size local operator. Why is buying faster, and why does it almost always cost more?
cards.takeaway: Buying skips the ramp-up years, and the seller charges you for the profits you skipped.
cards.a: Building means years of losing money while you sign customers, hire people and grind toward the scale where the unit economics finally work. Buying hands you all of that on closing day, which is precisely the point. The price reflects it, because you are paying the seller today for the future profits of a business that already runs, plus a premium to persuade them to give up control, so the cheaper-looking build wins on price and loses on time. Which one is right depends on how fast the window is closing, and a good answer says so rather than picking a side on instinct.

cards.q: You already know barriers to entry as the thing that protects incumbents. On a live case you are the one standing outside. What do those barriers actually cost you?
cards.takeaway: From the outside, barriers are the bill you pay before your first profitable unit.
cards.a: Capital requirements mean a plant, a fleet or a licence you have to fund before a single sale. Scale economies mean the incumbents’ cost per unit is already lower than yours will be for years, so you either lose money or price above them. Switching costs, whether contracts, habits or integration work, mean even a genuinely better product moves slowly. Regulation and locked-up distribution can simply shut the door. Adding all of that up gives you the real cost of entry, and that number, rather than the market size, is what usually kills a case.

cards.q: You have built a model showing Ferrow Retail at 6 percent share in three years. Your partner asks what the incumbents are doing while that happens. Why does that question matter so much?
cards.takeaway: Incumbents fight back, so a plan that assumes they stand still is not a plan.
cards.a: Share does not sit unclaimed, it gets taken from someone, and that someone can cut price, tie customers into longer contracts, flood the channel with promotions, or simply copy whatever you launched with. The usual pattern is that the strongest incumbent defends hardest in the segment where it earns the most. So build the response into the case: assume price falls a few points, ask whether your economics still hold at that price, and check who can afford a long fight. A recommendation that survives the counterattack is the only one worth giving.

cards.q: Halden Dairy wants to enter a country where it has never operated. Beyond the numbers, what non-financial barriers should you raise, and how do you keep that from sounding like hand-waving?
cards.takeaway: Rules and local habits change your cost, product and timeline, so price them rather than just naming them.
cards.a: Regulation shows up as licences, ownership limits that force you into a local partner, labelling and safety standards, tariffs and data rules, each of which is a delay and a cost you can put a number on. Culture shows up as different tastes, different buying occasions, different retail channels, and a workforce that expects to be managed differently. The way to stay credible is to convert all of it into figures, so a licence that takes nine months means revenue starts in year two, and reformulating for local taste adds four points to cost. Vague respect-the-culture comments land badly, quantified ones land well.

cards.q: Your client is already in its market and simply wants to grow. What is the full menu of growth levers, and how do you make sure you have not missed one?
cards.takeaway: Grow by winning more customers, more per customer, more often, new products, or new markets.
cards.a: Revenue is customers times what each one spends times how often they buy, so the first three levers fall straight out of that arithmetic: win more customers, get more out of each purchase through price or basket size, or get people buying more often. Beyond the existing business there are two more, selling new products to the customers you already have, and selling what you already make in new markets, which is exactly where market entry sits. Running the whole list out loud before you pick one is how you show an interviewer you are being exhaustive rather than lucky.

cards.q: A chief executive tells you she wants to double revenue in four years and asks whether to grow it herself or go and buy it. How do you frame organic versus inorganic growth?
cards.takeaway: Organic growth is cheaper but capped by your own capability, acquisition is the reverse.
cards.a: Organic growth means growing out of your own operations, more stores, more products, more customers, funded by your own cash and limited by how fast your own capability can expand. Inorganic growth means acquiring it, which delivers revenue immediately but costs a premium and leaves you with an integration job, which is where most of the promised value quietly disappears. The honest framing is that organic growth is limited by what you can build, while acquisition is limited by what happens to be for sale and what you can afford. Four years is short enough that most doubling plans need both, and saying so beats picking one.

cards.q: The client is nervous about committing $200 million to a full launch, so you suggest piloting first. What should that pilot actually be designed to test?
cards.takeaway: A pilot exists to test the assumption that would break the case, not to prove the plan works.
cards.a: A pilot is only worth running if it can change the decision, so pick the one or two assumptions the whole business case rests on and design around those. Usually that means customer take-up at the price you assumed and the true cost to serve once you are actually operating, not brand awareness. Set the number that means go and the number that means stop before you start, or the results become something everyone reads their own way. And run it somewhere representative, because a pilot in your friendliest city tells you almost nothing about the rest of the market.

cards.q: The client is going to spend real money on the back of your work. What does a defensible market-entry business case actually contain?
cards.takeaway: Revenue at a realistic share, cost to serve it, the one-off cost of entering, and when it pays back.
cards.a: Start with revenue built from the bottom up, your realistic share of the serviceable market at a price you can defend, not a share pulled out of the air. Take off the cost to serve that revenue, then the fixed cost of running in the market, then the one-off cost of getting in at all, the plant, the licences, the hiring, the losses of the early years. What falls out is a cash path over five years, and the number people argue about is the payback period, the year cumulative cash finally turns positive. Then flex the two assumptions you trust least and show whether the answer still holds.

cards.q: Halfway through the case the numbers stop supporting entry, and your interviewer is clearly enjoying the market. How do you say don’t enter without sounding like you gave up?
cards.takeaway: Say no by naming the number that fails and the condition that would change your mind.
cards.a: Recommend against entry exactly the way you would recommend for it, answer first, reasons behind it. Point at the specific thing that fails, that payback runs past eight years, that the client has no route onto the shelf, that the incumbent can undercut you at will, rather than saying the market looks hard. Then give the client somewhere to go: what would have to be true for the answer to flip, and what a better use of the same money looks like. Interviewers set this trap deliberately, because a candidate who cannot say no cannot be trusted when they say yes.

cards.q: Last question. Verrow Fitness can enter a $900 million market where the top two hold 70 percent, needs $120 million up front, and models 5 percent share by year four. Go or no go?
cards.takeaway: Commit to an answer, support it with the economics, and name the one risk that would break it.
cards.a: Do the arithmetic out loud: 5 percent of $900 million is $45 million of revenue, and at a plausible 15 percent margin that is under $7 million of profit a year against $120 million spent, so payback runs past a decade. On those numbers the answer is no, because a 5 percent share in a market where two players hold 70 percent is both small and expensive to defend. Then name the risk in your own answer, that share and margin are assumptions rather than facts, and say what would flip it, entry by acquisition or a niche the incumbents ignore.

name: M&A & Due Diligence Cases
description: How to judge whether a deal is worth doing and whether the value is real.
intro: Companies buy other companies all the time, and somebody has to tell them whether it is a good idea. That somebody is often a consultant, which is why acquisition cases turn up so heavily in interviews. This deck sits on the client’s side of the table: why buy at all, whether the target is really the business it claims to be, what it is genuinely worth to this particular buyer, and whether the two can be put together without breaking either one. You will lean on the structuring, market, profitability and strategy work you have already done, now applied to a decision with a price tag attached. No finance background assumed.

cards.q: Your engagement manager tells you Redmayne Group wants to buy a competitor and asks you to frame the work. How is a consultant’s job on an M&A case different from a banker’s?
cards.takeaway: A banker asks whether the deal can be done, a consultant asks whether it should be.
cards.a: A banker’s work sits around executing a transaction, finding a counterparty, running the process and settling on a price. A consultant is usually hired earlier and asks a blunter question: is this deal a good idea at all. That means testing whether the target’s market is genuinely growing, whether its profits will survive contact with reality, whether the benefits of combining are real, and whether the buyer can absorb the business afterwards. You can be handed a deal that is priced perfectly sensibly and still recommend the client walk away.

cards.q: An interviewer gives you almost nothing: “our client wants to buy this company, should they?” What is the core structure for an acquisition case?
cards.takeaway: Four questions: why buy at all, is the target good, what is it worth to us, can we integrate it.
cards.a: Work through four questions in order: why buy at all, meaning what the client is trying to achieve and whether buying beats building it or partnering; is the target a good business, which is where the market and profitability work you already know earns its keep; what is it worth to this particular buyer, which is standalone value plus whatever the two create together; and can the client actually integrate it. A convincing no on any one of those is a finished answer, not a failure to reach the end.

cards.q: The CEO of Halverson Packaging tells your team he wants to double revenue in three years and acquisitions are the fastest route. Why should that make you uneasy, and what is a real reason to buy a company?
cards.takeaway: A good rationale names a specific advantage the two companies only have together.
cards.a: Speed is a motive, not a rationale. The legitimate reasons all name something the combination creates that neither side has alone: scale that lowers unit costs in a business where scale genuinely matters, a capability or technology the client cannot build fast enough, access to customers or a geography that would take years to win, or consolidating a fragmented market. The weak ones are growth for its own sake, diversification with no shared logic, buying because debt is cheap, and the quiet one nobody says out loud, a chief executive who wants a bigger company to run.

cards.q: What is commercial due diligence, and what is it actually trying to do?
cards.takeaway: Commercial diligence tries to break the target’s growth story before the client pays for it.
cards.a: Due diligence is the investigation a buyer runs before committing, and the commercial piece is the outside-in view: how big the market really is, how fast it is really growing, how defensible the target’s position is, and whether its customers would stay if a rival called tomorrow. The useful framing is disproof. The seller’s plan is a hypothesis, and your job is to find the evidence that would kill it, usually from customer interviews and independent market data rather than from the seller’s own pack. Failing to break the story is the strongest thing you can honestly say.

cards.q: A partner asks who needs to be in the room for diligence on Sennen Coatings before the client commits. What are the main diligence workstreams, and what does each one own?
cards.takeaway: Six workstreams, commercial, financial, operational, legal, tech and people, each test a different risk.
cards.a: Commercial owns the demand story, the market and the customers. Financial checks that reported earnings are real and repeatable rather than flattered by one-off gains, while operational asks whether the plants, the network and the supply chain can deliver the volumes the plan assumes. Legal hunts for what is buried, contracts, disputes and licences that transfer badly, and technology asks whether two sets of systems can ever be joined. People covers who stays. They run in parallel, and the real value tends to come from where their findings contradict each other.

cards.q: Your client’s model shows $90 million of synergies on a deal, $60 million from cost and $30 million from revenue. Why will a good adviser treat those two numbers very differently?
cards.takeaway: Cost synergies are inside your control, revenue synergies need customers to agree.
cards.a: A synergy is value the two businesses produce together that neither produces alone. Cost synergies come from removing duplication, one head office instead of two, one distribution network, better purchasing terms across a bigger order book. The buyer can name those line items and act on them unilaterally. Revenue synergies, mostly cross-selling and wider distribution, require customers to behave in a way nobody has yet asked them about, so experienced teams discount them heavily or strip them out of the price entirely and treat them as upside rather than as something worth paying for.

cards.q: An interviewer says “we’ll save money by combining the two head offices.” How would you turn that sentence into a number you would actually defend?
cards.takeaway: Build a synergy from a driver you can count, then split recurring savings from one-time costs.
cards.a: Go bottom-up from something countable: how many duplicated roles exist, at what fully loaded cost including benefits and property, and how quickly they can realistically come out given notice periods and the risk of gutting the business. Then sanity check the total against the target’s whole overhead line, because a number that lands at forty per cent of it is not credible. Finally separate recurring savings, which repeat every year and therefore carry real value, from one-time items like severance and a building sale, which happen once and cannot be capitalised as if they were permanent.

cards.q: Your team has stacked up $90 million of synergies on Sennen Coatings. The partner asks what has to come back out of that number before it goes in front of the client. What does she mean?
cards.takeaway: Gross synergies minus dis-synergies and cost to achieve is the only number worth paying for.
cards.a: Dis-synergies are value the combination destroys: customers who deliberately keep two suppliers and drop one of you, large buyers who use the merger to demand a single lower price, salespeople who leave and take accounts with them, and the general drag of managers spending a year on integration instead of on customers. Cost to achieve is the cash you spend getting there, severance, systems, rebranding, advisers. Both are real and both are usually missing from the seller’s pack, which is exactly why the net number, not the headline, is what belongs in a price.

cards.q: Diligence on Brackley Tools shows its three largest customers are 55% of revenue, and two of those already buy from your client. Why does that combination worry you more than either fact alone?
cards.takeaway: Shared customers can consolidate spend, so overlap often shrinks combined revenue instead of adding to it.
cards.a: Concentration means a single lost account moves the whole investment case, so you check contract lengths, renewal dates and whether the relationship sits with the company or with one departing salesperson. Overlap makes it worse. A customer buying from both sides today can renegotiate one contract at the better of the two prices, or decide it no longer wants a single supplier for a critical input and drop one of you on purpose. So combined revenue is frequently less than the sum of the parts, which turns a headline revenue synergy into a quiet revenue dis-synergy.

cards.q: An interviewer says culture is a soft factor and pushes you on why a consulting team would burn real diligence hours on it. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: When the value walks out at night, retention is the number that decides the outcome.
cards.a: In people-heavy businesses, software, professional services, anything sales-led, the assets are relationships and know-how, and they can resign. That makes it measurable rather than soft: voluntary attrition before the deal was announced, how many revenue-owning staff are under retention agreements, how differently the two sides pay and promote, and how long each takes to make a decision. If a third of the target’s engineers leave in year one, the roadmap slips, the cross-selling never happens and the revenue synergies you were counting on quietly disappear.

cards.q: Your client asks what actually happens the morning after the deal closes on Trelane Logistics. What does integration planning cover, and where does it usually go wrong?
cards.takeaway: Plan day one, the first hundred days and the long tail separately, and staff the plan before closing.
cards.a: Day one is about nothing breaking: people get paid, orders get filled, customers get a call, and everyone knows who they report to. The first hundred days is where visible decisions get made, the operating model is settled and every synergy gets a named owner and a date. The long tail, systems, sites and brands, runs for years. What goes wrong is rarely the plan itself. It is leaders pulled off the base business, decisions deferred until the vacuum sends the best people to competitors, and a synergy number nobody was ever personally accountable for.

cards.q: Your team concludes Oakhurst Medical is an excellent business and a perfect strategic fit, and the client is ready to pay a 60% premium. Why is that still not a recommendation to buy?
cards.takeaway: A great company bought at too high a price is still a bad investment.
cards.a: What the target is worth to your client is its standalone value plus the net synergies you were able to defend. The premium is what the client pays the seller above the standalone value, and it is paid on day one, in cash, before a single synergy has been delivered. If the premium is larger than the net synergies, the client has handed the seller the value its own people still have to go and create, and has taken all the execution risk in exchange. Good target, good fit, bad deal is a completely coherent recommendation.

cards.q: Halverson Packaging is now in a competitive auction and the CEO tells your partner he refuses to lose this one. What discipline should the team have put in place before the bidding started?
cards.takeaway: Set the maximum price from your own analysis before the auction, and write down what could move it.
cards.a: A walk-away price is the highest number at which the deal still creates value for the client: standalone value plus net synergies, less a margin for everything diligence could not verify. It gets set in writing before the emotion of an auction arrives, along with the specific facts that would justify moving it. That distinction matters because auctions reward optimism, and the winner is often simply the bidder who believed the rosiest forecast. Raising a bid because a new fact emerged is analysis, raising it because you want to win is not.

cards.q: Your client wants to buy one division of Redmayne Group rather than the whole company. Why is a carve-out harder to diligence than buying a standalone business?
cards.takeaway: A carve-out’s reported profit is an allocation, not a business that has ever stood on its own.
cards.a: A carve-out is a division separated from its parent, and it has never had its own finance, HR, IT or leadership team. The profit it reports rests on an internal overhead charge from the parent, which is almost never what those functions cost to build and run alone, so the first job is rebuilding a genuine standalone cost base. Then you ask which contracts, licences and customer relationships actually transfer, and you price the transition services agreement, the temporary deal where the seller keeps running things for a fee while the buyer stands the business up.
